items.title: Tracing Labeled Sulfur and Phosphorus into Macromolecules
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain why the ³⁵S in Culture 1 was incorporated into the protein fraction.

(b) In Culture 2, ³²P was incorporated into two different fractions. Explain why each of these two fractions became labeled.

(c) Cellulose is a carbohydrate. A researcher grows cotton plants with ³²P in their water and then purifies cellulose from the cotton fibers. Predict whether the purified cellulose will contain ³²P, and justify your prediction.
items.stimulus:
Researchers grew two cultures of the same bacterium. Each culture's food source contained one radioactively labeled element. Cells use a radioactive form of an element in the same way as the ordinary form.

Culture 1: sulfur-35 (³⁵S)
Culture 2: phosphorus-32 (³²P)

After several generations, the cells from each culture were broken open and their molecules were separated into four fractions: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. The radioactivity of each fraction was measured in counts per minute (cpm). Readings below 100 cpm are background and show that the label was not incorporated.

Fraction | Culture 1 (³⁵S), cpm | Culture 2 (³²P), cpm
Carbohydrates | 30 | 40
Lipids | 25 | 2100
Proteins | 8800 | 35
Nucleic acids | 20 | 6400
items.answer:
(a) Sulfur is one of the elements used in building proteins. As the bacteria made new proteins, they used the ³⁵S from their food, so the label appeared in the protein fraction (8800 cpm), while the other fractions stayed at background.

(b) Phosphorus is used in building nucleic acids, so the cells built ³²P into their nucleic acids, labeling the nucleic acid fraction (6400 cpm).
Phosphorus is also used in building phospholipids, which are a type of lipid, so ³²P was built into phospholipids and the lipid fraction was labeled (2100 cpm).

(c) The purified cellulose will not contain ³²P. Cellulose is a carbohydrate, and carbohydrates are built from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen; they do not contain phosphorus. This matches the data: the carbohydrate fraction in Culture 2 stayed at background (40 cpm).

criteria.text: Explains that sulfur is an element used in building proteins, so the cells built ³⁵S into the proteins they made.
criteria.evidence: Response states that sulfur is used to build proteins (is part of proteins) and connects this to the label appearing in the protein fraction.
criteria.fix: Memorize the element linked to each macromolecule: sulfur is used in building proteins, so a sulfur label marks protein.

criteria.text: Explains that phosphorus is used in building nucleic acids, so ³²P was incorporated into the nucleic acid fraction (6400 cpm).
criteria.evidence: Response links the labeled nucleic acid fraction to phosphorus being an element used to build nucleic acids.
criteria.fix: Recall phosphorus is used in building nucleic acids; check that fraction first when a phosphorus label is used.

criteria.text: Explains that phosphorus is used in building phospholipids, a type of lipid, so ³²P was incorporated into the lipid fraction (2100 cpm).
criteria.evidence: Response links the labeled lipid fraction to phosphorus being an element used to build phospholipids.
criteria.fix: Recall phosphorus also builds phospholipids, which are lipids; a phosphorus label therefore appears in the lipid fraction too.

criteria.text: Predicts that the purified cellulose will not contain ³²P (it will not be radioactive).
criteria.evidence: Response states the cellulose will not be labeled with ³²P.
criteria.fix: Decide whether the molecule class contains the labeled element; if not, predict no label in the purified molecule.

criteria.text: Justifies the prediction: carbohydrates such as cellulose are built from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen and do not contain phosphorus.
criteria.evidence: Response states that carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (no phosphorus), so phosphorus is not built into cellulose.
criteria.fix: Justify with elemental composition: carbohydrates are built of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen only, so they lack phosphorus.

items.title: Linear and Branched Storage Polysaccharides
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the type of bond that links the glucose monomers together in both polysaccharides.

(b) For one molecule of each polysaccharide, calculate how many times faster glucose is released from Polysaccharide B than from Polysaccharide L at the start of the test.

(c) Animals store glucose in glycogen, a highly branched polysaccharide, in cells such as muscle cells that may need glucose very quickly. Using the results of the test, explain how a branched structure suits this function.

(d) One molecule of L and one molecule of B are each completely broken down into glucose. Predict whether the two molecules release the same or different numbers of glucose monomers, and justify your prediction.
items.stimulus:
Two storage polysaccharides were purified. Every molecule of each polysaccharide is built from exactly 1,200 glucose monomers.

Polysaccharide L: one unbranched (linear) chain.
Polysaccharide B: highly branched; it consists of 100 chains joined to one another.

Cells break these polysaccharides down by removing glucose monomers one at a time, and a monomer can be removed only from the free end of a chain. Each chain, in either polysaccharide, has exactly one free end from which monomers can be removed. In a test, glucose was removed from every free end at the same rate, 10 glucose monomers per second per free end.
items.answer:
(a) The glucose monomers (monosaccharides) are linked by covalent bonds to form the polysaccharide polymers.

(b) Polysaccharide L has one chain and therefore 1 free end: 1 × 10 = 10 glucose monomers per second.
Polysaccharide B has 100 chains and therefore 100 free ends: 100 × 10 = 1,000 glucose monomers per second.
1,000 ÷ 10 = 100, so B releases glucose 100 times faster than L at the start.

(c) Glucose can be removed only from free chain ends. A highly branched polysaccharide such as glycogen contains many chains and so has many free ends, so glucose can be removed from all of these ends at the same time. As the test shows, this releases glucose much faster than from a linear chain, which suits muscle cells that may need glucose quickly.

(d) Both molecules release the same number of glucose monomers, 1,200 each. Both are polymers built from 1,200 glucose monomers, and complete breakdown releases every monomer. Being linear or branched changes how the monomers are connected and how fast they can be removed, not how many monomers the molecule contains.

criteria.text: Identifies the bonds between monomers as covalent bonds.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the glucose monomers are joined by covalent bonds.
criteria.fix: Remember monosaccharide monomers are joined into polysaccharides by covalent bonds, not hydrogen or ionic bonds.

criteria.text: Calculates that B releases glucose 100 times faster: L has 1 free end (10 monomers per second) and B has 100 free ends (1,000 monomers per second); 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the number of free ends (100 versus 1), or the release rates (1,000 versus 10 monomers per second), and obtains a factor of 100.
criteria.fix: Count free ends in each molecule, multiply by the rate per end, then divide the two release rates.

criteria.text: Explains that branching produces many chains and therefore many free ends, so glucose can be removed from many ends at the same time, releasing glucose quickly when the cell needs it.
criteria.evidence: Response connects the many free chain ends of a branched polymer to simultaneous removal of monomers and faster glucose release, using the test result.
criteria.fix: Link structure to function: more branches mean more free ends, and more ends mean more monomers released at once.

criteria.text: Predicts that both molecules release the same number of glucose monomers, 1,200 each.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the numbers are the same (1,200 glucose monomers from each molecule).
criteria.fix: Compare total monomer counts, not rates; complete breakdown of a polymer releases every monomer it contains.

criteria.text: Justifies that both are polymers of 1,200 glucose monomers; branching changes how the monomers are connected (and how fast they can be removed), not how many monomers the polymer contains.
criteria.evidence: Response explains that complete breakdown releases every monomer in each polymer and that branched versus linear arrangement does not change the number of monomers.
criteria.fix: Separate structure from composition: linear or branched describes how monomers are joined, while the monomer count sets total glucose released.

items.title: Double Bonds and the Physical State of Fatty Acids
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the fatty acid in the table that is saturated.

(b) Describe the relationship between the number of carbon–carbon double bonds and the melting point shown in the data.

(c) At a room temperature of 20 °C, fatty acid W is solid and fatty acid Y is liquid. Explain this difference in terms of the structure of the carbon chains of W and Y.

(d) Seals live in very cold ocean water and have a thick layer of fat beneath the skin. Other than serving as a store of energy, explain how this fat layer helps a seal maintain its body temperature in this environment.
items.stimulus:
A student compares four fatty acids. Each has a chain of 18 carbon atoms, and they differ only in the number of carbon–carbon double bonds (C=C) in the chain. A fatty acid is liquid at temperatures above its melting point and solid at temperatures below it.

Fatty acid | Number of C=C double bonds | Approximate melting point (°C)
W | 0 | 69
X | 1 | 13
Y | 2 | −5
Z | 3 | −11
items.answer:
(a) Fatty acid W is saturated. It has no carbon–carbon double bonds, so its chain contains only single bonds between carbon atoms.

(b) As the number of carbon–carbon double bonds increases, the melting point decreases: 69 °C with 0 double bonds, 13 °C with 1, −5 °C with 2, and −11 °C with 3.

(c) Fatty acid W is saturated: its carbon chain has only single bonds. Fatty acid Y is unsaturated: it has two double bonds, and each double bond causes a kink in the carbon chain. The more unsaturated a lipid is, the more liquid it is at room temperature, so Y is liquid at 20 °C (above its melting point of −5 °C) while W is solid (below its melting point of 69 °C).

(d) Fat provides insulation. The thick fat layer beneath the skin slows the loss of heat from the seal's body to the cold water, helping the seal stay warm.

criteria.text: Identifies fatty acid W, the fatty acid with zero carbon–carbon double bonds.
criteria.evidence: Response names W.
criteria.fix: A saturated fatty acid has only single bonds between carbons; pick the one with zero C=C double bonds.

criteria.text: As the number of carbon–carbon double bonds increases, the melting point decreases (from 69 °C with 0 double bonds to −11 °C with 3).
criteria.evidence: Response states that more double bonds is associated with a lower melting point across the four fatty acids.
criteria.fix: Describe the trend across all rows in one sentence: as the first variable increases, the second variable decreases.

criteria.text: Explains that Y's two double bonds put kinks in its carbon chain, making Y unsaturated, and that unsaturated fatty acids are more liquid at room temperature than saturated ones such as W, whose chain has only single bonds.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the double bonds in Y cause kinks in the carbon chain and links being unsaturated (kinked) to being liquid at room temperature, in contrast to saturated W.
criteria.fix: Connect each double bond to a kink in the carbon chain, then state that more unsaturated lipids are more liquid at room temperature.

criteria.text: Explains that the fat layer provides insulation, reducing the loss of heat from the seal's body to the cold water and helping keep the seal warm.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies insulation (reduced heat loss to the surroundings) as the function of the fat layer.
criteria.fix: Recall that besides energy storage, fats can insulate mammals, slowing heat loss to a cold environment.

items.title: Base Composition and Structure of Nucleic Acid Samples
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify which sample (1, 2, or 3) is RNA, and justify your answer using a structural difference between DNA and RNA shown in the data.

(b) A fourth virus is found to have double-stranded DNA in which 18% of the bases are guanine. Calculate the percentage of bases in this DNA that are adenine. Show your work.

(c) Make a claim about whether the DNA in Sample 2 is double-stranded, and justify your claim using the data.

(d) For the DNA segment 5′-ATGCCA-3′: (i) write the sequence of the complementary strand, labeled with its 5′ and 3′ ends, and (ii) identify the end of the given strand (5′ or 3′) to which a new nucleotide would be added if the strand were being extended, and name the chemical group found at that end.
items.stimulus:
A research team isolates nucleic acid from three different viruses. Some viruses carry DNA and others carry RNA as their genetic material, and the genetic material may be single-stranded or double-stranded. The team measures the percentage of each nitrogenous base in each sample. A dash (—) means the base was not detected.

Sample | %A | %T | %G | %C | %U
1 | 30 | 30 | 20 | 20 | —
2 | 25 | 33 | 24 | 18 | —
3 | 22 | — | 30 | 20 | 28

The team also studies a short segment of one DNA strand with the sequence 5′-ATGCCA-3′.
items.answer:
(a) Sample 3 is RNA. It contains uracil (28%) and no thymine. RNA contains the base uracil, while DNA contains thymine, so Samples 1 and 2 (which contain thymine) are DNA.

(b) In double-stranded DNA, C pairs with G and A pairs with T, so %C = %G = 18%. G + C = 36%, so A + T = 100% − 36% = 64%. Since %A = %T, adenine = 64% ÷ 2 = 32%.

(c) Sample 2 is not double-stranded; it is single-stranded DNA. In double-stranded DNA every A is hydrogen-bonded to a T and every C to a G, so %A would equal %T and %G would equal %C. In Sample 2, A is 25% but T is 33%, and G is 24% but C is 18%, so the bases are not paired in complementary strands.

(d) (i) The complementary strand is 5′-TGGCAT-3′ (aligned with the given strand it reads 3′-TACGGT-5′), because A pairs with T, G pairs with C, and the two strands run antiparallel.
(ii) A new nucleotide would be added to the 3′ end of the strand, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the sugar; the new nucleotide forms a covalent bond there.

criteria.text: Identifies Sample 3 as RNA because it contains uracil and no thymine.
criteria.evidence: Names Sample 3 and justifies with the presence of uracil (U) in place of thymine (T), since RNA contains uracil while DNA contains thymine.
criteria.fix: Remember RNA contains uracil instead of thymine; look for the sample with U present and T absent.

criteria.text: Calculates adenine = 32% using complementary base pairing.
criteria.fix: In double-stranded DNA set C equal to G and A equal to T, subtract G + C from 100, then halve.

criteria.text: Claims Sample 2 is not double-stranded (single-stranded) because A does not equal T and G does not equal C.
criteria.evidence: States Sample 2 is single-stranded (not double-stranded) and cites that %A (25) ≠ %T (33) and/or %G (24) ≠ %C (18), whereas complementary pairing in a double strand would make these equal.
criteria.fix: Compare %A with %T and %G with %C; double-stranded DNA pairs A–T and C–G, so those percentages must match.

criteria.text: Writes the antiparallel complementary strand 5′-TGGCAT-3′.
criteria.evidence: Gives 5′-TGGCAT-3′, or equivalently 3′-TACGGT-5′ aligned under the given strand, with correct base pairing (A–T, C–G) and opposite orientation.
criteria.fix: Pair each base (A with T, G with C), then remember strands are antiparallel; read the new strand 5′ to 3′.

criteria.text: Identifies the 3′ end, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group, as the end where new nucleotides are added.
criteria.evidence: States nucleotides are added to the 3′ end and names the hydroxyl group of the sugar at that end.
criteria.fix: Recall nucleic acid synthesis adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end, defined by the sugar's 3′ hydroxyl group.

items.title: Surface Area-to-Volume Ratio in Cells and in Mammals
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the surface area-to-volume ratio of cell A. Include units.

(b) Calculate how many times greater the surface area-to-volume ratio of cell A is than that of cell B.

(c) Using your calculated values, explain why cell B is less efficient than cell A at exchanging materials with its environment.

(d) Predict which animal, the shrew or the moose, has the higher metabolic rate per unit body mass, and justify your prediction using surface area-to-volume ratio.
items.stimulus:
Two spherical cells are compared.

Cell | Shape | Radius (μm)
A | sphere | 2
B | sphere | 6

For a sphere, surface area SA = 4πr² and volume V = (4/3)πr³.

In a separate comparison, researchers study two mammals that both keep a constant body temperature: a shrew with a body mass of about 5 g and a moose with a body mass of about 400 kg.
items.answer:
(a) For cell A, r = 2 μm.
SA = 4π(2)² = 16π μm².
V = (4/3)π(2)³ = (32/3)π μm³.
SA/V = 16π ÷ (32π/3) = 48/32 = 1.5 μm⁻¹.

(b) For cell B, r = 6 μm: SA = 4π(6)² = 144π μm² and V = (4/3)π(6)³ = 288π μm³, so SA/V = 0.5 μm⁻¹.
1.5 μm⁻¹ ÷ 0.5 μm⁻¹ = 3, so cell A's surface area-to-volume ratio is 3 times that of cell B.

(c) Cell B's SA:V (0.5 μm⁻¹) is only one-third of cell A's (1.5 μm⁻¹). Materials are exchanged across the plasma membrane, so cell B has much less membrane surface for each unit of volume that needs nutrients and produces wastes. Exchange across the membrane therefore cannot keep up with the needs of B's volume as well as it can in A, so B is less efficient at exchanging materials.

(d) The shrew has the higher metabolic rate per unit body mass. Because it is much smaller, the shrew has a much higher surface area-to-volume ratio, so it exchanges heat with its environment proportionally faster and loses heat quickly for its mass. To keep its body temperature constant, it must produce more heat through metabolism per unit of body mass than the moose does.

criteria.text: Calculates SA:V of cell A = 1.5 μm⁻¹, by any valid method, for example SA = 16π μm² and V = (32/3)π μm³, so SA/V = 16π ÷ (32π/3) = 1.5 μm⁻¹, or SA/V = 3/r = 3/2.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a correct calculation for a sphere of radius 2 μm and reports 1.5 μm⁻¹ (1.5 per μm).
criteria.fix: Substitute r into both sphere formulas, or simplify SA/V to 3/r first, and report the ratio with units of μm⁻¹.

criteria.text: Calculates that cell A's SA:V is 3 times that of cell B, by any valid method, for example 1.5 μm⁻¹ ÷ 0.5 μm⁻¹ = 3 (cell B: SA/V = 3/6 = 0.5 μm⁻¹).
criteria.evidence: Response shows cell B's ratio (0.5 μm⁻¹) or the radius ratio reasoning and obtains a factor of 3.
criteria.fix: Compute the second cell's ratio the same way, then divide the larger ratio by the smaller one.

criteria.text: Explains, citing the calculated values, that cell B has a lower SA:V (0.5 μm⁻¹ versus 1.5 μm⁻¹, one-third as much), so it has less plasma membrane surface per unit of volume through which nutrients can enter and wastes can leave, relative to the needs of its larger volume.
criteria.evidence: Response cites B's lower calculated SA:V and explains that less membrane area is available per unit volume for taking in nutrients or removing wastes.
criteria.fix: Quote both calculated ratios, then link a lower ratio to less membrane surface available to serve each unit of cell volume.

criteria.text: Predicts that the shrew has the higher metabolic rate per unit body mass.
criteria.evidence: Response names the shrew.
criteria.fix: Smaller organisms typically have higher metabolic rates per unit body mass; choose the smaller animal.

criteria.text: Justifies that the smaller shrew has a higher SA:V, so it exchanges (loses) heat with its environment proportionally faster, and must produce more heat by metabolism per unit body mass to keep its body temperature constant.
criteria.evidence: Response links the shrew's higher SA:V to proportionally greater heat loss and to a greater need for metabolic heat production per unit mass.
criteria.fix: Chain the reasoning: smaller size, higher SA:V, faster heat loss per unit mass, so more metabolism is needed to stay warm.

items.title: Permeability of Protein-Free Phospholipid Vesicles
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate how many times faster O₂ crosses the protein-free bilayer than H₂O does. Then explain, based on the structure of the membrane interior, why O₂ crosses much faster than H₂O.

(b) Explain why the rate at which K⁺ crosses the protein-free bilayer is below detection, even though K⁺ is smaller than glucose.

(c) The student makes a second set of vesicles that are identical except that K⁺ channel proteins are embedded in the bilayer. Predict how the rate of K⁺ crossing will compare with the rate in the protein-free vesicles, and justify your prediction.

(d) Plant cells with intact cell walls and plant cells whose cell walls have been removed by enzymes are both placed in distilled water, which causes water to enter the cells. Predict which group of cells is more likely to burst, and describe the role of the cell wall that accounts for the difference.
items.stimulus:
A student prepares artificial vesicles whose membranes are pure phospholipid bilayers with no embedded proteins. The student measures how quickly each of four substances crosses the vesicle membrane when it is added at the same concentration to the solution outside the vesicles. Rates are reported in the same arbitrary units for every substance.

Substance | Description | Relative rate of crossing the protein-free bilayer
O₂ | small, nonpolar | 5000
H₂O | small, polar, uncharged | 50
Glucose | large, polar | 0.05
K⁺ | ion (charged) | below detection (less than 0.0001)
items.answer:
(a) O₂ rate ÷ H₂O rate = 5000 ÷ 50 = 100, so O₂ crosses 100 times faster than H₂O. The interior of the bilayer is made of the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails of phospholipids, so it is hydrophobic. Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ pass freely through this nonpolar region. Water is small and uncharged but polar, so the hydrophobic interior restricts it and only small amounts pass through.

(b) K⁺ is an ion with a charge. The nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the middle of the bilayer prevent ions from crossing, so even though K⁺ is small, its charge keeps it from moving through the hydrophobic interior. Charge matters more than size here.

(c) The rate of K⁺ crossing will increase and become detectable in the vesicles with K⁺ channel proteins. The embedded channel proteins provide a hydrophilic passage through the membrane, so the charged ions can cross without moving through the hydrophobic tails.

(d) The cells whose walls were removed are more likely to burst. As water enters, the cell swells. The cell wall is a rigid structural boundary around the plasma membrane that resists this expansion, which protects walled cells from osmotic lysis. Cells without walls have no such protection.

criteria.text: Correct calculation: O₂ crosses 100 times faster than H₂O (5000 ÷ 50 = 100).
criteria.evidence: Shows the division of the O₂ rate by the H₂O rate and reports 100 (100 times faster).
criteria.fix: Divide the larger rate by the smaller rate from the table, show the setup, and report the result as 'times faster'.

criteria.text: Explanation: the bilayer interior is hydrophobic (nonpolar hydrocarbon tails), so small nonpolar O₂ passes freely, while polar H₂O passes only in small amounts.
criteria.evidence: Links the hydrophobic/nonpolar interior of the bilayer to free passage of nonpolar O₂ and to restricted passage of polar water.
criteria.fix: State that the membrane interior is made of nonpolar hydrocarbon tails, then connect each molecule's polarity to how easily it passes through.

criteria.text: K⁺ is charged (an ion), and the nonpolar hydrocarbon tails in the bilayer interior prevent the movement of ions, so size alone does not allow passage.
criteria.evidence: Identifies the charge of K⁺ as the key property and states that the hydrophobic/nonpolar interior blocks charged particles regardless of small size.
criteria.fix: Identify the property (charge) that matters more than size, and say how the nonpolar interior of the bilayer blocks ions.
variants: ions are blocked by the hydrophobic interior
charged particles cannot pass through nonpolar tails

criteria.text: Prediction that the K⁺ rate increases (becomes detectable), justified because channel proteins provide a hydrophilic pathway through the membrane that lets ions bypass the hydrophobic interior.
criteria.evidence: States that K⁺ crossing increases AND justifies it by explaining that embedded channel proteins give ions a passage through the membrane that avoids the nonpolar tails.
criteria.fix: Pair the prediction with a reason: explain what an embedded channel protein provides that the bare bilayer lacks for charged ions.

criteria.text: Prediction that the cells without cell walls are more likely to burst, because the cell wall is a rigid structural boundary that resists expansion and protects the cell from osmotic lysis.
criteria.evidence: Identifies the wall-less cells as the group that bursts AND describes the cell wall as a structural boundary that protects against osmotic lysis (bursting) as water enters.
criteria.fix: Name the group that bursts and state that the cell wall provides structural support that prevents osmotic lysis when water enters.

items.title: Passive, Active, and Bulk Transport in an Amoeba
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using Table 1, explain why solute K must be moved into the cell by active transport.

(b) Using Table 2, describe the evidence that solute G enters the cell by passive transport.

(c) Describe how the plasma membrane brings the beads into the cell.

(d) Inside the amoeba, undigested material is enclosed in vesicles that normally fuse with the plasma membrane to release the material outside the cell. Predict the effect of the energy-blocking chemical on the release of this material, and justify your prediction.
items.stimulus:
A freshwater amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote. Researchers measured the concentrations of two small solutes, G and K, inside the amoeba and in the surrounding water. Both solutes show net movement into the cell.

Table 1
Solute | Concentration inside cell (mM) | Concentration in surrounding water (mM) | Direction of net movement
G | 0.8 | 6.0 | into cell
K | 25.0 | 1.5 | into cell

The researchers also added tiny plastic beads to the water. Each bead is far too large to pass through the plasma membrane. After 20 minutes, beads were found inside small membrane-bound vesicles in the amoeba's cytoplasm. The researchers then repeated the measurements on amoebas treated with a chemical that blocks the cell's supply of metabolic energy.

Table 2
Measurement | Untreated amoebas | Energy-blocked amoebas
Uptake rate of G (relative units) | 100 | 98
Uptake rate of K (relative units) | 100 | 3
Beads taken in per cell in 20 minutes | 40 | 0
items.answer:
(a) Solute K is 1.5 mM in the surrounding water but 25.0 mM inside the cell, yet its net movement is into the cell. K is therefore moving from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration, against its concentration gradient. Passive transport only produces net movement from high to low concentration, so moving K inward requires the direct input of energy: active transport.

(b) When the cell's supply of metabolic energy is blocked, the uptake rate of G stays almost the same (98 compared with 100), while the uptake of K drops to 3. G's movement into the cell therefore does not depend on a direct input of metabolic energy. This fits passive transport: G moves from high concentration outside (6.0 mM) to low concentration inside (0.8 mM).

(c) The beads enter by endocytosis. The plasma membrane folds inward around the beads, and the folded region closes and pinches off as a new small vesicle that contains the beads inside the cell.

(d) Release of the undigested material will stop (or nearly stop) in the energy-blocked amoebas. The material is released by exocytosis, in which a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, and exocytosis requires energy. The bead data show the same dependence for vesicle transport in the other direction: endocytosis fell from 40 beads to 0 when energy was blocked.

criteria.text: Explains that K moves from a lower concentration outside (1.5 mM) to a higher concentration inside (25.0 mM), against its concentration gradient, and moving a substance from low to high concentration requires the direct input of energy (active transport).
criteria.evidence: Response cites K's concentrations (or states K moves from low to high concentration) and states that this movement requires an input of energy.
criteria.fix: Compare outside and inside concentrations; net movement from low to high concentration cannot be passive and requires energy input.

criteria.text: Describes that G's uptake rate is almost unchanged when the energy supply is blocked (100 versus 98), showing that G's net movement into the cell, from 6.0 mM outside to 0.8 mM inside, does not require a direct input of metabolic energy.
criteria.evidence: Response cites G's nearly unchanged uptake rate under the energy block (100 versus 98) as evidence that no direct energy input is needed.
criteria.fix: Compare each solute's rate with and without energy; a rate that barely changes shows the movement does not depend on metabolic energy.

criteria.text: Describes endocytosis: the plasma membrane folds inward around the beads and pinches off, forming a new small vesicle that encloses them inside the cell.
criteria.evidence: Response describes the membrane folding in (or surrounding the beads) and forming a vesicle containing the beads; naming endocytosis or phagocytosis without describing the membrane movement is not enough.
criteria.fix: Describe the membrane's movement step by step: it folds in around the material, then closes off as a vesicle inside the cell.

criteria.text: Predicts that release of the undigested material will stop or greatly decrease in energy-blocked amoebas.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the energy-blocked amoebas will release little or none of the material.
criteria.fix: State the direction of the change clearly: release stops, decreases, or stays the same.

criteria.text: Justifies that release by vesicle fusion is exocytosis, which requires energy (consistent with bead uptake by endocytosis falling from 40 to 0 when energy was blocked).
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the release as exocytosis (vesicle fusing with the membrane) and states that this process requires energy, optionally citing the bead data.
criteria.fix: Remember both endocytosis and exocytosis move large amounts of material in vesicles and both require an input of energy.

items.title: Internal Membranes Separate and Support Cellular Reactions
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the percent decrease in the amount of Q present at 30 minutes in Extract 2 compared with Extract 1.

(b) Using the data in Table 1, explain how the membrane of compartment K allows Q to accumulate in Extract 1, and why much less Q accumulated in Extract 2.

(c) Describe the relationship between internal membrane surface area and the rate of reaction R shown in Table 2.

(d) Explain how a larger area of internal membranes leads to the higher rate of reaction R in cell type N.
items.stimulus:
Liver cells make a molecule, Q, in the cytosol. The reactions that break Q down occur only inside a membrane-bound organelle, compartment K. Researchers prepared two extracts from the same liver tissue and supplied each with the raw materials needed to make Q.

Extract 1: cells were broken open gently, so the organelles, including compartment K, stayed intact.
Extract 2: cells were broken open harshly, so organelle membranes ruptured and the contents of compartment K mixed with the cytosol.

Table 1: Amount of Q present (μmol per gram of tissue)
Time (min) | Extract 1 | Extract 2
0 | 0 | 0
10 | 4.0 | 0.6
20 | 8.1 | 1.0
30 | 12.0 | 1.5

In a second study, the researchers compared two cell types in which reaction R is carried out by proteins embedded in internal membranes.

Table 2
Cell type | Internal membrane surface area per cell (μm²) | Rate of reaction R (relative units)
M | 1,500 | 30
N | 4,500 | 90
items.answer:
(a) Percent decrease = (12.0 − 1.5) ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 10.5 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 87.5%.

(b) In Extract 1, compartment K is intact, so its membrane keeps the reactions that break down Q inside the compartment, separate from the cytosol where Q is made. Because the opposing reactions are kept apart, they do not compete, and Q builds up steadily, reaching 12.0 μmol per gram at 30 minutes. In Extract 2, the ruptured membrane lets the contents of compartment K mix with the cytosol, so Q is broken down in the same space where it is being made. Much of the Q is broken down as soon as it forms, so only 1.5 μmol per gram accumulates.

(c) The rate of reaction R increases as internal membrane surface area increases. Cell type N has 3 times the internal membrane surface area of M (4,500 versus 1,500 μm²) and 3 times the rate (90 versus 30), so the rate rises in proportion to the membrane area.

(d) Reaction R is carried out by proteins embedded in internal membranes, so the reaction can occur only on membrane surfaces. A larger area of internal membrane increases the surface area where the reaction can occur and holds more of the embedded proteins, so more reaction R takes place at the same time and the rate is higher.

criteria.text: Calculates a percent decrease of 87.5%: (12.0 − 1.5) ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 87.5%.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the difference (10.5 μmol per gram) divided by the Extract 1 value (12.0) and expresses the result as 87.5%, or uses an equivalent valid method such as (1 − 1.5/12.0) × 100.
criteria.fix: For percent decrease, divide the drop by the original (reference) value, then multiply by 100.

criteria.text: Explains that the membrane of compartment K keeps the reactions that break down Q separate from the cytosol where Q is made, minimizing competing reactions; when the membrane ruptures (Extract 2), breakdown occurs in the same space as synthesis, so Q is broken down as it is made and only 1.5 μmol per gram accumulates versus 12.0.
criteria.evidence: Response links the intact membrane to separation of the competing synthesis and breakdown reactions, and links rupture to Q being broken down in the mixed extract, citing the lower amount of Q.
criteria.fix: Name the two opposing processes, state where each happens, and explain that the membrane keeps them apart so they cannot compete.

criteria.text: Describes that the rate of reaction R increases as internal membrane surface area increases, in proportion: tripling the area (1,500 to 4,500 μm²) triples the rate (30 to 90).
criteria.evidence: Response states that greater internal membrane surface area is associated with a higher rate of reaction R, and notes the threefold change in both.
criteria.fix: Describe the direction of the trend and its size: compare how many times each variable changed between the two cell types.

criteria.text: Explains that internal membranes increase the surface area where membrane-associated reactions can occur, providing room for more of the embedded proteins that carry out reaction R, so more reaction R can happen at the same time.
criteria.evidence: Response states that more internal membrane provides more surface area on which reaction R can take place (more embedded proteins), increasing the rate.
criteria.fix: Connect membrane area to reaction sites: more membrane surface holds more embedded proteins, so more reactions run at once.

items.title: Charge Compatibility at an Enzyme's Active Site
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate how many times faster product forms in tube 1 than in tube 3.

(b) Explain how the normal enzyme causes the rate of product formation in tube 1 to be much higher than in tube 3.

(c) Explain why the mutant enzyme in tube 2 has much lower activity than the normal enzyme.

(d) The normal enzyme acts slowly on substrate S′ even though S′ has the same shape as S. Explain why.
items.stimulus:
An enzyme catalyzes the breakdown of substrate S. The part of S that binds to the enzyme carries a negative charge, and the enzyme's active site contains amino acids with positively charged R groups. Researchers measured the initial rate of product formation in four tubes kept at the same temperature and pH. Every tube starts with the same concentration of substrate, and every tube that contains enzyme has the same enzyme concentration.

Tube | Contents | Initial rate of product formation (μmol/min)
1 | Substrate S + normal enzyme | 48
2 | Substrate S + mutant enzyme | 2
3 | Substrate S, no enzyme | 0.5
4 | Substrate S′ + normal enzyme | 4

In the mutant enzyme, one positively charged R group in the active site is replaced by a negatively charged R group; the overall shape of the active site is unchanged. Substrate S′ has the same shape as substrate S but carries no charge.
items.answer:
(a) 48 μmol/min ÷ 0.5 μmol/min = 96. Product forms 96 times faster in tube 1 than in tube 3.

(b) The enzyme is a biological catalyst. It lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so far more substrate molecules can react per minute than in tube 3, where the reaction occurs without the enzyme.

(c) Substrate S binds through a negatively charged region, which is attracted to the positively charged R groups in the normal active site. In the mutant, a negatively charged R group replaces a positive one, so the active site's charge is no longer compatible with S; the like charges repel. S therefore binds poorly, few enzyme–substrate complexes form, and the rate drops to 2 μmol/min.

(d) For an enzyme-mediated reaction to occur, both the shape and the charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site. S′ has the right shape but no charge, so it is not attracted to the positively charged R groups in the active site. S′ binds poorly, few enzyme–substrate complexes form, and the rate is only 4 μmol/min.

criteria.text: Calculates 48 ÷ 0.5 = 96, so product forms 96 times faster in tube 1.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the tube 1 rate by the tube 3 rate and obtains 96.
criteria.fix: To find how many times faster, divide the larger rate by the smaller rate; do not subtract.

criteria.text: Explains that the enzyme is a biological catalyst that lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so the reaction proceeds much faster than without the enzyme.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the enzyme lowers the activation energy (energy needed to start the reaction), which increases the reaction rate.
criteria.fix: When explaining an enzyme's effect on rate, name activation energy and state that the enzyme lowers it.

criteria.text: Explains that the substituted negatively charged R group makes the charge of the active site incompatible with the negatively charged substrate S (like charges repel), so S binds poorly and few enzyme–substrate complexes form.
criteria.evidence: Response links the new negative charge in the active site to loss of charge compatibility with negative S and to reduced substrate binding or reduced enzyme–substrate complex formation.
criteria.fix: Compare the charges of active site and substrate; like charges repel, which reduces binding and enzyme–substrate complex formation.

criteria.text: Explains that for the reaction to occur, both the shape and the charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site; S′ fits the shape but lacks the negative charge attracted by the positive R groups, so it binds poorly and forms few enzyme–substrate complexes.
criteria.evidence: Response states that charge, not only shape, must match the active site and that uncharged S′ is not attracted to the positively charged R groups, so binding is reduced.
criteria.fix: Remember the enzyme–substrate model requires compatible shape and charge; check both properties for any substrate.

items.title: A Sequential Pathway and Energy Coupling in a Bacterium
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data, identify the step that is blocked in the mutant strain.

(b) The enzyme for step 3 works normally in the mutant cells. Explain why the mutant cells contain no D.

(c) Explain how coupling step 3 to reaction E allows step 3 to occur in the cell.

(d) Calculate the amount of energy per mole released by reaction E that is not used to drive step 3, and describe what happens to this energy.
items.stimulus:
A bacterium makes molecule D from molecule A through a three-step pathway. Each step is catalyzed by a different enzyme.

Step 1: A → B
Step 2: B → C
Step 3: C → D

Researchers measured the concentrations of the pathway molecules in normal cells and in a mutant strain that lacks a working enzyme for one of the three steps.

Molecule | Normal cells (mM) | Mutant cells (mM)
A | 1.0 | 1.1
B | 0.4 | 6.5
C | 0.3 | 0.0
D | 2.0 | 0.0

Step 3 requires an input of energy. In the cell, step 3 is coupled to reaction E, which releases energy. Reaction E releases 30 kJ of energy per mole, and step 3 requires 21 kJ of energy per mole.
items.answer:
(a) Step 2 (B → C) is blocked. In the mutant, B builds up to 6.5 mM (compared with 0.4 mM in normal cells), while C is absent (0.0 mM). B is the reactant of step 2 and C is its product, so the block is at step 2.

(b) The pathway is sequential: the product of one step is the reactant for the next. C, the product of step 2, is the reactant for step 3. Because step 2 is blocked, no C is made, so even though the step 3 enzyme works, step 3 has no reactant and no D is produced.

(c) Step 3 requires an input of energy that it cannot supply itself. When step 3 is coupled to reaction E, the energy released by reaction E is used to provide the energy step 3 requires. Reaction E releases 30 kJ per mole, more than the 21 kJ per mole step 3 needs, so the coupled processes can proceed together.

(d) 30 kJ − 21 kJ = 9 kJ per mole is not used to drive step 3. This energy is released to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy). It is not destroyed, consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.

criteria.text: Identifies step 2 (B → C) as the blocked step.
criteria.evidence: Response names step 2 (B → C).
criteria.fix: Find where a pathway molecule piles up and the next molecule is missing; the blocked step lies between them.

criteria.text: Explains that in a sequential pathway the product of one step is the reactant for the next step: C, the product of step 2, is the reactant for step 3, so with no C made, step 3 cannot produce D.
criteria.evidence: Response states that step 3 needs C as its reactant and that C is not made because step 2 is blocked, so no D is formed.
criteria.fix: Trace the pathway forward: each step's product feeds the next step, so a missing reactant stops every later step.

criteria.text: Explains that the energy released by reaction E is used to supply the energy that step 3 requires; because E releases more energy (30 kJ per mole) than step 3 needs (21 kJ per mole), the coupled processes can proceed together.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the energy-releasing reaction E provides the energy input required by the energy-requiring step 3, and notes that E releases at least as much energy as step 3 needs.
criteria.fix: Describe coupling as an energy-releasing process paying for an energy-requiring one, and check that energy released exceeds energy required.

criteria.text: Calculates 30 kJ − 21 kJ = 9 kJ per mole not used by step 3.
criteria.evidence: Response subtracts the energy required by step 3 from the energy released by E and obtains 9 kJ per mole.
criteria.fix: Subtract energy required from energy released; the difference is the energy left over from the coupled reactions.

criteria.text: Describes that the extra energy is released to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy); it is not destroyed, consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the unused energy is lost to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy), not destroyed or stored.
criteria.fix: Remember energy transfers are never complete: energy not captured is released as heat, and energy is never destroyed.

items.title: Intervals of Continuity for Log, Rational and Piecewise Functions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Determine all intervals on which h is continuous. Justify your answer using properties of the functions that make up h.

(b) Is h continuous on the closed interval [2, 5]? Is h continuous on the closed interval [0, 2]? Explain each answer.

(c) Find the value of k for which f is continuous for all real numbers x. Show the work that leads to your answer.
items.stimulus:
Let h be the function defined by h(x) = ln(x + 2)/(x² − 1).

Let f be the function defined, for a constant k, by
f(x) = k·cos(πx) + 3 for x ≤ 1
f(x) = x² + k for x > 1.
items.answer:
(a) The numerator ln(x + 2) is defined only when x + 2 > 0, so x > −2. The denominator x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) equals 0 at x = −1 and x = 1, so h is undefined there. Logarithmic functions and polynomials are continuous on their domains, and a quotient of continuous functions is continuous wherever the denominator is nonzero. Therefore h is continuous at every point of its domain, which is the intervals (−2, −1), (−1, 1) and (1, ∞).

(b) Yes, h is continuous on [2, 5]. Every x with 2 ≤ x ≤ 5 lies in (1, ∞), where h is continuous at each point, so h is continuous at each point of [2, 5].
No, h is not continuous on [0, 2]. The value x = 1 is in [0, 2], and h(1) is undefined because the denominator is 0, so h is not continuous at x = 1 and therefore not continuous on [0, 2].

(c) For x < 1, f(x) = k·cos(πx) + 3 is continuous (cosine is continuous everywhere), and for x > 1, f(x) = x² + k is a polynomial, which is continuous everywhere. So f can fail to be continuous only at x = 1.
f(1) = k·cos(π) + 3 = 3 − k, and lim x→1⁻ f(x) = 3 − k.
lim x→1⁺ f(x) = 1² + k = 1 + k.
For continuity at x = 1: 3 − k = 1 + k, so 2k = 2 and k = 1. Check: both one-sided limits and f(1) equal 2.

criteria.text: Excludes x ≤ −2 because ln(x + 2) is defined only when x + 2 > 0, that is, x > −2.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the logarithm requires x + 2 > 0, so values with x ≤ −2 are not in the domain of h.
criteria.fix: Before listing intervals, write the domain condition for every logarithm: its argument must be strictly positive.

criteria.text: Excludes x = −1 and x = 1 because they make the denominator x² − 1 equal to 0.
criteria.evidence: Response solves x² − 1 = 0 (or factors (x − 1)(x + 1)) and states that h is undefined at x = −1 and x = 1.
criteria.fix: Set the denominator equal to zero, solve, and remove each solution from the domain, even when the numerator is also zero.

criteria.text: States h is continuous on (−2, −1), (−1, 1) and (1, ∞), justified because ln and polynomials are continuous on their domains and a quotient is continuous where the denominator is nonzero.
criteria.evidence: Response lists exactly the three open intervals (−2, −1), (−1, 1), (1, ∞) and cites continuity of logarithmic and polynomial (or rational) functions on their domains.
criteria.fix: After finding the domain, name the function types involved and state they are continuous on their domains, so h is continuous on its domain.

criteria.text: Yes, h is continuous on [2, 5] because [2, 5] lies inside (1, ∞), where h is continuous at every point.
criteria.evidence: Response answers yes and explains that every point of [2, 5] belongs to an interval on which h is continuous (or is in the domain of h).
criteria.fix: Check whether the whole interval lies inside one interval of continuity; if so, h is continuous at each of its points.

criteria.text: No, h is not continuous on [0, 2] because x = 1 is in [0, 2] and h(1) is undefined.
criteria.evidence: Response answers no and identifies x = 1 as a point of [0, 2] where h is not defined, so h is not continuous at every point of the interval.
criteria.fix: Test each excluded value against the interval; one point where the function is undefined breaks continuity on the whole interval.

criteria.text: Explains that each piece of f is continuous on its own interval (a trigonometric plus constant function and a polynomial), so only x = 1 needs to be checked.
criteria.evidence: Response states that k·cos(πx) + 3 and x² + k are continuous everywhere, so continuity of f can fail only at x = 1.
criteria.fix: Begin piecewise continuity problems by stating each piece is continuous on its interval because of its function type, then check the boundary.

criteria.text: Sets up the continuity condition at x = 1: lim x→1⁻ f(x) = 3 − k equals lim x→1⁺ f(x) = 1 + k, and f(1) = 3 − k.
criteria.evidence: Response computes the left-hand limit (or f(1)) as k·cos(π) + 3 = 3 − k and the right-hand limit as 1 + k and sets them equal.
criteria.fix: Evaluate both one-sided limits at the boundary using cos(π) = −1, then require they agree with f(1).

criteria.text: Finds k = 1.
criteria.evidence: Response solves 3 − k = 1 + k correctly to obtain k = 1.
criteria.fix: Solve the equation from equal one-sided limits carefully and substitute back to confirm both sides give the same value, here 2.

items.title: Velocity at an Instant from Average Velocities
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) A student says: "To find the particle's velocity at exactly t = 1, I will use the average velocity formula [s(b) − s(a)] / (b − a) on the interval from t = 1 to t = 1." Explain why this does not work.

(b) Find the average velocity of the particle on each of these intervals: [0.9, 1], [0.99, 1], [0.999, 1], [1, 1.1], [1, 1.01] and [1, 1.001]. Show the calculation for the interval [1, 1.01]. Give each answer to four decimal places.

(c) Use your results from part (b) to estimate the velocity of the particle at the instant t = 1. Explain how the values support your estimate.

(d) The average velocity of the particle over the interval [1, 4] is 17 meters per second. Explain what your answer to part (c) tells you about the particle's motion at the instant t = 1 that the average velocity over [1, 4] does not.
items.stimulus: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is s(t) = t³ − 4t + 2, where s(t) is measured in meters and t is measured in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5.
items.answer:
(a) On the interval from t = 1 to t = 1, b − a = 0, so the formula divides by zero and the average velocity is undefined. An average velocity needs two different times.

(b) s(1) = −1 and s(1.01) = −1.009699, so the average velocity on [1, 1.01] is (−1.009699 − (−1)) / 0.01 = −0.009699 / 0.01 = −0.9699 m/s.
Average velocities: [0.9, 1]: −1.2900 m/s; [0.99, 1]: −1.0299 m/s; [0.999, 1]: −1.0030 m/s; [1, 1.1]: −0.6900 m/s; [1, 1.01]: −0.9699 m/s; [1, 1.001]: −0.9970 m/s.

(c) The velocity at t = 1 is about −1 m/s. As the intervals shrink toward t = 1, the averages from the left (−1.29, −1.0299, −1.0030) and from the right (−0.69, −0.9699, −0.9970) close in on −1 from both sides.

(d) At t = 1 the particle is moving backward, in the negative direction, at about 1 meter per second. The average velocity of 17 m/s over [1, 4] only describes the net change in position from t = 1 to t = 4; it suggests steady forward motion and hides that the particle is moving backward at t = 1.

criteria.text: Explains that the interval has length 0, so b − a = 0 and the formula divides by zero, which is undefined.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the change in time is 0 (b − a = 0) and that dividing by 0 makes the average velocity undefined.
criteria.fix: Check the denominator: an average rate needs two different times, so b − a cannot be 0.

criteria.text: Shows a valid calculation of the average velocity on [1, 1.01], such as [s(1.01) − s(1)] / (1.01 − 1) = (−1.009699 − (−1)) / 0.01.
criteria.evidence: Response shows correct work for [1, 1.01] by any valid method: the difference quotient with s(1.01) = −1.009699 and s(1) = −1 over 0.01, or an equivalent simplified quotient such as b² + ab + a² − 4 at a = 1, b = 1.01.
criteria.fix: Write s(b) − s(a) over b − a with both position values before dividing.

criteria.text: Gives all six average velocities correctly: −1.2900, −1.0299, −1.0030, −0.6900, −0.9699 and −0.9970 m/s.
criteria.evidence: Response lists the six values for the intervals in the order given, each correct to four decimal places.
criteria.fix: Recompute s at each endpoint and keep s(1) = −1 the same in every quotient.

criteria.text: Estimates the velocity at t = 1 as −1 m/s.
criteria.evidence: Response states a single estimate of −1 meter per second for the velocity at t = 1, or the value toward which the response's own part (b) averages correctly point.
criteria.fix: State one value with units, read from where the averages are heading.

criteria.text: Justifies that as the intervals shrink toward t = 1 from both sides, the average velocities approach −1.
criteria.evidence: Response notes that the left-interval values (−1.29, −1.0299, −1.0030) and the right-interval values (−0.69, −0.9699, −0.9970) both close in on −1 as the intervals get smaller.
criteria.fix: Describe what the averages do as the intervals shrink, from the left and from the right.

criteria.text: States that at t = 1 the particle is moving in the negative direction (backward) at about 1 meter per second.
criteria.evidence: Response interprets the negative velocity at t = 1 as motion in the negative direction with speed about 1 meter per second, or interprets the sign and size of the response's own estimate in part (c) correctly.
criteria.fix: Interpret the sign of a velocity as a direction of motion.

criteria.text: Contrasts this with the 17 m/s average, which describes the overall change in position over the 3 seconds and hides the backward motion at t = 1.
criteria.evidence: Response explains that the average over [1, 4] reflects only the net change in position over the whole interval, so it does not show the direction or speed at the instant t = 1.
criteria.fix: Contrast one instant with a whole interval, in the context of the particle.

items.title: Interpreting and Writing Limits with Correct Notation
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use the definition of a limit to determine lim x→3 f(x). Explain your reasoning, referring to the values of f(x) for x close to 3.

(b) A student claims that lim x→3 f(x) = 10 because f(3) = 10. Explain why the student's reasoning is incorrect.

(c) The temperature T(t) can be made arbitrarily close to 68 degrees Fahrenheit by taking t sufficiently close to 5 minutes, but not equal to 5. Write this statement using correct limit notation.

(d) Interpret the statement lim x→−2 h(x) = −4 in words. Then state whether h(−2) must equal −4, and explain.
items.stimulus:
A function f is defined for all real numbers. For every x ≠ 3, f(x) = 2x + 1, and f(3) = 10.

A second function h has the property lim x→−2 h(x) = −4. No other information about h is given.

The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, t minutes after a heater is switched off is T(t).
items.answer:
(a) The definition of a limit only considers x close to 3 with x ≠ 3. For all such x, f(x) = 2x + 1. As x gets sufficiently close to 3, 2x + 1 gets arbitrarily close to 2(3) + 1 = 7. Therefore lim x→3 f(x) = 7.

(b) The student is using the value of f at x = 3, but a limit as x→3 is determined by the values f(x) for x near 3 and not equal to 3. The value f(3) = 10 plays no role. Near 3, f(x) = 2x + 1 is close to 7, not 10, so the limit is 7, and the fact that f(3) = 10 does not change it.

(c) lim t→5 T(t) = 68.

(d) The statement means that the values h(x) can be made arbitrarily close to −4 by taking x sufficiently close to −2, but not equal to −2. No, h(−2) does not have to equal −4. The limit depends only on the values of h near −2, so h(−2) could be a different number or could be undefined. For example, h(x) = x − 2 for x ≠ −2 with h undefined at x = −2 has limit −4 as x→−2.

criteria.fix: Use the formula f(x) = 2x + 1, which holds for x ≠ 3, to find what value f(x) approaches near 3.

criteria.evidence: The response explains that only values of x near 3 with x ≠ 3 matter, and for those x the values f(x) = 2x + 1 get arbitrarily close to 7.
criteria.fix: State the definition: the limit is R if f(x) is arbitrarily close to R for x sufficiently close to c, but not equal to c.

criteria.text: Explains that the limit does not depend on the value of f at x = 3, so f(3) = 10 does not determine the limit; the limit is 7.
criteria.evidence: The response states that the definition of a limit uses x near 3 but not equal to 3, so the value f(3) is irrelevant, and the values f(x) near 3 approach 7, not 10.
criteria.fix: Remember the limit as x→c ignores x = c itself; compare f(c) with the values f(x) takes near c.

criteria.text: Writes lim t→5 T(t) = 68.
criteria.evidence: The response uses limit notation with the variable t approaching 5, the function T(t), and the limit value 68.
criteria.fix: Put the approached input under lim (t→5), write the function T(t), then set it equal to the value approached, 68.

criteria.evidence: The response says no, h(−2) is not required to be −4, and explains that the limit depends only on x near −2, not at −2.
criteria.fix: Recall that a limit describes behavior near c, not at c; the function value at c may differ or not exist.

items.title: Reading Limits from a Described Piecewise Graph
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the description of the graph, find lim x→-1⁻ g(x) and lim x→-1⁺ g(x). Does lim x→-1 g(x) exist? Explain.

(b) Find lim x→2 g(x) and g(2). Explain why these two values can be different.

(c) Describe the behavior of g(x) as x approaches 4 from each side, using limit notation. Does lim x→4 g(x) exist as a real number? Explain.

(d) Find lim x→-4⁺ g(x) and lim x→6⁻ g(x). Then list every value of c with -4 < c < 6 for which lim x→c g(x) does not exist, giving a reason for each value.
items.stimulus:
A function g is defined for -4 ≤ x ≤ 6 except at x = 4. Its graph is described in words below. A closed point is part of the graph. An open circle marks a point that is not on the graph.

1. For -4 ≤ x < -1, the graph is a straight line segment. It starts at the closed point (-4, 0) and ends at an open circle at (-1, 3).
2. At x = -1 there is a single closed point at (-1, 1), so g(-1) = 1.
3. For -1 < x < 2, the graph is a straight line segment. It runs from an open circle at (-1, -2) to an open circle at (2, 4).
4. At x = 2 there is a single closed point at (2, 0), so g(2) = 0.
5. For 2 < x < 4, the graph is an unbroken increasing curve. It starts at the open circle at (2, 4) and rises without bound as x approaches 4 from the left.
6. The vertical line x = 4 is a vertical asymptote, and g(4) is not defined.
7. For 4 < x ≤ 6, the graph is an unbroken decreasing curve. It comes down from arbitrarily large values just to the right of x = 4 and ends at the closed point (6, 1).
items.answer:
(a) As x → -1 from the left, the first segment approaches the open circle at (-1, 3), so lim x→-1⁻ g(x) = 3. As x → -1 from the right, the second segment approaches the open circle at (-1, -2), so lim x→-1⁺ g(x) = -2. Since 3 ≠ -2, the left-hand and right-hand limits are not equal. Therefore lim x→-1 g(x) does not exist. The closed point (-1, 1) does not affect this.

(b) From the left, the segment on (-1, 2) approaches the height 4 at x = 2. From the right, the curve on (2, 4) starts at the open circle (2, 4), so it also approaches 4. Both one-sided limits equal 4, so lim x→2 g(x) = 4. The closed point at (2, 0) gives g(2) = 0. These values can differ because a limit describes the values g(x) approaches as x gets close to 2, not the value of g at x = 2 itself.

(c) As x approaches 4 from the left, the graph rises without bound, so lim x→4⁻ g(x) = ∞. As x approaches 4 from the right, the graph comes down from arbitrarily large values, so lim x→4⁺ g(x) = ∞. Thus lim x→4 g(x) = ∞. This means g is unbounded near x = 4, so the limit does not exist as a real number.

(d) As x → -4 from the right, the first segment approaches its starting point (-4, 0), so lim x→-4⁺ g(x) = 0. As x → 6 from the left, the decreasing curve approaches (6, 1), so lim x→6⁻ g(x) = 1.
The limit fails to exist at exactly two values of c.
At c = -1, the one-sided limits are 3 and -2, which are unequal.
At c = 4, g is unbounded on both sides.
At c = 2, the limit exists and equals 4, even though g(2) = 0. Everywhere else in (-4, 6), the graph is an unbroken segment or curve, so the limit exists.

criteria.text: States lim x→-1⁻ g(x) = 3 and lim x→-1⁺ g(x) = -2.
criteria.evidence: Both one-sided limit values are correct. Each is read from the segment that approaches x = -1 from that side, not from the closed point (-1, 1).
criteria.fix: For a one-sided limit, follow the graph toward x = -1 from that side only and ignore the isolated point at x = -1.

criteria.text: Concludes lim x→-1 g(x) does not exist because the left-hand limit (3) does not equal the right-hand limit (-2).
criteria.evidence: The response states that the limit does not exist. It justifies this by comparing the two unequal one-sided limits.
criteria.fix: State that a two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal, then compare the two values.

criteria.text: States lim x→2 g(x) = 4, supported by both one-sided limits equal to 4.
criteria.evidence: The response gives the value 4. It notes that the graph approaches the height 4 from both the left and the right of x = 2.
criteria.fix: Check both sides of x = 2. If the left-hand and right-hand heights agree, that common height is the limit.

criteria.text: States g(2) = 0 and explains that the limit depends on values of g near x = 2, not on the value at x = 2.
criteria.evidence: The response correctly gives g(2) = 0 from the closed point. It gives a reason that the limit describes behavior as x approaches 2 and does not depend on g(2).
criteria.fix: Read g(2) from the closed point, then explain that a limit describes nearby behavior and ignores the function value itself.

criteria.text: States lim x→4⁻ g(x) = ∞ and lim x→4⁺ g(x) = ∞.
criteria.evidence: The response uses correct one-sided limit notation showing that g increases without bound from both sides of x = 4.
criteria.fix: Near a vertical asymptote, describe each side separately and write ∞ or -∞ according to the direction the graph goes.

criteria.text: Concludes lim x→4 g(x) does not exist as a real number because g is unbounded near x = 4. The response may also write lim x→4 g(x) = ∞.
criteria.evidence: The response states that the limit is not a real number and attributes this to the unbounded behavior of g near x = 4.
criteria.fix: Remember that writing a limit equals ∞ describes unbounded growth. The limit still does not exist as a finite real number.

criteria.text: States lim x→-4⁺ g(x) = 0 and lim x→6⁻ g(x) = 1.
criteria.evidence: Both endpoint one-sided limits are correct. Each is read from the graph approaching the endpoint from inside the domain.
criteria.fix: At an endpoint of the domain, use the one-sided limit from inside the interval and read the height the graph approaches.

criteria.text: Lists exactly c = -1 and c = 4, giving a reason for each.
criteria.evidence: The response lists c = -1, where the one-sided limits are unequal, and c = 4, where g is unbounded. It does not include c = 2 or any other value.
criteria.fix: Test each break in the graph. A limit fails only for unequal one-sided limits, unbounded behavior, or oscillation, not for a misplaced point.

items.title: Estimating One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits from Tables
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use the table to estimate lim x→1 f(x). Explain your reasoning using values from the table.

(b) A student claims that because f(1) = 5, the answer to part (a) must be 5. Explain why the student is incorrect.

(c) Use the table to estimate lim x→2⁻ g(x) and lim x→2⁺ g(x).

(d) Based on your answers to part (c), does lim x→2 g(x) exist? Explain.
items.stimulus:
The functions f and g are defined for all real numbers. Selected values of f near x = 1 and selected values of g near x = 2 are shown in the tables below. Assume that the trends shown in each table continue as x gets closer to the indicated value. It is also given that f(1) = 5.

Table for f:
x    | 0.9  | 0.99   | 0.999    | 1.001    | 1.01   | 1.1
f(x) | 2.71 | 2.9701 | 2.997001 | 3.003001 | 3.0301 | 3.31

Table for g:
x    | 1.9 | 1.99 | 1.999 | 2.001  | 2.01  | 2.1
g(x) | 3.8 | 3.98 | 3.998 | −0.997 | −0.97 | −0.7
items.answer:
(a) As x approaches 1 from the left, f(0.9) = 2.71, f(0.99) = 2.9701, f(0.999) = 2.997001, which get closer to 3. As x approaches 1 from the right, f(1.1) = 3.31, f(1.01) = 3.0301, f(1.001) = 3.003001, which also get closer to 3. Since the values approach 3 from both sides, lim x→1 f(x) = 3.

(b) The limit as x→1 is determined by the values of f(x) for x close to 1 but not equal to 1. The value f(1) = 5 is the function value at x = 1 itself and does not affect the limit. The table shows f(x) approaching 3 near x = 1, so lim x→1 f(x) = 3, not 5.

(c) For x < 2: g(1.9) = 3.8, g(1.99) = 3.98, g(1.999) = 3.998, approaching 4, so lim x→2⁻ g(x) = 4. For x > 2: g(2.1) = −0.7, g(2.01) = −0.97, g(2.001) = −0.997, approaching −1, so lim x→2⁺ g(x) = −1.

(d) No. lim x→2 g(x) does not exist because the left-hand limit, 4, is not equal to the right-hand limit, −1.

criteria.text: Estimates lim x→1 f(x) = 3.
criteria.evidence: States that the limit of f(x) as x approaches 1 is 3.
criteria.fix: Look at the f(x) values in the columns closest to x = 1 and identify the single number they approach.

criteria.text: Supports the estimate with table values from both sides of x = 1 approaching 3.
criteria.evidence: Cites values for x < 1 (such as f(0.999) = 2.997001) and values for x > 1 (such as f(1.001) = 3.003001) and notes that both sets get closer to 3.
criteria.fix: Quote at least one table value from each side of x = 1 and state that both sides approach the same number.

criteria.text: Explains that a limit depends on the values of f near x = 1, not on the value at x = 1, so the limit remains 3.
criteria.evidence: States that lim x→1 f(x) describes the values f(x) approaches as x gets close to (but not equal to) 1, so f(1) = 5 does not affect the limit, which is still 3.
criteria.fix: Remember that a limit as x→c uses inputs close to c but not equal to c; the value f(c) is irrelevant.

criteria.text: Estimates lim x→2⁻ g(x) = 4, based on values for x < 2.
criteria.evidence: States the left-hand limit is 4 and refers to values such as g(1.99) = 3.98 and g(1.999) = 3.998 approaching 4.
criteria.fix: For a left-hand limit, use only the table columns with x less than 2 and identify the number they approach.

criteria.text: Estimates lim x→2⁺ g(x) = −1, based on values for x > 2.
criteria.evidence: States the right-hand limit is −1 and refers to values such as g(2.01) = −0.97 and g(2.001) = −0.997 approaching −1.
criteria.fix: For a right-hand limit, use only the table columns with x greater than 2 and identify the number they approach.

criteria.text: Concludes lim x→2 g(x) does not exist because the one-sided limits are not equal.
criteria.evidence: States the limit does not exist and gives the reason that the left-hand limit (4) and right-hand limit (−1) are different (or consistent with the student's part (c) values).
criteria.fix: A two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal; compare your two one-sided estimates.

items.title: Limit Theorems with Given Limits and a Piecewise Function
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find lim x→2 [2f(x) − 3g(x)]. Show the limit properties you use.

(b) Find lim x→2 [f(x)·g(x)] / [f(x) + 1]. Explain why the quotient property of limits may be applied.

(c) Find lim x→2 √( [f(x)]² + 7 ). Justify your answer by referring to the appropriate limit property.

(d) Find lim x→2⁻ q(x) and lim x→2⁺ q(x) in terms of k. Then find the value of k for which lim x→2 q(x) exists, and explain why.
items.stimulus:
The functions f and g are defined for all real numbers, and it is known that lim x→2 f(x) = 3 and lim x→2 g(x) = −4. No other information about f and g is given.

The function q is defined by
q(x) = x³ − 2x for x < 2
q(x) = kx + 1 for x > 2
where k is a constant. The function q is not defined at x = 2.
items.answer:
(a) By the difference and constant multiple properties, lim x→2 [2f(x) − 3g(x)] = 2·lim x→2 f(x) − 3·lim x→2 g(x) = 2(3) − 3(−4) = 6 + 12 = 18.

(b) Denominator: lim x→2 [f(x) + 1] = 3 + 1 = 4. Since this limit is 4 ≠ 0, the quotient property applies. Numerator, by the product property: lim x→2 f(x)·g(x) = (3)(−4) = −12. So the limit is −12/4 = −3.

(c) Inner expression: lim x→2 ([f(x)]² + 7) = (3)² + 7 = 16, using the product (or power) and sum properties. The square root function is continuous at 16, so by the limit property for composite functions, lim x→2 √([f(x)]² + 7) = √16 = 4.

(d) For x < 2, q(x) = x³ − 2x, so lim x→2⁻ q(x) = 2³ − 2(2) = 8 − 4 = 4. For x > 2, q(x) = kx + 1, so lim x→2⁺ q(x) = 2k + 1. The two-sided limit lim x→2 q(x) exists if and only if the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal (q(2) being undefined does not affect the limit). Setting 2k + 1 = 4 gives k = 3/2.

criteria.text: Finds lim x→2 [2f(x) − 3g(x)] = 18 using the sum/difference and constant multiple properties.
criteria.evidence: Response writes the limit as 2·lim f(x) − 3·lim g(x) = 2(3) − 3(−4) and obtains 18.
criteria.fix: Split the limit into 2·lim f(x) − 3·lim g(x), substitute the given limits, and watch the sign when subtracting a negative.

criteria.text: States that the limit of the denominator is lim x→2 [f(x) + 1] = 4, which is not 0, so the quotient property applies.
criteria.evidence: Response computes the denominator's limit as 4 and explicitly notes it is nonzero as the condition for the quotient property.
criteria.fix: Before using the quotient property, compute the limit of the denominator and state that it is not zero.

criteria.text: Finds the limit value −3.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the numerator limit (3)(−4) = −12 from the product property and divides by 4 to get −3.
criteria.fix: Use the product property for the numerator, lim f · lim g = (3)(−4), then divide by the denominator's limit.

criteria.text: Finds the limit value 4 with justification that the limit of a composite function can be found by applying the continuous outer square-root function to the limit of the inner expression.
criteria.evidence: Response finds lim x→2 ([f(x)]² + 7) = 9 + 7 = 16, states that the square root function is continuous at 16 (composite limit property), and obtains √16 = 4.
criteria.fix: Find the inner limit first, then state that √u is continuous at that value so the limit passes inside the root.

criteria.text: Finds lim x→2⁻ q(x) = 4.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the x < 2 piece and evaluates 2³ − 2(2) = 4.
criteria.fix: For a left-hand limit at 2, use the piece defined for x < 2 and substitute x = 2 into that polynomial.

criteria.text: Finds lim x→2⁺ q(x) = 2k + 1.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the x > 2 piece and evaluates k(2) + 1 = 2k + 1.
criteria.fix: For a right-hand limit at 2, use the piece defined for x > 2 and substitute x = 2.

criteria.text: Finds k = 3/2 because the two-sided limit exists exactly when the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal.
criteria.evidence: Response sets 2k + 1 = 4, solves k = 3/2, and states that the two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits are equal (the fact that q(2) is undefined does not matter).
criteria.fix: State that a two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits are equal, then set them equal and solve for k.

items.title: Table and Algebraic Views of a Limit at a Hole
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using only the values in the table, estimate lim x→2 f(x). Explain how the table supports your estimate.

(b) Use algebra to find lim x→2 f(x) exactly, showing the work that confirms your estimate from part (a).

(c) Find the value of k for which lim x→2 g(x) exists. Show the work that leads to your answer.

(d) With k equal to the value found in part (c), state the value of lim x→2 g(x). Explain why the given value g(2) = 5 does not change your answer.
items.stimulus:
The function f is defined by f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² − 5x + 6) for all x ≠ 2 and x ≠ 3. Selected values of f, rounded to four decimal places, are shown in the table below.

x    | 1.9     | 1.99    | 1.999   | 2.001   | 2.01    | 2.1
f(x) | −3.5455 | −3.9505 | −3.9950 | −4.0050 | −4.0505 | −4.5556

The function g is defined piecewise by g(x) = f(x) for x < 2, g(2) = 5, and g(x) = kx + 1 for x > 2, where k is a constant.
items.answer:
(a) As x approaches 2 from the left (1.9, 1.99, 1.999), f(x) takes the values −3.5455, −3.9505, −3.9950, which approach −4. As x approaches 2 from the right (2.1, 2.01, 2.001), f(x) takes the values −4.5556, −4.0505, −4.0050, which also approach −4. Since both sides approach the same value, lim x→2 f(x) ≈ −4.

(b) Direct substitution gives 0/0. Factoring, f(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/((x − 2)(x − 3)) = (x + 2)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 2. So lim x→2 f(x) = lim x→2 (x + 2)/(x − 3) = (2 + 2)/(2 − 3) = 4/(−1) = −4, which confirms the estimate.

(c) lim x→2⁻ g(x) = lim x→2⁻ f(x) = −4 from part (b). lim x→2⁺ g(x) = lim x→2⁺ (kx + 1) = 2k + 1. For the limit to exist the one-sided limits must be equal: 2k + 1 = −4, so 2k = −5 and k = −5/2.

(d) With k = −5/2, both one-sided limits equal −4, so lim x→2 g(x) = −4. The limit depends only on the values of g(x) as x gets close to 2, not on the value of g at x = 2 itself, so g(2) = 5 does not affect the limit.

criteria.text: Estimates lim x→2 f(x) = −4 from the table.
criteria.evidence: States the estimate −4 for lim x→2 f(x).
criteria.fix: Look at the trend in f(x) as x gets closer to 2 and name the single number the outputs approach.

criteria.text: Explains that values from both the left (x < 2) and the right (x > 2) approach −4.
criteria.evidence: Refers to inputs on both sides of 2 (for example 1.999 and 2.001) and notes the outputs on each side get close to −4.
criteria.fix: For a two-sided limit from a table, check inputs below and above the target separately and state that both sides approach the same value.

criteria.text: Factors and simplifies: f(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/((x − 2)(x − 3)) = (x + 2)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 2.

criteria.text: Sets the right-hand limit equal to the left-hand limit: lim x→2⁺ g(x) = 2k + 1 and lim x→2⁻ g(x) = −4, so 2k + 1 = −4.

criteria.text: Solves to get k = −5/2.

criteria.text: States lim x→2 g(x) = −4 and explains that a limit depends only on values of g near x = 2, not on the value at x = 2.
criteria.evidence: Gives −4 and states that the limit describes the behavior of g(x) as x approaches 2, so the single value g(2) = 5 is irrelevant.
criteria.fix: Remember a limit describes outputs as x approaches a point; the function's value at that exact point does not affect the limit.
