items.title: Paired Forces Between a Tow Truck, a Cable, and a Car
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Determine the magnitude and direction of the force that the car exerts on the cable at this instant. Justify your answer.

(b) Determine the magnitude and direction of the force that the cable exerts on the truck at this instant. Justify your answer using a property of the cable.

(c) A student says: "The car pulls back on the cable with a force equal in size and opposite in direction to the cable's pull on the car, so these two forces cancel and the car cannot speed up." Explain the error in the student's reasoning.

(d) Consider the system made up of the truck, the cable, and the car. Explain whether the forces that the cable exerts on the truck and on the car can change the velocity of this system's center of mass.
items.stimulus: A tow truck pulls a car east along a straight, level road using a horizontal cable. The truck is east of the car. Treat the cable as ideal: its mass is negligible and it does not stretch. At one instant, the cable exerts a force of 1500 N directed east on the car.
items.answer:
(a) By Newton's third law, the force the car exerts on the cable is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force the cable exerts on the car: F(car on cable) = −F(cable on car). So the car exerts 1500 N directed west on the cable.

(b) The cable is ideal, so the tension is the same at all points along it. The cable pulls on each attached object along the cable toward the other object. It pulls the car east with 1500 N, so it pulls the truck with 1500 N directed west, toward the car.

(c) The two forces the student describes form a third-law pair, and they are exerted on different objects: one is exerted on the car and the other on the cable. Forces exerted on different objects cannot cancel each other. Only forces exerted on the car itself determine whether the car speeds up, so the student's conclusion does not follow.

(d) No. The cable, truck, and car are all inside the chosen system, so the forces the cable exerts on the truck and on the car are internal forces. Internal forces do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass, so they cannot change the velocity of the center of mass of the truck–cable–car system.

criteria.text: The car exerts a force of 1500 N directed west on the cable, by Newton's third law: the force of the car on the cable is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force of the cable on the car.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1500 N, west, and justifies it with Newton's third law (paired forces equal in magnitude and opposite in direction).
criteria.fix: For a force of A on B, the third-law partner is B on A: same magnitude, opposite direction, exerted on the other object.

criteria.text: The cable exerts a force of 1500 N directed west on the truck, justified by a property of the ideal cable: its tension is the same at all points, or its negligible mass means the forces on it balance.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1500 N, west, and justifies the magnitude either by uniform tension in an ideal cable or by the cable's negligible mass requiring zero net force on it, with the third-law partner on the truck.
criteria.fix: In an ideal string or cable, tension is equal at every point; each end pulls on its attached object along the cable, toward the middle.

criteria.text: Explains that the two forces in a third-law pair are exerted on different objects (one on the car, one on the cable), so they cannot cancel; only forces exerted on the car itself combine to determine the car's motion.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the paired forces act on different objects and therefore do not add together or cancel in describing the car's motion.
criteria.fix: Check which object each force is exerted on; third-law partners are always on different objects, so never cancel them against each other.

criteria.text: They cannot: the cable's forces on the truck and car are interactions between objects inside the chosen system (internal forces), and internal forces do not influence the motion of the system's center of mass.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the cable forces as internal to the truck–cable–car system and states that internal forces do not change the motion of the system's center of mass.
criteria.fix: First decide whether both interacting objects are inside the system; if so, the forces are internal and cannot change the center-of-mass motion.

items.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces in Three Situations
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) For Situation 1, calculate the magnitude of the friction force and the magnitude of the normal force that the snow exerts on the sled.

(b) For Situation 2, describe what happens after t = 0 to the east component and to the north component of the puck's velocity. Justify your answer.

(c) For Situation 3, is the bus an inertial reference frame? Justify your answer using Newton's first law.
items.stimulus:
Situation 1: A child pulls a sled across level snow with a rope. The rope is at 37° above the horizontal and the tension in the rope is 50 N. The sled moves east in a straight line at a constant speed of 1.5 m/s. The gravitational force exerted on the sled by Earth is 300 N. The snow exerts a normal force and a horizontal friction force on the sled. Use sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80.

Situation 2: A hockey puck slides east at 3.0 m/s across frictionless, level ice. Starting at time t = 0, a steady wind exerts a constant horizontal force on the puck directed north. The vertical forces on the puck remain balanced.

Situation 3: A bus on a straight, level road is speeding up while moving east. A small block of ice is placed on the floor of the bus, and friction between the ice and the floor is negligible. A passenger in the bus sees the block slide toward the back of the bus, even though no horizontal force is exerted on the block.
items.answer:
(a) The sled moves at constant velocity, so by Newton's first law the net force on it is zero.
Horizontal: the rope's horizontal component is 50 N × 0.80 = 40 N east, so the friction force has magnitude 40 N (directed west).
Vertical: the rope's vertical component is 50 N × 0.60 = 30 N up. F_N + 30 N − 300 N = 0, so the normal force has magnitude 270 N.

(b) After t = 0 there is still no force on the puck in the east–west direction, so the forces in that direction are balanced and the east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s. The wind's force makes the net force point north, so the forces are unbalanced in that direction and the north component of velocity changes: it increases from zero, directed north.

(c) No. The net force on the ice block is zero: the vertical forces balance and no horizontal force is exerted on it. Yet an observer in the bus sees the block's velocity change as it starts sliding toward the back. Newton's first law says an object with zero net force keeps a constant velocity, so this observer would not verify the first law. The speeding-up bus is therefore not an inertial reference frame.

criteria.text: Friction force magnitude = 50 N × cos 37° = 50 × 0.80 = 40 N, because the sled's velocity is constant, so the net force is zero and the horizontal forces balance.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the horizontal net force to zero (constant velocity) and finds friction = 40 N from the rope's horizontal component.
criteria.fix: Constant velocity means zero net force; balance the rope's horizontal component, T cos θ, against friction.

criteria.text: Normal force magnitude = 300 N − 50 N × sin 37° = 300 − 30 = 270 N, from balancing the vertical forces.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the vertical net force to zero, including the rope's upward component of 30 N, and finds the normal force = 270 N.
criteria.fix: Include the rope's upward component when balancing vertical forces; the normal force equals 300 N minus T sin θ, not 300 N.

criteria.text: The east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s, because there is no east–west force on the puck, so the forces are balanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the east component remains 3.0 m/s (unchanged) and justifies it with zero net force in the east–west direction.
criteria.fix: Treat each direction separately: if forces along a direction are balanced, the velocity component along that direction stays constant.

criteria.text: The north component of velocity changes, increasing from zero in the northward direction, because the wind's force makes the net force northward, unbalanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the north component of velocity changes (grows from zero, directed north) and justifies it with the unbalanced northward force.
criteria.fix: Velocity changes only in the direction of the unbalanced force; identify that direction and state that component changes.

criteria.text: No: in the bus's frame the ice block's velocity changes (it starts moving toward the back) even though the net force on it is zero, so an observer in the bus would not verify Newton's first law, and the bus is not an inertial frame.
criteria.evidence: Response says the bus is not inertial and justifies it by noting the block accelerates relative to the bus while the net force on it is zero, contradicting Newton's first law.
criteria.fix: Test a frame by asking whether objects with zero net force keep constant velocity there; if not, the frame is noninertial.

items.title: Weight and Apparent Weight on a Larger Planet
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Planet P.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut when the astronaut stands on its surface.

(c) The astronaut later travels in a spacecraft to a point that is a distance 3R from the center of Planet P, where R is the radius of Planet P. Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut at that point.

(d) Back on the surface of Planet P, the astronaut stands on a scale in an elevator that has an upward acceleration of magnitude 2.0 m/s². Calculate the astronaut's apparent weight.
items.stimulus: Planet P has twice the mass of Earth and twice the radius of Earth. Treat both planets as spheres with symmetrically distributed mass, and ignore their rotation. At Earth's surface the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. Ignore gravitational forces from all objects other than the planet being discussed.
items.answer:
(a) The field strength at a planet's surface is g = GM/R². For Planet P, g_P = G(2M)/(2R)² = (2/4)(GM/R²) = (1/2)(10 N/kg) = 5.0 N/kg.

(b) F_g = m·g_P = (60 kg)(5.0 N/kg) = 300 N.

(c) The gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between centers. On the surface the distance is R; at the new point it is 3R, three times larger, so the force is 1/9 as large: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.

(d) The apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the scale. Taking up as positive, F_N − m·g_P = m·a, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = (60 kg)(5.0 m/s² + 2.0 m/s²) = 420 N. The apparent weight is 420 N, greater than the 300 N gravitational force because the astronaut accelerates upward.

criteria.evidence: Response applies g = GM/r² with doubled mass and doubled radius and obtains 5.0 N/kg (or 5.0 m/s²).
criteria.fix: Write g = GM/r², replace M and r by their multiples, and simplify: doubling r divides g by four.

criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the astronaut's 60 kg mass by the surface field strength of Planet P to obtain 300 N (a consistent follow-through value from the previous part also earns this point).
criteria.fix: Weight is mass times the local field strength; use the field strength for Planet P, not Earth's 10 N/kg.

criteria.text: The distance from the center triples, so F_g falls by a factor of 3² = 9: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the inverse-square dependence on distance from the planet's center (3R, not 2R) and obtains about 33 N (100/3 N).
criteria.fix: Measure r from the planet's center; with F ∝ 1/r², tripling r divides the force by nine.

criteria.text: Apparent weight = normal force: F_N − mg_P = ma, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = 60(5.0 + 2.0) = 420 N.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies apparent weight as the normal (scale) force and obtains 420 N from F_N − mg = ma with upward acceleration.
criteria.fix: Apparent weight is the normal force; apply net force = ma with the acceleration's direction, so F_N exceeds mg when accelerating upward.

items.title: Kinetic Energy of a Car Measured by Different Observers
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the car's translational kinetic energy as measured by the roadside observer.

(b) A truck with twice the mass of the car travels at half the car's speed, as measured by the roadside observer. Determine the ratio of the truck's kinetic energy to the car's kinetic energy.

(c) A second car, identical to the first, travels west at 15 m/s. A student says this car has negative kinetic energy because its velocity is negative. Explain whether the student is correct.

(d) An observer riding in a van that moves west at 5.0 m/s, as measured by the roadside observer, measures the motion of the first car. Calculate the first car's translational kinetic energy as measured by the observer in the van.
items.stimulus: A car of mass 1200 kg travels east along a straight, level road at 15 m/s, as measured by an observer standing beside the road. Take east as the positive direction.
items.answer:
(a) K = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)(1200 kg)(15 m/s)² = (600)(225) = 135,000 J.

(b) K_truck = (1/2)(2m)(v/2)² = (1/2)(2m)(v²/4) = (1/2)·(1/2)mv². So K_truck/K_car = 1/2. Doubling the mass doubles K, but halving the speed divides K by 4.

(c) The student is not correct. Kinetic energy is a scalar, K = (1/2)mv², and v² is positive whether the velocity is +15 m/s or −15 m/s. The westbound car has the same kinetic energy, 135,000 J, not a negative value.

(d) Relative to the van, the car's velocity is (+15 m/s) − (−5.0 m/s) = +20 m/s. The van observer measures K = (1/2)(1200 kg)(20 m/s)² = (600)(400) = 240,000 J. Kinetic energy depends on the observer's reference frame.

criteria.evidence: Response substitutes m = 1200 kg and v = 15 m/s into K = (1/2)mv² and obtains 135,000 J.
criteria.fix: Square the speed before multiplying: K = (1/2)mv², with v² = 225 m²/s² here.

criteria.evidence: Response obtains a ratio of 1/2, either by proportional reasoning (mass factor 2 times speed factor squared, 1/4) or by computing both kinetic energies (67,500 J and 135,000 J).
criteria.fix: Use K ∝ mv²: multiply the mass factor by the square of the speed factor.

criteria.text: The student is incorrect: kinetic energy is a scalar that depends on v², which is positive for either direction of velocity, so the westbound car's kinetic energy is positive.
criteria.evidence: Response states the student is wrong and explains either that kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction or that K = (1/2)mv² uses v², which is positive for negative velocity.
criteria.fix: Remember kinetic energy is a scalar: squaring velocity gives a positive value, so direction never affects K.

criteria.text: Car's velocity relative to the van = (+15 m/s) − (−5.0 m/s) = +20 m/s, so K = (1/2)(1200 kg)(20 m/s)² = 240,000 J.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the car's speed relative to the van as 20 m/s and obtains 240,000 J, recognizing that kinetic energy depends on the observer's reference frame.
criteria.fix: Find the object's velocity relative to the observer first (subtract the observer's signed velocity), then compute K with that speed.

items.title: Elastic and Gravitational Potential Energy and the Choice of Zero
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the elastic potential energy of the block–spring system when the spring is compressed 0.15 m.

(b) The spring is instead compressed 0.30 m from its equilibrium length. Determine the factor by which the elastic potential energy of the system changes compared with the 0.15 m compression.

(c) Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy of the book–Earth system as the book moves from the shelf to the tabletop, according to Student A and according to Student B.

(d) Explain why the two students assign different values to the gravitational potential energy of the system when the book is on the shelf but agree on the change in potential energy.
items.stimulus:
System 1: A block on a horizontal surface rests against an ideal spring with spring constant 400 N/m. The block is pushed so that the spring is compressed 0.15 m from its equilibrium length, and the block is held at rest.

System 2: A 2.0 kg book and Earth form a system. The book is moved from a shelf 1.50 m above the floor to a tabletop 0.80 m above the floor. Use g = 10 N/kg. Student A chooses the floor as the zero of gravitational potential energy, and Student B chooses the tabletop as the zero.
items.answer:
(a) U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)² = (1/2)(400 N/m)(0.15 m)² = (200)(0.0225) = 4.5 J.

(b) U_s is proportional to (Δx)². Doubling the compression from 0.15 m to 0.30 m multiplies U_s by 2² = 4. Check: (1/2)(400)(0.30)² = 18 J, and 18 J/4.5 J = 4.

(c) Student A (zero at floor): U_shelf = (2.0)(10)(1.50) = 30 J and U_table = (2.0)(10)(0.80) = 16 J, so ΔU_g = 16 J − 30 J = −14 J.
Student B (zero at tabletop): U_shelf = (2.0)(10)(0.70) = 14 J and U_table = 0 J, so ΔU_g = 0 J − 14 J = −14 J.
Both find ΔU_g = −14 J; the potential energy of the system decreases by 14 J.

(d) The position of zero potential energy is a choice made by the observer. Measuring heights from the tabletop instead of the floor lowers every potential energy value by the same amount, mg(0.80 m) = 16 J. The values at a single position differ (30 J versus 14 J at the shelf), but when one value is subtracted from another the shared 16 J cancels, so the change in potential energy is the same for both students.

criteria.evidence: Response substitutes k = 400 N/m and Δx = 0.15 m into U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)² and obtains 4.5 J.
criteria.fix: Square the compression before multiplying: U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)², with Δx measured from the spring's equilibrium length.

criteria.text: The elastic potential energy increases by a factor of 4 (to 18 J), because U_s is proportional to (Δx)² and the compression doubles.
criteria.evidence: Response states a factor of 4 (or computes 18 J ÷ 4.5 J = 4) using the squared dependence on compression.
criteria.fix: Use U_s ∝ (Δx)²: the energy factor is the square of the compression factor, so doubling Δx gives four times.

criteria.text: Both students find ΔU_g = mgΔy = (2.0 kg)(10 N/kg)(0.80 m − 1.50 m) = −14 J (Student A: 16 J − 30 J; Student B: 0 J − 14 J).
criteria.evidence: Response obtains −14 J (a decrease of 14 J) for both Student A and Student B, by direct use of mgΔy or by subtracting each student's values.
criteria.fix: Compute ΔU as final minus initial; with Δy negative here, the potential energy decreases.
variants: a decrease of 14 J for both students

criteria.text: Explains that the location of zero potential energy is a choice made by the observer; changing it shifts every potential energy value by the same constant (here 16 J), so individual values differ but the difference between two positions is unchanged.
criteria.evidence: Response states the zero of potential energy is arbitrary (chosen by the observer) and that this choice adds the same constant to both values, which cancels when finding the change.
criteria.fix: Remember only changes in potential energy are fixed by physics; the zero level is a choice that shifts all values equally.

items.title: Coulomb Force and Gravity Between Two Charged Spheres
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the magnitude of the electric force that sphere A exerts on sphere B, and state the direction of that force.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force between the two spheres.

(c) The spheres are moved apart until their centers are 0.090 m apart; the charges and masses are unchanged. By what factor does the magnitude of the electric force change? Does the ratio of the electric force magnitude to the gravitational force magnitude increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answers.
items.stimulus:
Two small spheres, A and B, are held at rest on insulating stands so that their centers are 0.030 m apart. Sphere A has charge +4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C and sphere B has charge −2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C. Each sphere has mass 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg. The spheres are small compared with their separation, so each can be modeled as a point charge and a point mass.

Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².
items.answer:
(a) |F_E| = k|q_A q_B|/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.030)² = (7.2 × 10⁻⁸)/(9.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ N.
The charges have opposite signs, so the force is attractive: the force on B points toward A, along the line joining the centers.

(b) F_G = G m_A m_B / r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(2.0 × 10⁻³)(2.0 × 10⁻³)/(0.030)² = (2.668 × 10⁻¹⁶)/(9.0 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 2.96 × 10⁻¹³ N.

(c) The separation triples from 0.030 m to 0.090 m. The electric force is inversely proportional to r², so it changes by a factor of 1/3² = 1/9, to about 8.9 × 10⁻⁶ N.
The ratio stays the same. The gravitational force is also inversely proportional to r², so it also becomes 1/9 as large. In the ratio F_E/F_G the factor 1/9 cancels, and the ratio remains about 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ / 2.96 × 10⁻¹³ ≈ 2.7 × 10⁸ at both separations.

criteria.text: Calculates the electric force magnitude as 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ N using Coulomb's law.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes into |F| = k|q_A q_B|/r² with r = 0.030 m and obtains 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ N (or an equivalent value).
criteria.fix: Square the separation before dividing, and use the magnitudes of both charges in Coulomb's law.

criteria.text: States that the force on B is directed toward A (attractive), along the line joining the centers.
criteria.evidence: Response says the force on B points toward A, or describes it as attractive.
criteria.fix: After finding the magnitude, compare the signs of the two charges: opposite signs attract along the line joining them.

criteria.text: Calculates the gravitational force magnitude as about 3.0 × 10⁻¹³ N.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes into F_G = G m_A m_B / r² with m = 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg and r = 0.030 m and obtains about 2.96 × 10⁻¹³ N.
criteria.fix: Multiply the two masses, divide by the separation squared, then multiply by G; keep the powers of ten carefully.

criteria.text: States that the electric force becomes 1/9 of its original value because it is inversely proportional to the square of the separation, which tripled.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the separation tripling and uses the inverse-square dependence to give a factor of 1/9.
criteria.fix: When the distance changes by a factor n, an inverse-square force changes by 1/n²; here n = 3.

criteria.text: States that the ratio stays the same (about 2.7 × 10⁸) because both forces are inversely proportional to the square of the separation.
criteria.evidence: Response answers 'stays the same' and justifies it by noting both the electric and gravitational forces depend on 1/r², so the factor cancels in the ratio.
criteria.fix: Check how each force depends on r; if both scale as 1/r², the distance cancels when you divide them.

items.title: Charging by Friction, Then by Induction with Grounding
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use conservation of charge to determine the net charge on the wool.

(b) With the switch open, the negatively charged rod is brought near the left side of the metal sphere without touching it. Describe how charge is distributed on the sphere, and state the sphere's net charge.

(c) With the rod still held near the sphere, the switch is closed. Next the switch is opened, and only after that is the rod taken away. State the direction in which electrons move through the wire while the switch is closed, and state the sign of the sphere's final net charge. Justify your answers.
items.stimulus:
A rubber rod and a piece of wool are both initially electrically neutral. The rod is rubbed with the wool, and afterward the rod has a net charge of −4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C. Assume charge was transferred only between the rod and the wool.

Separately, an initially neutral metal sphere sits on an insulating stand. A thin wire with a switch connects the sphere to Earth (ground). The switch is initially open.
items.answer:
(a) The rod became negative, so it gained electrons: the electrons moved from the wool to the rod.
Charge is conserved. The rod and wool started neutral and charge moved only between them, so their total charge is still zero. The wool's net charge is therefore +4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C.

(b) The negative rod repels electrons in the metal sphere, so electrons shift to the right side, away from the rod. The left side (nearest the rod) is left with positive charge and the right side has negative charge. No charge has been transferred to or from the sphere, so its net charge is still zero; it is only polarized.

(c) With the switch closed, electrons are repelled by the negative rod and move from the sphere through the wire into Earth.
The sphere has lost electrons, so it has more protons than electrons. Because the switch is opened while the rod is still nearby, those electrons cannot return, and the net charge of the sphere stays constant after that. The sphere's final net charge is positive.

criteria.text: Uses conservation of charge to find the wool's net charge as +4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C: the wool lost exactly the electrons the rod gained.
criteria.evidence: Response gives +4.8 × 10⁻⁹ C for the wool and justifies it with conservation of charge (total charge of rod plus wool stays zero).
criteria.fix: Apply conservation of charge: two objects that start neutral and only exchange charge end with equal and opposite charges.

criteria.text: States that electrons in the sphere are repelled toward the right side, leaving the left side (near the rod) positive and the right side negative.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies positive charge on the side nearest the rod and negative charge on the far side.
criteria.fix: For induction without contact, describe both sides: electrons are pushed away from a negative rod, leaving the near side positive.
variants: near side positive, far side negative

criteria.text: States that the sphere's net charge remains zero, because no charge is transferred to or from it.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the sphere's net charge is zero (it is polarized but still neutral).
criteria.fix: An object's net charge changes only when charge is transferred to or from it; polarization alone leaves it neutral.

criteria.text: States that electrons move from the sphere through the wire to Earth, because they are repelled by the negatively charged rod.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the direction as sphere to Earth (out of the sphere) and attributes it to repulsion by the negative rod.
criteria.fix: Ask which way the nearby charge pushes electrons; grounding gives them a path to move in that direction.
variants: from the sphere to the ground

criteria.text: States that the sphere's final net charge is positive, because it lost electrons and opening the switch before removing the rod prevents any charge from returning.
criteria.evidence: Response answers positive and explains that the sphere has fewer electrons than protons and that, once the switch is open, its net charge cannot change.
criteria.fix: Track electrons that left the system: losing electrons makes an object positive, and its net charge stays fixed once the ground path is broken.

items.title: Net Electric Field of Two Positive Point Charges on a Line
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the electric field at point P due to each charge. Then calculate the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at point P.

(b) There is one point between the two charges where the net electric field is zero. Determine the x-coordinate of that point.

(c) An electron is placed at point P. Calculate the magnitude of the electric force on the electron and state its direction.
items.stimulus:
Point charge q₁ = +8.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed at x = 0 on the x-axis, and point charge q₂ = +2.0 × 10⁻⁹ C is fixed at x = 0.30 m. Point P is on the x-axis at x = 0.10 m. The +x direction points from q₁ toward q₂.

Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.answer:
(a) Field from q₁ at P (r = 0.10 m): E₁ = k q₁/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(8.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.10)² = 7.2 × 10³ N/C, pointing away from q₁, in the +x direction.
Field from q₂ at P (r = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 m): E₂ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.20)² = 4.5 × 10² N/C, pointing away from q₂, in the −x direction.
Net field: E = 7.2 × 10³ − 4.5 × 10² = 6.75 × 10³ N/C, in the +x direction.

(b) Between the charges the two fields point in opposite directions, so the net field is zero where their magnitudes are equal:
k(8.0 × 10⁻⁹)/x² = k(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.30 − x)²
(0.30 − x)²/x² = 1/4, so (0.30 − x)/x = 1/2 (taking the positive root, since 0 < x < 0.30 m).
0.60 − 2x = x, so x = 0.20 m.

(c) |F| = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(6.75 × 10³ N/C) ≈ 1.08 × 10⁻¹⁵ N.
The electron is negative, so the force on it is opposite the field: in the −x direction (toward q₁).

criteria.text: Finds the field at P due to q₁ as 7.2 × 10³ N/C in the +x direction and the field due to q₂ as 4.5 × 10² N/C in the −x direction.
criteria.evidence: Response uses E = k|q|/r² with r = 0.10 m for q₁ and r = 0.20 m for q₂, and gives each field's direction as away from its positive charge.
criteria.fix: Compute each charge's field separately with its own distance to P, and point each away from a positive charge.

criteria.text: Finds the net field at P as 6.75 × 10³ N/C in the +x direction.
criteria.evidence: Response combines the two fields as vectors (subtracting because they point in opposite directions) to get about 6.8 × 10³ N/C, directed in +x.
criteria.fix: Add fields as vectors: when they point in opposite directions, subtract magnitudes and take the direction of the larger one.

criteria.text: Finds x = 0.20 m, the point between the charges where the field magnitudes from q₁ and q₂ are equal.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the two field magnitudes are equal there (for example by solving k q₁/x² = k q₂/(0.30 m − x)²) and obtains x = 0.20 m.
criteria.fix: Between two like charges the fields point opposite ways; set the magnitudes equal and solve, taking the root between the charges.

criteria.text: Calculates the force magnitude as about 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ N using F = qE.
criteria.evidence: Response multiplies e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C by the net field from the first part (6.75 × 10³ N/C) to get about 1.08 × 10⁻¹⁵ N.
criteria.fix: Use F = |q|E with the net field at that point, not either individual field.

criteria.text: States that the force on the electron is in the −x direction (toward q₁), opposite the field.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the direction of the force as −x (toward q₁).
criteria.fix: The field direction is the force direction on a positive charge; reverse it for an electron.

items.title: Assembling a Three-Charge System: Work and Potential Energy
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Before q₃ is brought in, only q₁ and q₂ are in place. Calculate the electric potential energy of the system of q₁ and q₂.

(b) Charge q₃ is then moved slowly from very far away to its position while q₁ and q₂ are held fixed, so that q₃ is at rest at the start and the end. Calculate the work done by the external force on q₃.

(c) Calculate the total electric potential energy of the three-charge system.

(d) All three charges are then moved, starting and ending at rest, until each is very far from the other two. Is the total work done by external forces positive, negative, or zero? Justify your answer.
items.stimulus:
Three point charges are placed in a plane:
q₁ = +3.0 μC at the origin, (0, 0)
q₂ = −2.0 μC at (0.40 m, 0)
q₃ = +1.0 μC at (0, 0.30 m)

The electric potential energy of a pair of point charges is zero when they are infinitely far apart. Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
items.answer:
(a) U₁₂ = k q₁q₂/r₁₂ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(−2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.40) = −0.135 J.

(b) Distances from q₃: r₁₃ = 0.30 m, and r₂₃ = √(0.40² + 0.30²) = 0.50 m.
U₁₃ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.30) = +0.090 J.
U₂₃ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(−2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.50) = −0.036 J.
q₃ starts and ends at rest, so the external work equals the change in electric potential energy of the system: W = U₁₃ + U₂₃ = 0.090 − 0.036 = +0.054 J.

(c) U_total = U₁₂ + U₁₃ + U₂₃ = −0.135 + 0.090 − 0.036 = −0.081 J.

(d) Positive. When the charges are all very far apart, the system's electric potential energy is zero. It starts at −0.081 J, so it must increase by 0.081 J. The charges start and end at rest, so the total external work equals this increase: W = +0.081 J, which is positive.

criteria.text: Calculates U₁₂ = −0.135 J.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes into U = k q₁q₂/r with r = 0.40 m, keeping the signs of the charges, and obtains −0.135 J.
criteria.fix: Keep the signs of both charges in U = kq₁q₂/r; opposite charges give a negative potential energy.

criteria.text: Accounts for both new interactions: U₁₃ = +0.090 J (r = 0.30 m) and U₂₃ = −0.036 J (r = 0.50 m), separately or in one combined expression.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the q₂–q₃ distance as 0.50 m and includes the interaction of q₃ with q₁ (+0.090 J) and with q₂ (−0.036 J) with correct signs, as separate pair energies or correctly substituted terms of a combined expression such as kq₃(q₁/r₁₃ + q₂/r₂₃).
criteria.fix: List every new pair the arriving charge forms, find each distance, and compute each pair energy with its sign.

criteria.text: States the external work is W = U₁₃ + U₂₃ = +0.054 J, because the work equals the increase in the system's electric potential energy when kinetic energy does not change.
criteria.evidence: Response sums the two new pair energies to get +0.054 J and identifies this as the external work.
criteria.fix: With no change in kinetic energy, the external work equals the change in electric potential energy, the sum of the new pair terms.

criteria.text: Calculates U_total = −0.135 J + 0.090 J − 0.036 J = −0.081 J.
criteria.evidence: Response sums the potential energies of all three pairs and obtains −0.081 J.
criteria.fix: Add the energy of every pair exactly once: three charges form three pairs.

criteria.text: States the total external work is positive (+0.081 J) because the system's potential energy must increase from −0.081 J to zero with no change in kinetic energy.
criteria.evidence: Response answers positive and supports it with the change in potential energy from the negative total in the previous part to zero at large separation.
criteria.fix: Compare the final potential energy (zero when far apart) with the starting value; external work equals that change.

items.title: Current, Charge Carriers, and Conventional Current Direction
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the current in the wire.

(b) Calculate the number of electrons that pass through a cross section of the wire each second.

(c) State the direction in which the electrons in the wire actually move, and explain how this is related to the direction of the conventional current.

(d) The circuit is then opened, and the current in the wire becomes zero. A student claims that every electron in the wire is now at rest. Evaluate the student's claim.
items.stimulus: A copper wire is part of a closed circuit that contains a battery and a heating element. While the circuit is closed, charge passes through a cross section of the wire at a steady rate, and a total of 360 C passes through that cross section in 4.0 minutes. The conventional current in this wire is directed from end X of the wire toward end Y. The elementary charge is e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.answer:
(a) Δt = 4.0 min × 60 s/min = 240 s. I = Δq/Δt = 360 C / 240 s = 1.5 A.

(b) Each second 1.5 C passes a cross section. Number of electrons per second = (1.5 C/s)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) ≈ 9.4 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.

(c) The electrons move from Y toward X. Conventional current is defined as the direction in which positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so they actually move opposite to the conventional current, which points from X to Y.

(d) The claim is incorrect. Zero current means that the net motion of the charge carriers through any cross section is zero, so there is no net flow of charge. Individual electrons still move with nonzero speeds in random directions; their motions simply produce no net transfer of charge.

criteria.text: Calculates I = Δq/Δt = 1.5 A.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the charge by the elapsed time with consistent units (for example 360 C / 240 s, or 90 C/min converted to C/s) to obtain 1.5 A.
criteria.fix: Express the time in seconds, or convert coulombs per minute to coulombs per second, since 1 A means 1 C per second.

criteria.text: Finds about 9.4 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.
criteria.evidence: Response divides 1.5 C/s by e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, or divides the total number of electrons (360 C / e = 2.25 × 10²¹) by 240 s, to obtain about 9.4 × 10¹⁸ electrons each second.
criteria.fix: The current gives coulombs per second; divide by the charge of one electron to count electrons per second.

criteria.text: States that electrons move from Y toward X, opposite the conventional current, because conventional current is the direction positive charge would move and electrons are negative.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the electron motion as from end Y to end X and explains that conventional current is defined by positive charge motion, so negative carriers move the opposite way.
criteria.fix: Remember conventional current follows positive charge; in metal wires the moving carriers are electrons, so reverse the stated direction.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect: zero current means zero net motion of charge carriers through a cross section, but individual electrons still move with nonzero speeds in random directions.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and distinguishes zero net (average) motion of electrons from individual electrons having zero speed.
criteria.fix: Separate net flow from individual motion: zero current only means equal numbers of carriers cross a section each way.

items.title: Open, Closed, and Short Circuits in a Three-Bulb Circuit
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Both switches are open. State which bulbs are lit and which are unlit. Justify your answer in terms of closed and open circuits.

(b) Switch S is closed while switch T stays open. State whether bulb 2 is lit, and explain using the idea of a short circuit.

(c) Both switches are now closed. State whether bulb 3 is lit, and explain why. Then identify two different closed loops that both contain the battery, listing the circuit elements each loop passes through.
items.stimulus:
An ideal battery has a positive terminal P and a negative terminal N. The circuit is connected as follows.
- Bulb 1 connects terminal P to junction B.
- Bulb 2 connects junction B to junction C.
- Switch S also connects junction B directly to junction C, giving a second path from B to C that contains nothing except the switch.
- A wire connects junction C to terminal N.
- Bulb 3 connects terminal P to point D, and switch T connects point D to terminal N.

All wires and closed switches have negligible resistance. A bulb is lit only when charge flows through it.
items.answer:
(a) Bulbs 1 and 2 are lit. The path P → bulb 1 → B → bulb 2 → C → N is a closed loop through the battery, so charge can flow through both bulbs. Switch S is open, so the only path from B to C is through bulb 2.
Bulb 3 is unlit. Its only path back to the battery goes through switch T, which is open, so that path is an open circuit and no charge can flow through bulb 3.

(b) Bulb 2 is unlit. Closing S gives charge a path from B to C through the switch alone, with no change in electric potential; this is a short circuit across bulb 2. Because bulb 2 is connected between the same points B and C, the potential difference across it is zero, so no charge flows through it and it does not light.

(c) Bulb 3 is lit, because closing T completes the closed loop P → bulb 3 → D → switch T → N.
Two closed loops that contain the battery:
Loop 1: battery (P) → bulb 1 → B → switch S → C → battery (N).
Loop 2: battery (P) → bulb 3 → D → switch T → battery (N).
The battery is part of both loops.

criteria.text: States that bulbs 1 and 2 are lit because the path P → bulb 1 → B → bulb 2 → C → N is a closed loop through the battery.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies bulbs 1 and 2 as lit and describes the closed path from the battery through bulb 1 and bulb 2 back to the battery.
criteria.fix: Trace each bulb's path from one battery terminal to the other; a bulb lights only if that path forms a complete loop.

criteria.text: States that bulb 3 is unlit because open switch T breaks its only path back to the battery, so it is in an open circuit.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies bulb 3 as unlit and explains that charge cannot flow through it because switch T is open.
criteria.fix: Check every switch along a bulb's path; one open switch makes that path an open circuit with no charge flow.

criteria.text: States that bulb 2 is unlit because closed switch S lets charge flow from B to C with no change in electric potential (a short circuit), so the potential difference across bulb 2 is zero and no charge flows through it.
criteria.evidence: Response says bulb 2 goes out and explains that the switch path from B to C has no potential difference, so bulb 2, connected between the same two points, has none either.
criteria.fix: When a wire or closed switch joins a bulb's two ends, the bulb has zero potential difference across it; say so explicitly.

criteria.text: States that bulb 3 is lit because closing T completes the closed loop P → bulb 3 → D → switch T → N.
criteria.evidence: Response says bulb 3 is lit and identifies the now-complete path through bulb 3 and switch T back to the battery.
criteria.fix: After a switch closes, retrace the bulb's path to the battery and confirm it now forms a complete loop.

criteria.text: Identifies two valid closed loops containing the battery, chosen from: battery–bulb 1–switch S; battery–bulb 3–switch T; battery–bulb 1–bulb 2.
criteria.evidence: Response lists two of these three loops by their elements, each starting and ending at the battery, showing the battery belongs to more than one loop.
criteria.fix: Start at a battery terminal, follow connected elements without retracing, and stop when you return to the other terminal; repeat along a different route.

items.title: Resistance of a Nichrome Wire and a Non-Ohmic Filament
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the resistance of the nichrome wire.

(b) The ends of the nichrome wire are connected across a potential difference of 6.6 V. Calculate the current in the wire.

(c) A second wire is made of the same nichrome but has twice the length and twice the diameter of the first wire. Determine the resistance of the second wire.

(d) Using the filament data, determine whether the filament is ohmic. Then give a physical explanation for the trend in its resistance.
items.stimulus:
A uniform nichrome wire has length 2.0 m, cross-sectional area 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², and resistivity 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m. Treat the wire as ohmic.

Separately, a student measures the current in a lightbulb filament for several potential differences across it. The filament is not assumed to be ohmic. The data are:
ΔV (V) | I (A)
1.0 | 0.20
2.0 | 0.36
4.0 | 0.60
8.0 | 0.90
items.answer:
(a) R = ρℓ/A = (1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m)(2.0 m)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 4.4 Ω.

(b) I = ΔV/R = 6.6 V / 4.4 Ω = 1.5 A.

(c) R = ρℓ/A. The length doubles, which doubles R. The diameter doubles, so the cross-sectional area (proportional to diameter squared) becomes 4 times larger, which divides R by 4. The new resistance is 4.4 Ω × 2/4 = 2.2 Ω.

(d) ΔV/I for each row: 1.0/0.20 = 5.0 Ω, 2.0/0.36 ≈ 5.6 Ω, 4.0/0.60 ≈ 6.7 Ω, 8.0/0.90 ≈ 8.9 Ω. The resistance is not constant, so the filament is not ohmic.
As the current increases, the filament converts electrical energy to thermal energy at a greater rate and its temperature rises. The resistivity of a conductor typically increases with temperature, so the filament's resistance increases as the current increases.

criteria.text: Calculates R = ρℓ/A = 4.4 Ω.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes ρ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m, ℓ = 2.0 m and A = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² into R = ρℓ/A and obtains 4.4 Ω.
criteria.fix: Multiply resistivity by length, then divide by cross-sectional area, tracking powers of ten.

criteria.text: Calculates I = ΔV/R = 6.6 V / 4.4 Ω = 1.5 A.
criteria.evidence: Response applies Ohm's law with the resistance from the first part, or computes I = ΔV·A/(ρℓ) directly, to get 1.5 A.
criteria.fix: Use I = ΔV/R with the resistance you found, and check that volts divided by ohms gives amperes.

criteria.text: Finds 2.2 Ω, because doubling the length doubles R while doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, so R is multiplied by 2/4 = 1/2.
criteria.evidence: Response recognizes that area scales with diameter squared (factor 4), combines this with the length factor 2, and gives 2.2 Ω.
criteria.fix: Area depends on diameter squared; find the factors for length and area separately, then combine them in R = ρℓ/A.

criteria.text: States that the filament is not ohmic because ΔV/I is not constant (current is not proportional to ΔV): ΔV/I rises from 5.0 Ω at 1.0 V to about 8.9 Ω at 8.0 V.
criteria.evidence: Response shows from the data that ΔV/I is not constant, by computing it for at least two rows (for example 5.0 Ω and 8.9 Ω) or by showing doubling ΔV does not double I (0.20 A to 0.36 A), and concludes not ohmic.
criteria.fix: Compute ΔV/I for several rows, or check whether doubling ΔV doubles I; an ohmic element keeps a constant ratio.

criteria.text: Explains that resistance increases as current increases because the filament converts more electrical energy to thermal energy and gets hotter, and the resistivity of a conductor typically increases with temperature.
criteria.evidence: Response links larger current to higher filament temperature and states that resistivity (and so resistance) increases with temperature.
criteria.fix: Connect the change in resistance to temperature: more current heats the filament, and hotter conductors have greater resistivity.

items.title: Power and Energy of a Heater and Bulb Brightness
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the power delivered to the heater.

(b) Calculate the electrical energy converted to thermal energy by the heater in 2.0 hours of operation at 120 V.

(c) The heater is instead connected to a 60 V source, and its resistance does not change. Calculate the power delivered to the heater now.

(d) Derive an expression for the ratio P_X/P_Y of the power delivered to bulb X to the power delivered to bulb Y. Then state which bulb is brighter.
items.stimulus:
A space heater connected to a 120 V outlet has a current of 12.5 A. Treat the heater as an ohmic resistor.

Separately, bulb X and bulb Y are each connected alone across its own ideal battery, and the two batteries have the same potential difference ΔV. Both bulbs are ohmic, and the resistance of bulb Y is twice the resistance of bulb X: R_Y = 2R_X.
items.answer:
(a) P = IΔV = (12.5 A)(120 V) = 1500 W.

(b) Δt = 2.0 h × 3600 s/h = 7200 s. Energy = PΔt = (1500 W)(7200 s) = 1.08 × 10⁷ J.

(c) The heater's resistance is R = ΔV/I = 120 V / 12.5 A = 9.6 Ω. At 60 V: P = (ΔV)²/R = (60 V)²/(9.6 Ω) = 375 W. (Equivalently, halving ΔV at constant R multiplies the power by 1/4: 1500 W × 1/4 = 375 W.)

(d) Each bulb has potential difference ΔV across it, so P = (ΔV)²/R for each.
P_X/P_Y = [(ΔV)²/R_X] / [(ΔV)²/R_Y] = R_Y/R_X = 2R_X/R_X = 2.
Bulb X receives twice the power, and brightness increases with power, so bulb X is brighter.

criteria.text: Calculates P = IΔV = (12.5 A)(120 V) = 1500 W.
criteria.evidence: Response obtains 1500 W by any valid route, such as P = IΔV, or R = ΔV/I = 9.6 Ω followed by P = (ΔV)²/R or P = I²R.
criteria.fix: Multiply the current through the heater by the potential difference across it to calculate its power.

criteria.text: Calculates E = PΔt = (1500 W)(7200 s) = 1.08 × 10⁷ J.
criteria.evidence: Response obtains 1.08 × 10⁷ J (or the equivalent 3.0 kWh) by any valid route, such as PΔt with Δt = 7200 s, or IΔVΔt.
criteria.fix: Power is energy per unit time: multiply the power by the operating time, using seconds to get joules.

criteria.text: Calculates 375 W, using the unchanged resistance of 9.6 Ω (for example P = (ΔV)²/R, so halving ΔV gives one quarter of 1500 W).
criteria.evidence: Response obtains 375 W by any valid route, such as (60 V)²/(9.6 Ω), or I = 60 V/9.6 Ω = 6.25 A then P = IΔV, or scaling 1500 W by (1/2)².
criteria.fix: When resistance is fixed, use P = (ΔV)²/R: power depends on the square of the potential difference.

criteria.text: Derives P_X/P_Y = R_Y/R_X = 2.
criteria.evidence: Response uses a valid power relation with the same ΔV for both bulbs (P = (ΔV)²/R, or I = ΔV/R with P = IΔV) and simplifies the ratio to 2.
criteria.fix: With the same potential difference across each bulb, write each bulb's power in terms of ΔV and R, then cancel ΔV in the ratio.

criteria.text: States that bulb X is brighter.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies bulb X as the brighter bulb.
criteria.fix: Brightness increases with power; once you know which bulb gets more power, that bulb is brighter.

items.title: Loop Rule and Potential Around a Three-Resistor Loop
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the current in the loop.

(b) Use Kirchhoff's loop rule to determine the potential difference across R₃. Then determine the resistance R₃.

(c) Determine the electric potential at point K.

(d) A charge of +2.0 C passes through R₃ in the direction of the conventional current. Calculate the change in the electric potential energy associated with this charge, and state whether it increases or decreases.
items.stimulus: An ideal battery with emf 12.0 V is connected in a single loop with three resistors. Going around the loop in the direction of the conventional current, starting from the battery's positive terminal, charge passes through resistor R₁ = 2.0 Ω, then point M, then resistor R₂ = 4.0 Ω, then point K, then resistor R₃ of unknown resistance, and then returns to the battery's negative terminal. An ideal voltmeter connected across R₂ reads 4.0 V. Take the electric potential of the battery's negative terminal to be 0 V.
items.answer:
(a) The voltmeter shows ΔV₂ = 4.0 V across R₂ = 4.0 Ω, so I = ΔV₂/R₂ = 4.0 V / 4.0 Ω = 1.0 A. This is the current everywhere in the single loop.

(b) ΔV₁ = IR₁ = (1.0 A)(2.0 Ω) = 2.0 V.
Loop rule, going around in the direction of the current: +12.0 V − 2.0 V − 4.0 V − ΔV₃ = 0, so ΔV₃ = 6.0 V.
R₃ = ΔV₃/I = 6.0 V / 1.0 A = 6.0 Ω.

(c) The ideal battery raises the potential from 0 V at the negative terminal to 12.0 V at the positive terminal. Stepping along the current: at M (after R₁) the potential is 12.0 V − 2.0 V = 10.0 V, and at K (after R₂) it is 10.0 V − 4.0 V = 6.0 V.
The electric potential at K is 6.0 V. (Check: after R₃ the potential is 6.0 V − 6.0 V = 0 V, matching the negative terminal.)

(d) The charge goes from K (6.0 V) to the negative terminal (0 V), so ΔV = −6.0 V.
ΔU = qΔV = (2.0 C)(−6.0 V) = −12 J. The electric potential energy decreases by 12 J.

criteria.text: Calculates I = ΔV₂/R₂ = 4.0 V / 4.0 Ω = 1.0 A.
criteria.evidence: Response applies Ohm's law to R₂ using the voltmeter reading and obtains 1.0 A.
criteria.fix: Use the element whose potential difference and resistance are both known to find the current in a single loop.

criteria.text: Applies the loop rule: 12.0 V − 2.0 V − 4.0 V − ΔV₃ = 0, so ΔV₃ = 6.0 V (with ΔV₁ = IR₁ = 2.0 V).
criteria.evidence: Response writes a loop equation in which the battery's 12.0 V gain equals the sum of the drops across the three resistors and solves for 6.0 V, or the value that follows correctly from the response's own current in part (a).
criteria.fix: Go once around the loop adding the battery's gain and each resistor's drop, set the sum to zero, then solve.

criteria.text: Calculates R₃ = 6.0 Ω (for example ΔV₃/I = 6.0 V / 1.0 A).
criteria.evidence: Response obtains 6.0 Ω by any valid route, such as dividing the potential difference across R₃ by the loop current, or R₃ = 12.0 V/I − R₁ − R₂; or the value that follows correctly from its own earlier answers.
criteria.fix: Once the potential difference across a resistor is known, divide by the current through it to find its resistance.

criteria.text: Gives the electric potential at K as 6.0 V (for example 12.0 V − 2.0 V − 4.0 V).
criteria.evidence: Response gives 6.0 V at K by any valid stepping around the loop, such as subtracting the drops across R₁ and R₂ from 12.0 V or adding the rise across R₃ to 0 V; or the value following correctly from its own parts (a) and (b).
criteria.fix: Start at a point of known potential and step around the loop, subtracting each drop along the current or adding it going against the current.

criteria.text: Calculates ΔU = qΔV = (2.0 C)(0 V − 6.0 V) = −12 J, a decrease of 12 J.
criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the charge by the change in potential from K (6.0 V) to the negative terminal (0 V), giving −12 J, and states the energy decreases; or the result that follows correctly from its own potential at K in part (c).
criteria.fix: Use ΔU = qΔV with ΔV = final potential minus initial potential, keeping the sign to decide increase or decrease.

items.title: Junction Rule at a Wire Junction and in Parallel Branches
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) In Situation 1, determine the magnitude of the current in wire 3 and state whether it is directed into or out of junction J.

(b) In Situation 1, calculate the amount of charge that passes through wire 3 in 5.0 s.

(c) In Situation 2, determine the current in the lightbulb.

(d) In Situation 2, a student claims that the current in the wire from junction L back to the battery's negative terminal is less than 6.0 A, because the resistors and the bulb use up some of the current. Evaluate the student's claim.
items.stimulus:
Situation 1: Three wires meet at junction J. Wire 1 carries a steady current of 3.0 A into J. Wire 2 carries a steady current of 1.2 A out of J. The current in wire 3 is unknown.

Situation 2: An ideal battery with a potential difference of 12.0 V is connected to three parallel branches. Each branch runs from junction H, which is connected by a wire to the battery's positive terminal, to junction L, which is connected by a wire to the battery's negative terminal. Branch 1 contains a 6.0 Ω resistor, branch 2 contains a 4.0 Ω resistor, and branch 3 contains a lightbulb of unknown resistance. An ideal ammeter in the wire between the positive terminal and junction H reads 6.0 A. All wires have negligible resistance.
items.answer:
(a) Junction rule at J: total current in = total current out. 3.0 A = 1.2 A + I₃, so I₃ = 1.8 A. The current in wire 3 is directed out of J.

(b) Δq = IΔt = (1.8 A)(5.0 s) = 9.0 C.

(c) Each branch is connected between H and L, so each has the battery's 12.0 V across it.
Branch 1: I₁ = 12.0 V / 6.0 Ω = 2.0 A. Branch 2: I₂ = 12.0 V / 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.
Junction rule at H: 6.0 A = 2.0 A + 3.0 A + I_bulb, so I_bulb = 1.0 A.

(d) The claim is incorrect. The three branch currents, 2.0 A + 3.0 A + 1.0 A = 6.0 A, all enter junction L, and the only path out of L is the wire to the negative terminal. By the junction rule, the current in that wire is 6.0 A. Charge is conserved: the resistors and bulb transfer electrical energy, but charge is not used up, so the charge per unit time returning to the battery equals the charge per unit time leaving it.

criteria.text: Finds 1.8 A directed out of J, using the junction rule: current in equals current out, so 3.0 A = 1.2 A + I₃.
criteria.evidence: Response applies ΣI_in = ΣI_out at J to get 1.8 A and states the current in wire 3 leaves the junction.
criteria.fix: Add all currents entering and all leaving a junction, set the totals equal, and solve for the missing current and its direction.

criteria.text: Calculates Δq = IΔt = (1.8 A)(5.0 s) = 9.0 C.
criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the current in wire 3 by 5.0 s to obtain 9.0 C.
criteria.fix: Current is charge per unit time, so multiply the current by the time interval in seconds.

criteria.text: Finds the current through the two resistors from the 12.0 V across each parallel branch: 2.0 A and 3.0 A separately, or 5.0 A combined.
criteria.evidence: Response divides 12.0 V by each resistance to get 2.0 A and 3.0 A, or divides 12.0 V by the resistors' equivalent resistance 2.4 Ω to get 5.0 A.
criteria.fix: Each parallel branch has the full battery potential difference across it; divide that by each branch's resistance.

criteria.text: Uses the junction rule at H to find the bulb current: 6.0 A = 2.0 A + 3.0 A + I_bulb (or 5.0 A + I_bulb), so I_bulb = 1.0 A.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the 6.0 A entering H equal to the total current leaving H through the branches and obtains 1.0 A.
criteria.fix: At the junction where branches split, the incoming current equals the sum of the branch currents; subtract the known branches.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect: by the junction rule at L, the branch currents 2.0 A + 3.0 A + 1.0 A = 6.0 A all leave L in the return wire, because charge is conserved and is not used up in the elements.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim, applies the junction rule at L to get 6.0 A in the return wire, and cites conservation of charge.
criteria.fix: Apply the junction rule where branches rejoin, and remember elements transfer energy, not charge, so charge entering equals charge leaving.

items.title: Rigid-Container Gas Data: Zero-Pressure Temperature and Moles
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data, determine the temperature, in degrees Celsius, at which the pressure of the gas would be zero if the trend in the data continued.

(b) Calculate the number of moles of gas in the container.

(c) All of the gas is moved into a different container with half the volume, and it is heated until its absolute temperature is twice its absolute temperature at 20 °C. No gas escapes. Determine the new pressure of the gas.

(d) The ideal-gas model becomes less accurate when a gas is compressed into a very small volume. Identify one assumption of the ideal-gas model that fails under these conditions and explain why it fails.
items.stimulus:
A fixed amount of an ideal gas is sealed in a rigid container of volume 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. A student measures the gas pressure at several temperatures:
T (°C) | P (kPa)
20 | 120.0
50 | 132.3
80 | 144.6
110 | 156.9

Use R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) and T(K) = T(°C) + 273.
items.answer:
(a) Each 30 °C increase raises the pressure by 12.3 kPa, so the pressure is linear in temperature with slope 12.3/30 = 0.41 kPa/°C. Starting at 20 °C and 120.0 kPa, the pressure reaches zero after a decrease of 120.0/0.41 ≈ 293 °C, at T ≈ 20 − 293 ≈ −273 °C.

(b) P = 120.0 kPa = 1.200 × 10⁵ Pa, T = 20 + 273 = 293 K.
n = PV/(RT) = (1.200 × 10⁵ Pa)(4.0 × 10⁻³ m³)/[(8.31 J/(mol·K))(293 K)] = 480/2435 ≈ 0.197 mol.

(c) From PV = nRT, P = nRT/V. The amount of gas n is constant. T doubles, which doubles P, and V is halved, which doubles P again. P_new = 2 × 2 × 120.0 kPa = 480 kPa.

(d) The model assumes the volume of the atoms is negligible compared with the volume occupied by the gas. When the gas is squeezed into a very small volume, the atoms take up a significant fraction of that volume, so this assumption fails. (Also acceptable: the model assumes the only appreciable forces act during collisions, but when atoms are packed close together the forces between them at other times are no longer negligible.)

criteria.text: Finds about −273 °C by extending the linear trend (slope 0.41 kPa per °C) to zero pressure.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the pressure rises by 12.3 kPa per 30 °C (0.41 kPa/°C) and extrapolates from a data point to P = 0, getting a value between −276 °C and −270 °C.
criteria.fix: Find the constant change in P per degree, then work backward from a data point until the pressure reaches zero.

criteria.text: Calculates n = PV/(RT) ≈ 0.197 mol, using the absolute temperature 293 K.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes into PV = nRT with consistent units (pascals, m³ and R = 8.31 J/(mol·K), or kPa, L and R = 8.31 kPa·L/(mol·K)) and T in kelvins, obtaining about 0.197 mol (or uses another row consistently).
criteria.fix: Match units to R: with R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) use pascals and cubic meters, and always use absolute temperature in kelvins.

criteria.text: Finds the pressure increases by a factor of 4, to 480 kPa, because P = nRT/V with n constant, T doubled, and V halved.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the ideal gas law with n fixed to combine a factor of 2 from temperature and a factor of 2 from volume, giving 4 × 120.0 kPa = 480 kPa.
criteria.fix: Write P = nRT/V and apply each change as a factor: doubling T doubles P, and halving V doubles P again.

criteria.text: Identifies a relevant assumption and explains its failure: the atoms' own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume, or the atoms are close enough that forces between them other than during collisions become appreciable.
criteria.evidence: Response names one of these two assumptions and connects its failure to the atoms being packed closely together in a small volume.
criteria.fix: Recall the model's assumptions (negligible atomic volume, forces only during collisions) and ask which depend on atoms being far apart.

items.title: Hot Block in Cool Water: Direction of Transfer and Equilibrium
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Immediately after the block is placed in the water, state the direction of the net energy transfer by thermal processes, and identify which system is being heated and which is being cooled. Then name the thermal process by which energy is transferred from the surface of the block into the water in contact with it.

(b) Explain, in terms of collisions between particles, why the net energy transfer is in the direction you stated.

(c) After a long time, both thermometers read the same temperature, and the reading no longer changes. Name the condition the block and water have reached and describe the net energy transfer between them. Do individual collisions between particles of the block and particles of the water still transfer energy? Explain.
items.stimulus: A metal block at 80 °C is placed into water at 20 °C inside a closed, well-insulated container, so energy exchange with the surroundings is negligible. The block is fully submerged. One thermometer is embedded in the block and another is in the water, and both are read over time.
items.answer:
(a) The net energy transfer is from the block to the water, because energy is transferred spontaneously from the higher-temperature system (the block at 80 °C) to the lower-temperature system (the water at 20 °C). The water is being heated and the block is being cooled.
Energy passes from the block's surface into the water touching it by conduction. (Convection then carries warmed water away within the container.)

(b) The block's higher temperature means its atoms have a higher average kinetic energy than the water molecules. When a particle of the block collides with a water molecule, energy is most likely transferred from the higher-energy particle to the lower-energy one. Over many collisions this produces a net transfer of energy from the block to the water.

(c) The block and water have reached thermal equilibrium. There is no net energy transfer by thermal processes between them, which is why the temperatures stay equal and constant.
Yes, individual collisions still transfer energy. Particles keep moving and colliding, and in some collisions energy goes from block to water while in others it goes from water to block. These transfers balance on average, so the net transfer is zero.

criteria.text: States that the net energy transfer is from the block to the water, so the water is heated and the block is cooled.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the direction block → water and identifies the water as heated and the block as cooled.
criteria.fix: Energy flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature; name the higher-temperature system as cooled and the other as heated.
variants: from the block to the water

criteria.text: Names conduction as the process transferring energy from the block's surface into the water touching it.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies conduction (energy transfer through direct contact and collisions) at the block–water surface; mentioning convection within the water as well does not lose the point.
criteria.fix: Match each process to its mechanism: direct contact is conduction, bulk fluid motion is convection, and electromagnetic waves are radiation.

criteria.text: Explains that the block's atoms have a higher average kinetic energy, and in collisions between particles of the two systems energy is most likely transferred from the higher-energy particles to the lower-energy ones.
criteria.evidence: Response connects higher temperature to higher average kinetic energy of the block's atoms and states that collisions tend to transfer energy from higher-energy to lower-energy particles.
criteria.fix: Describe temperature as average particle kinetic energy, then state which particle usually gains energy when a fast one hits a slow one.

criteria.text: Names thermal equilibrium and states that there is no net energy transfer by thermal processes between the block and the water.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies thermal equilibrium and says the net energy transfer between the two systems is zero.
criteria.fix: Define thermal equilibrium by net energy transfer, not by particles stopping: equal temperatures mean zero net transfer.

criteria.text: States that individual collisions still transfer energy in both directions, but on average the transfers balance, so the net transfer is zero.
criteria.evidence: Response says particles keep colliding and exchanging energy, with transfers from block to water balanced by transfers from water to block.
criteria.fix: Distinguish individual exchanges from the net result: particles keep colliding at equilibrium, but energy moves equally in both directions.

items.title: Heating Water, Conduction Through a Window, and Specific Heat
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the energy that must be transferred to 0.50 kg of water to raise its temperature from 20 °C to 80 °C.

(b) Calculate the rate at which energy is conducted through the window pane.

(c) The pane is replaced by a pane of the same glass and area but twice the thickness, and the temperature difference across it becomes 20 °C. Determine the new rate of energy conduction.

(d) Equal masses of aluminum and copper each absorb the same amount of energy. Which block has the larger temperature increase? Determine the ratio of the copper block's temperature increase to the aluminum block's temperature increase.
items.stimulus:
Specific heats: water 4190 J/(kg·°C), aluminum 900 J/(kg·°C), copper 385 J/(kg·°C).

A glass window pane has area 1.2 m², thickness 4.0 × 10⁻³ m, and thermal conductivity 0.80 W/(m·K). The inner surface of the glass is at 15 °C and the outer surface is at 5 °C, and these temperatures stay constant. Specific heats are independent of temperature.
items.answer:
(a) Q = mcΔT = (0.50 kg)(4190 J/(kg·°C))(80 °C − 20 °C) = (0.50)(4190)(60) = 125,700 J ≈ 1.26 × 10⁵ J.

(b) ΔT = 15 °C − 5 °C = 10 °C, which is a difference of 10 K.
Q/Δt = kAΔT/L = (0.80 W/(m·K))(1.2 m²)(10 K)/(4.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 2400 W.

(c) The rate is proportional to ΔT and inversely proportional to L. ΔT doubles (10 °C to 20 °C), multiplying the rate by 2, and L doubles, multiplying the rate by 1/2. The net factor is 1, so the rate is unchanged: 2400 W.

(d) ΔT = Q/(mc). With the same Q and m, ΔT is inversely proportional to c. Copper has the smaller specific heat, so copper has the larger temperature increase.
ΔT_Cu/ΔT_Al = c_Al/c_Cu = 900/385 ≈ 2.3.

criteria.text: Calculates Q = mcΔT = (0.50 kg)(4190 J/(kg·°C))(60 °C) ≈ 1.26 × 10⁵ J.
criteria.evidence: Response uses ΔT = 60 °C and obtains 125,700 J (about 1.26 × 10⁵ J).
criteria.fix: Use the temperature change, not a single temperature, in Q = mcΔT, and check the units of c.

criteria.evidence: Response uses ΔT = 10 K (or 10 °C) and L = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m to obtain 2400 W (2.4 × 10³ W).
criteria.fix: In Q/Δt = kAΔT/L use the temperature difference across the material and its thickness in meters.

criteria.text: Finds the new rate is 2400 W (unchanged): doubling ΔT doubles the rate while doubling L halves it.
criteria.evidence: Response obtains 2400 W either by applying the factors (2 for ΔT, 1/2 for L) or by substituting ΔT = 20 K and L = 8.0 × 10⁻³ m into kAΔT/L.
criteria.fix: The rate is proportional to ΔT and inversely proportional to thickness; apply both changes as factors, or substitute the new values directly.

criteria.text: States that the copper block has the larger temperature increase.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies copper as the block with the larger temperature increase.
criteria.fix: With the same energy and mass, ΔT = Q/(mc), so the material with the smaller specific heat warms more.

criteria.text: Determines ΔT_Cu/ΔT_Al = c_Al/c_Cu = 900/385 ≈ 2.3.
criteria.evidence: Response uses ΔT = Q/(mc) with equal Q and m to obtain a ratio c_Al/c_Cu of about 2.3.
criteria.fix: Write ΔT = Q/(mc) for each block, divide the two expressions, and cancel Q and m to leave a ratio of specific heats.

items.title: Entropy Changes in an Isolated and a Closed System
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) For System 1, state whether the total entropy of the two blocks increases, decreases, or stays the same as they approach the common temperature. Justify your answer using the second law of thermodynamics.

(b) Explain why the blocks will not spontaneously return to temperatures of 90 °C and 10 °C.

(c) The entropy of the water in System 2 decreases as it freezes. A student says this violates the second law of thermodynamics. Evaluate the student's claim.

(d) For System 1, a second student claims that if the blocks had reached the same final state by a slower process, the entropy of that final state would be different. Evaluate this claim.
items.stimulus:
System 1: Two copper blocks, one at 90 °C and one at 10 °C, are placed in contact inside a closed, perfectly insulated container. The two blocks together form an isolated system, and they eventually reach a common final temperature.

System 2: A tray of liquid water is placed in a freezer, and the water freezes into ice. Energy is transferred between the water and the air in the freezer, but no matter enters or leaves the water.
items.answer:
(a) The total entropy increases. The two blocks form an isolated system, and energy spreads spontaneously from the hot block to the cold block. This process is irreversible. The second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases and stays constant only when every process is reversible, so the entropy of the blocks increases.

(b) The equal-temperature state is thermodynamic equilibrium, where the entropy of the isolated system is at its maximum. Returning to 90 °C and 10 °C would require the energy to become concentrated again and the total entropy of the isolated system to decrease, which the second law does not allow. So this never happens spontaneously.

(c) The claim is incorrect. The water is a closed system, not an isolated one: energy is transferred out of the water to the air in the freezer. The entropy of a closed system can decrease when energy is transferred out of it. If the water is combined with its surroundings (the freezer and the room it operates in) to form an isolated system, the total entropy of that larger system does not decrease, so the second law is satisfied.

(d) The claim is incorrect. Entropy is a state function, so it depends only on the current state of the system, not on how the system reached it. The same final state of the two blocks has the same entropy whether it was reached quickly or slowly.

criteria.text: States that the total entropy increases, because the blocks form an isolated system undergoing an irreversible process (energy spreading from the hot block to the cold block), and the second law says entropy of an isolated system stays constant only for reversible processes.
criteria.evidence: Response answers 'increases' and justifies it by citing the isolated system, the irreversible (spontaneous) energy transfer or spreading of energy, and the second law.
criteria.fix: Identify the system as isolated, decide whether the process is reversible, then apply the second law's rule for isolated systems.

criteria.text: Explains that returning to 90 °C and 10 °C would decrease the total entropy of the isolated system, which the second law forbids; the equal-temperature equilibrium state has the maximum entropy.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the reverse process would require the isolated system's entropy to decrease (or to leave its maximum-entropy equilibrium state), which cannot happen.
criteria.fix: Ask what the reverse process would do to the isolated system's entropy, and compare that with what the second law allows.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect because the water is a closed system, not an isolated one: energy is transferred out of it to its surroundings, so its entropy can decrease.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and identifies the water as closed (exchanging energy with the freezer air), not isolated.
criteria.fix: Before applying the second law, check whether the system is isolated; a closed system that loses energy can lose entropy.

criteria.text: States that the total entropy of a larger isolated system that includes the water and its surroundings does not decrease, so the second law is satisfied.
criteria.evidence: Response explains that when the surroundings (freezer and room) are included to make an isolated system, the total entropy does not decrease.
criteria.fix: Enlarge the system until it is isolated, then apply the second law to that total entropy.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect because entropy is a state function: it depends only on the current state of the system, not on the process used to reach it.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and explains that entropy depends only on the state (temperature, configuration), not on the path or speed of the process.
criteria.fix: Recall that entropy is a state function; for any claim about a final state, ask whether the final state itself changed.
