items.title: Extrema and Inflection of a Polynomial on a Restricted Domain
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) On the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 10, identify every input value at which p has a local maximum and every input value at which p has a local minimum. Give a reason for each.

(b) Find the global maximum value and the global minimum value of p on its domain. Explain why p(3) is not the global minimum value of p.

(c) Identify the input values at which the graph of p has a point of inflection. Then state whether the graph of p is concave up or concave down for 6 < x < 10. Give a reason for each answer based on the rate of change of p.
items.stimulus:
Let p be the polynomial function defined by p(x) = −3x⁴ + 44x³ − 144x² + 200, with its domain restricted to 0 ≤ x ≤ 10. The following information about p is known.
• p is decreasing for 0 < x < 3, increasing for 3 < x < 8, and decreasing for 8 < x < 10.
• The rate of change of p is decreasing for 0 < x < 4/3, increasing for 4/3 < x < 6, and decreasing for 6 < x < 10.
The table gives selected values of p.
x | 0 | 3 | 8 | 10
p(x) | 200 | −151 | 1224 | −200
items.answer:
(a) Local maximums: at x = 0, because x = 0 is an included endpoint and p is decreasing for 0 < x < 3, so p(0) is greater than nearby outputs; and at x = 8, because p switches from increasing to decreasing there.
Local minimums: at x = 3, because p switches from decreasing to increasing there; and at x = 10, because x = 10 is an included endpoint and p is decreasing for 8 < x < 10, so p(10) is less than nearby outputs.

(b) The local maximum values are p(0) = 200 and p(8) = 1224. Since 1224 > 200, the global maximum value is 1224, at x = 8.
The local minimum values are p(3) = −151 and p(10) = −200. Since −200 < −151, the global minimum value is −200, at x = 10. So p(3) = −151 is only a local minimum, because p(10) = −200 is smaller.

(c) The rate of change of p switches from decreasing to increasing at x = 4/3 and from increasing to decreasing at x = 6, so the graph of p has points of inflection at x = 4/3 and x = 6.
For 6 < x < 10, the rate of change of p is decreasing, so the graph of p is concave down there.

criteria.text: Local maximums at x = 0 (an included endpoint, with p decreasing immediately after it) and at x = 8 (p switches from increasing to decreasing).
criteria.evidence: Response lists both x = 0 and x = 8 as local maximum locations with a correct reason for each.
criteria.fix: Check included endpoints as well as inputs where p switches between increasing and decreasing.

criteria.text: Local minimums at x = 3 (p switches from decreasing to increasing) and at x = 10 (an included endpoint, with p decreasing just before it).
criteria.evidence: Response lists both x = 3 and x = 10 as local minimum locations with a correct reason for each.
criteria.fix: At a right endpoint, a function that is decreasing up to that endpoint has a local minimum there.

criteria.text: The global maximum value is 1224 (it occurs at x = 8 and exceeds the other local maximum value, p(0) = 200).
criteria.evidence: Response gives the global maximum value 1224. The input x = 8 and a comparison with p(0) are not required.
criteria.fix: Compare the output values at every local maximum, including endpoints; the largest one is the global maximum.

criteria.text: The global minimum value is −200; p(3) = −151 is not the global minimum because p(10) = −200 is less than −151.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the global minimum value −200 and explains that p(3) = −151 is not the least value because p(10) = −200 is smaller. The input x = 10 is not required.
criteria.fix: Compare the output values at every local minimum, including endpoints; a local minimum is global only if it is the least.

criteria.text: Points of inflection at x = 4/3 and x = 6, because the rate of change of p switches from decreasing to increasing at x = 4/3 and from increasing to decreasing at x = 6.
criteria.evidence: Response gives both x = 4/3 and x = 6 and states that the rate of change of p changes between increasing and decreasing at each.
criteria.fix: Look for inputs where the rate of change switches between increasing and decreasing; those are the points of inflection.

criteria.text: Concave down for 6 < x < 10, because the rate of change of p is decreasing there.
criteria.evidence: Response states concave down on 6 < x < 10 and cites the decreasing rate of change.
criteria.fix: A decreasing rate of change means concave down; an increasing rate of change means concave up.

items.title: Zeros and Sign of a Rational Function
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find all real zeros of r. Explain why each value you give is a zero of r.

(b) The real zeros of the numerator and the real zeros of the denominator of r divide the real number line into intervals. List these values in increasing order, and determine whether r(x) is positive or negative on each interval.

(c) Solve the inequality r(x) ≥ 0. Give your answer as a union of intervals, and explain which of the values from the previous part are included.
items.stimulus: Let r be the rational function defined by r(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x² − 4x − 5).
items.answer:
(a) The numerator factors as x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), which is 0 at x = 3 and x = −2. The denominator factors as x² − 4x − 5 = (x − 5)(x + 1), which is 0 only at x = 5 and x = −1, so it is not zero at x = −2 (value 7) or at x = 3 (value −8). Both values are in the domain of r and make the numerator 0, so the real zeros of r are x = −2 and x = 3.

(b) r(x) = (x − 3)(x + 2)/((x − 5)(x + 1)). The dividing values are −2, −1, 3, 5.
x < −2: factors (−)(−)/((−)(−)), so r(x) > 0.
−2 < x < −1: (−)(+)/((−)(−)), so r(x) < 0.
−1 < x < 3: (−)(+)/((−)(+)), so r(x) > 0.
3 < x < 5: (+)(+)/((−)(+)), so r(x) < 0.
x > 5: all factors positive, so r(x) > 0.

(c) r(x) > 0 on x < −2, −1 < x < 3 and x > 5. The values x = −2 and x = 3 are included because r(x) = 0 there, which satisfies r(x) ≥ 0. The values x = −1 and x = 5 are excluded because the denominator is 0 there, so r is undefined. The solution is (−∞, −2] ∪ (−1, 3] ∪ (5, ∞).

criteria.text: Finds the numerator zeros x = 3 and x = −2 (for example, x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2)).
criteria.evidence: Response sets x² − x − 6 = 0 and finds x = 3 and x = −2 by any valid method, such as factoring, the quadratic formula or completing the square.
criteria.fix: Find the real zeros of the numerator first; those are the only possible zeros of a rational function.

criteria.text: Confirms that x = −2 and x = 3 are in the domain of r because the denominator is not zero there, so both are zeros of r.
criteria.evidence: Response checks the denominator: (−2)² − 4(−2) − 5 = 7 and 3² − 4(3) − 5 = −8 (or notes the denominator zeros are 5 and −1), so r(−2) = 0 and r(3) = 0.
criteria.fix: After finding numerator zeros, substitute each into the denominator to confirm it is nonzero before calling it a zero.

criteria.text: Lists the values −2, −1, 3 and 5, where −1 and 5 are the real zeros of the denominator x² − 4x − 5.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the denominator zeros x = 5 and x = −1 by any valid method (factoring as (x − 5)(x + 1) or the quadratic formula) and lists −2, −1, 3, 5 in order.
criteria.fix: Find the real zeros of both numerator and denominator, then list all of them in increasing order as the dividing points.

criteria.text: Gives the signs: r(x) > 0 for x < −2, r(x) < 0 for −2 < x < −1, r(x) > 0 for −1 < x < 3, r(x) < 0 for 3 < x < 5, r(x) > 0 for x > 5.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the correct sign of r(x) on all five intervals. Supporting work is not required.
criteria.fix: Test one value in each interval in the factored form, counting negative factors to get the sign of r.

criteria.evidence: Response gives exactly this union of intervals, or the equivalent inequalities x ≤ −2 or −1 < x ≤ 3 or x > 5.
criteria.fix: Combine the intervals where r is positive with the zeros of r, then write the union with correct brackets.

criteria.text: Explains that −2 and 3 are included because r equals 0 there, which satisfies r(x) ≥ 0, while −1 and 5 are excluded because r is undefined there.
criteria.evidence: Response justifies including the zeros of r and excluding the zeros of the denominator.
criteria.fix: Include zeros of the numerator for a ≥ inequality; always exclude inputs that make the denominator zero.

items.title: Comparing an Arithmetic and a Geometric Sequence
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the common difference of the sequence a, and write an expression for aₙ in terms of n.

(b) Find the common ratio of the sequence g, and write an expression for gₙ in terms of n.

(c) Find a₃ − a₂, a₄ − a₃, g₃ − g₂ and g₄ − g₃. Use these values to explain how the change from one term to the next differs between the two sequences.
items.stimulus: The sequence a is arithmetic, with a₂ = 17 and a₅ = 32. The sequence g is geometric, all of its terms are positive, and g₁ = 12 and g₃ = 27. Both sequences are defined for the whole numbers n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
items.answer:
(a) From n = 2 to n = 5 there are 3 steps, so d = (32 − 17)/3 = 15/3 = 5.
a₀ = a₂ − 2d = 17 − 10 = 7, so aₙ = 7 + 5n.

(b) g₃ = g₁·r², so r² = 27/12 = 9/4. Since all terms are positive, r = 3/2.
g₀ = g₁/r = 12/(3/2) = 8, so gₙ = 8(3/2)ⁿ.

(c) a₂ = 17, a₃ = 22, a₄ = 27, so a₃ − a₂ = 5 and a₄ − a₃ = 5.
g₂ = 8(3/2)² = 18, g₃ = 27, g₄ = 8(3/2)⁴ = 40.5, so g₃ − g₂ = 9 and g₄ − g₃ = 13.5.
The arithmetic sequence increases by the same amount, 5, at every step. The geometric sequence has positive terms and ratio 3/2 > 1, so it increases by a larger amount at each successive step (9, then 13.5).

criteria.text: The common difference is d = (32 − 17)/(5 − 2) = 5.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the change in terms, 15, by the 3 steps from n = 2 to n = 5 to get d = 5.
criteria.fix: Divide the change between two known terms by the number of steps between their indices.

criteria.evidence: Response gives aₙ = 7 + 5n or an equivalent form such as aₙ = 17 + 5(n − 2); finding a₀ = 7 is not required.
criteria.fix: Use aₙ = aₖ + d(n − k) with a known term, or find a₀ by stepping back to n = 0.

criteria.text: The common ratio is 3/2, because r² = 27/12 = 9/4 and r must be positive since all terms are positive.
criteria.evidence: Response obtains r = 3/2 by a valid method, for example solving g₁r² = g₃ to get r² = 9/4 and using the positive terms to reject −3/2, or g₂ = √(12·27) = 18.
criteria.fix: Two steps between g₁ and g₃ means dividing gives r²; use the sign information to choose the root.

criteria.evidence: Response gives gₙ = 8(3/2)ⁿ, with g₀ = 12/(3/2) = 8, or an equivalent form such as gₙ = 12(3/2)^(n − 1).
criteria.fix: Use gₙ = gₖ·r^(n − k) with a known term, or divide g₁ by r to find g₀.

criteria.text: a₃ − a₂ = 5, a₄ − a₃ = 5, g₃ − g₂ = 9 and g₄ − g₃ = 13.5.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the four differences 5, 5, 9 and 13.5, by computing the terms (a₃ = 22, a₄ = 27, g₂ = 18, g₄ = 40.5) or by any valid method, such as using d = 5 and g₄ = (3/2)g₃.
criteria.fix: Subtract consecutive terms, found from your formulas, or use the common difference and the common ratio directly.

criteria.text: Explains that the arithmetic sequence increases by the same amount (5) each step, while the geometric sequence of positive terms with ratio 3/2 increases by a larger amount each step.
criteria.evidence: Response contrasts a constant change for a with a growing change for g, referring to the computed differences.
criteria.fix: State that arithmetic sequences change by a constant difference, while increasing geometric sequences change by increasing amounts.

items.title: Key Characteristics of Exponential Functions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Does f demonstrate exponential growth or exponential decay? Explain. Then describe the behavior of f(x) as x increases without bound and as x decreases without bound.

(b) Find the maximum value and the minimum value of f on the closed interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3, and give the input value at which each occurs. Explain how you know where they occur.

(c) Show that the output values of h are not proportional over the equal-length input intervals in the table, but that the values of h(x) − 4 are. Then write an expression for h(x), as an additive transformation of an exponential function, that agrees with every value in the table.
items.stimulus:
Let f be the function defined by f(x) = 5(0.8)ˣ.

The function h is defined for all real numbers. The table gives selected values of h.
x | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3
h(x) | 7 | 10 | 16 | 28
items.answer:
(a) f is in the form a·bˣ with a = 5 > 0 and b = 0.8, where 0 < 0.8 < 1, so f demonstrates exponential decay.
As x increases without bound, (0.8)ˣ gets arbitrarily close to 0, so lim x→∞ f(x) = 0. As x decreases without bound, (0.8)ˣ = (1.25)^(−x) increases without bound, so lim x→−∞ f(x) = ∞.

(b) Because f is exponential decay, it is always decreasing. So on −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 its maximum is at the left endpoint and its minimum is at the right endpoint.
Maximum: f(−2) = 5(0.8)^(−2) = 5/0.64 = 7.8125, at x = −2.
Minimum: f(3) = 5(0.8)³ = 5(0.512) = 2.56, at x = 3.

(c) For h: 10/7 ≈ 1.43 and 16/10 = 1.6. These ratios are not equal, so the outputs of h are not proportional over equal-length intervals.
For h(x) − 4 the values are 3, 6, 12, 24, and 6/3 = 12/6 = 24/12 = 2, so these outputs are proportional with ratio 2.
So h(x) − 4 = 3(2)ˣ, and h(x) = 3(2)ˣ + 4. Check: 3 + 4 = 7, 6 + 4 = 10, 12 + 4 = 16, 24 + 4 = 28.

criteria.text: Exponential decay, because the initial value a = 5 is positive and the base b = 0.8 satisfies 0 < b < 1.
criteria.evidence: Response says decay and cites both a > 0 and 0 < b < 1.
criteria.fix: Check both conditions in the general form a·bˣ: the sign of a and whether b is between 0 and 1.

criteria.text: As x increases without bound, f(x) approaches 0 (lim x→∞ f(x) = 0); as x decreases without bound, f(x) increases without bound (lim x→−∞ f(x) = ∞).
criteria.evidence: Response gives both end behaviors correctly, in words or with limit notation.
criteria.fix: Test large positive and large negative inputs: (0.8)ˣ shrinks toward 0 for large x and grows without bound for very negative x.

criteria.text: Maximum value 7.8125 at x = −2, because f is always decreasing, so its largest output on the interval is at the left endpoint.
criteria.evidence: Response computes f(−2) = 5/(0.8)² = 5/0.64 = 7.8125 and explains the locations by f being always decreasing (or another valid reason), so the extremes are at the endpoints.
criteria.fix: For an always-decreasing exponential on a closed interval, evaluate at the left endpoint for the maximum.

criteria.text: Minimum value 2.56 at x = 3.
criteria.evidence: Response computes f(3) = 5(0.8)³ = 5(0.512) = 2.56 and identifies x = 3 as the location of the minimum.
criteria.fix: Evaluate the decreasing function at the right endpoint for the minimum, and compute 0.8³ = 0.512 carefully.

criteria.text: Shows 10/7 ≠ 16/10, so h is not proportional, while h(x) − 4 gives 3, 6, 12, 24, with constant ratio 2.
criteria.evidence: Response computes at least two unequal ratios of consecutive h values and the constant ratio 2 for consecutive values of h(x) − 4.
criteria.fix: Test proportional change by dividing consecutive outputs; repeat after subtracting the given constant from each output.

criteria.evidence: Response writes h(x) = 3·2ˣ + 4, with initial value 3 = h(0) − 4 and base 2.
criteria.fix: Write the exponential for h(x) − 4 using its value at x = 0 and its ratio, then add 4 back.

items.title: Rewriting Exponential Expressions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Rewrite f(x) in the form a·2ˣ, where a is a constant. Then describe the horizontal translation of y = 2ˣ that gives the graph of f, and the vertical dilation of y = 2ˣ that gives the same graph.

(b) Rewrite g(x) in the form bˣ, where b is a positive constant. Show how the value of b is found.

(c) Rewrite h(x) in the form a·bˣ, where a and b are positive constants. Show the properties of exponents you use.
items.stimulus:
Let f, g and h be the functions defined by
f(x) = 2^(x + 3)
g(x) = 16^(3x/4)
h(x) = 3·4^(1/2 − x)
items.answer:
(a) f(x) = 2^(x + 3) = 2ˣ·2³ = 8·2ˣ by the product property.
The graph of f is the graph of y = 2ˣ translated 3 units to the left. Because f(x) = 8·2ˣ, the same graph is also the graph of y = 2ˣ vertically dilated by a factor of 8.

(b) By the power property, g(x) = 16^(3x/4) = (16^(3/4))ˣ.
16^(3/4) = (fourth root of 16)³ = 2³ = 8.
So g(x) = 8ˣ, with b = 8.

(c) By the product property, h(x) = 3·4^(1/2)·4^(−x).
4^(1/2) is the square root of 4, which is 2, so 3·4^(1/2) = 6.
By the negative exponent property, 4^(−x) = 1/4ˣ = (1/4)ˣ.
So h(x) = 6(1/4)ˣ, with a = 6 and b = 1/4.

criteria.text: f(x) = 8·2ˣ, using the product property of exponents (2^(x + 3) = 2ˣ·2³).
criteria.evidence: Response gives f(x) = 8·2ˣ or an equivalent form such as 8(2ˣ); writing the step 2ˣ·2³ is not required.
criteria.fix: Split a sum in the exponent into a product of powers with the same base: b^(m + n) = bᵐ·bⁿ.

criteria.text: The graph of f is the graph of y = 2ˣ translated 3 units to the left, which is the same as a vertical dilation of y = 2ˣ by a factor of 8.
criteria.evidence: Response states both: horizontal translation 3 units left, and vertical dilation by a factor of 8.
criteria.fix: Read x + 3 inside the exponent as a shift left 3, and read the constant 8 in front as a vertical dilation.

criteria.text: Rewrites g(x) as a constant base raised to the power x, such as (16^(3/4))ˣ or (2³)ˣ, using the power property of exponents.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a valid power-property step, for example 16^(3x/4) = (16^(3/4))ˣ or 16^(3x/4) = (2⁴)^(3x/4) = 2^(3x) = (2³)ˣ.
criteria.fix: Use (bᵐ)ⁿ = b^(mn) to move the factor multiplying x out of the exponent and into the base.

criteria.text: b = 8, so g(x) = 8ˣ.
criteria.evidence: Response evaluates 16^(3/4) = (fourth root of 16)³ = 2³ = 8, or 2³ = 8, and writes g(x) = 8ˣ.
criteria.fix: Evaluate a fractional exponent by taking the root first, here the fourth root of 16, then raising to the power.

criteria.text: Finds a = 6 using properties of exponents, for example h(x) = 3·4^(1/2)·4^(−x) with 4^(1/2) = 2.
criteria.evidence: Response shows valid exponent-property work giving a = 6, such as 3·4^(1/2)·4^(−x) with 4^(1/2) = 2, or 3·2^(1 − 2x) = 6·2^(−2x).
criteria.fix: Separate the constant part of the exponent with the product property, then evaluate it, for example 4^(1/2) as a square root.

criteria.text: Rewrites 4^(−x) as (1/4)ˣ, giving h(x) = 6(1/4)ˣ.
criteria.evidence: Response uses a negative exponent property, such as 4^(−x) = 1/4ˣ = (1/4)ˣ or 2^(−2x) = (2^(−2))ˣ = (1/4)ˣ, and writes h(x) = 6(1/4)ˣ or 6(0.25)ˣ.
criteria.fix: Use b^(−n) = 1/bⁿ to turn a negative exponent into a base between 0 and 1.

items.title: Validating Models for App Growth with Residuals
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the residual of L at t = 3 and the residual of E at t = 3. Give each answer to three decimal places.

(b) Using the pattern in all six residuals of each model, explain which model is more appropriate for these data.

(c) The developer will use E to decide how much server capacity to buy. Having too little capacity causes the app to crash, while extra capacity costs little. Does E overestimate or underestimate the number of active users at t = 4? Explain whether overestimates or underestimates are preferable in this context.
items.stimulus:
An app developer recorded the number of active users U, in thousands, t months after the app's launch.
t (months) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
U (thousands) | 11.9 | 15.2 | 18.9 | 23.2 | 29.6 | 36.4

Using regression on these data, the developer found a linear model L(t) = 4.857t + 10.390 and an exponential model E(t) = 12.027(1.249)ᵗ. The coefficients are rounded to three decimal places; use the models exactly as written. The residuals of each model, except those at t = 3, are listed below (in thousands of users).
t (months) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Residual for L | 1.510 | −0.047 | −1.204 | ? | −0.218 | 1.725
Residual for E | −0.127 | 0.178 | 0.138 | ? | 0.331 | −0.157
items.answer:
(a) L(3) = 4.857(3) + 10.390 = 24.961, so the residual of L at t = 3 is 23.2 − 24.961 = −1.761.
E(3) = 12.027(1.249)³ ≈ 23.434, so the residual of E at t = 3 is 23.2 − 23.434 ≈ −0.234.

(b) The residuals of L in order of t are 1.510, −0.047, −1.204, −1.761, −0.218, 1.725: positive at both ends and negative in the middle. This systematic pattern means the linear model is not appropriate.
The residuals of E are −0.127, 0.178, 0.138, −0.234, 0.331, −0.157. They switch between positive and negative with no systematic pattern, so the exponential model E is more appropriate for these data.

(c) E(4) = 12.027(1.249)⁴ ≈ 29.269, and the residual is 29.6 − 29.269 ≈ 0.331 > 0. The actual value is greater than the predicted value, so E underestimates the number of active users at t = 4.
Overestimates are preferable. If the model overestimates users, the developer buys a little extra capacity, which costs little. If it underestimates, the developer may buy too little capacity and the app could crash.

criteria.text: The residual of L at t = 3 is 23.2 − L(3) = 23.2 − 24.961 = −1.761.
criteria.evidence: Response computes L(3) = 24.961 and the residual as actual minus predicted, −1.761.
criteria.fix: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value; compute the model value first, then subtract it from the data.

criteria.text: The residual of E at t = 3 is 23.2 − E(3) ≈ 23.2 − 23.434 = −0.234.
criteria.evidence: Response computes E(3) = 12.027(1.249)³ ≈ 23.434 and the residual −0.234 (actual minus predicted).
criteria.fix: Evaluate the exponential model without rounding the power early, then subtract the prediction from the actual value.

criteria.text: States that the residuals of L show a pattern: positive at t = 0 and t = 5 and negative for t = 1 through t = 4, so L is not appropriate.
criteria.evidence: Response describes the systematic sign pattern of the linear residuals (positive at both ends, negative in the middle) and concludes the linear model is not appropriate.
criteria.fix: Look at the signs of the residuals in order of t; a systematic arrangement such as positive, negative, positive shows a poor model.

criteria.text: States that the residuals of E, −0.127, 0.178, 0.138, −0.234, 0.331, −0.157, change sign without a pattern, so E is the more appropriate model.
criteria.evidence: Response notes the exponential residuals mix positive and negative values with no systematic pattern and concludes the exponential model is more appropriate.
criteria.fix: A model is justified as appropriate when its residuals, listed in order of t, appear without any pattern.

criteria.text: E underestimates at t = 4, because the residual 0.331 is positive (actual 29.6 is greater than predicted E(4) ≈ 29.269).
criteria.evidence: Response says underestimate and connects it to the positive residual, or to the actual value exceeding the predicted value.
criteria.fix: A positive residual means actual is greater than predicted, so the model underestimates; a negative residual means it overestimates.

criteria.text: Overestimates are preferable, because overestimating users leads to buying extra capacity, which costs little, while underestimating could leave too little capacity and make the app crash.
criteria.evidence: Response chooses overestimates and gives the contextual reason comparing the cost of too little and too much capacity.
criteria.fix: Compare the consequences of each error in the context, and prefer the error whose consequence is less harmful.

items.title: Evaluating, Building and Decomposing Composite Functions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find f(g(1)) and g(f(1)). What do your results show about the order in which two functions are composed?

(b) Write an expression for f(g(x)) and find the domain of the composite function f∘g. Explain why each excluded value is excluded.

(c) Write k as a composition u(v(x)) of two functions u and v, neither of which is the identity function. Then write w as a composition of t and f, and explain why composing them in the other order does not give w.
items.stimulus:
Let f and g be the functions defined by f(x) = 1/(x − 3) and g(x) = x² − 1.
Let k be the function defined by k(x) = (2x + 5)³.
Let w be the function defined by w(x) = f(x) + 7, and let t be the function defined by t(x) = x + 7.
items.answer:
(a) g(1) = 1² − 1 = 0, so f(g(1)) = f(0) = 1/(0 − 3) = −1/3.
f(1) = 1/(1 − 3) = −1/2, so g(f(1)) = (−1/2)² − 1 = 1/4 − 1 = −3/4.
Since −1/3 ≠ −3/4, f(g(1)) ≠ g(f(1)). The order of composition matters: composition of functions is not commutative.

(b) f(g(x)) = 1/(g(x) − 3) = 1/((x² − 1) − 3) = 1/(x² − 4).
g is defined for all real numbers, but g(x) must be in the domain of f, so g(x) ≠ 3. g(x) = 3 means x² − 1 = 3, so x² = 4 and x = 2 or x = −2. The domain of f∘g is all real numbers except x = 2 and x = −2.

(c) Let v(x) = 2x + 5 and u(x) = x³. Then u(v(x)) = (2x + 5)³ = k(x).
w(x) = f(x) + 7 = t(f(x)), so w = t∘f.
In the other order, f(t(x)) = 1/((x + 7) − 3) = 1/(x + 4), which is not equal to f(x) + 7 (for example, at x = 0, f(t(0)) = 1/4 while w(0) = −1/3 + 7 = 20/3). So only t∘f gives w.

criteria.evidence: Response evaluates g(1) = 0 first and then f(0) = −1/3.
criteria.fix: Evaluate the inner function first, then use its output as the input of the outer function.

criteria.text: g(f(1)) = −3/4, since f(1) = −1/2 and g(−1/2) = 1/4 − 1 = −3/4; the two results differ, so composition is not commutative (order matters).
criteria.evidence: Response obtains −3/4 and states that f(g(1)) ≠ g(f(1)), so changing the order of composition changes the result.
criteria.fix: Compute both orders separately and compare; composition generally gives different results when the order is reversed.

criteria.evidence: Response substitutes g(x) for x in f to get 1/((x² − 1) − 3) and simplifies to 1/(x² − 4).
criteria.fix: Replace every x in f with the whole expression g(x), using parentheses, then simplify the denominator.

criteria.text: The domain is all real x except x = 2 and x = −2, because g(2) = g(−2) = 3, and 3 is not in the domain of f.
criteria.evidence: Response excludes exactly x = ±2 and explains that these inputs make g(x) = 3, where f is undefined, or equivalently make the denominator (x² − 1) − 3 = x² − 4 equal 0.
criteria.fix: Exclude inputs whose inner output falls outside the domain of the outer function; solve g(x) = 3.

criteria.text: Gives a valid decomposition, such as v(x) = 2x + 5 and u(x) = x³, so that u(v(x)) = (2x + 5)³ = k(x).
criteria.evidence: Response names u and v explicitly, neither equal to x, and u(v(x)) simplifies to (2x + 5)³. Any valid pair, such as v(x) = 2x and u(x) = (x + 5)³, is accepted.
criteria.fix: Identify the inner expression that is being operated on, call it v(x), and let u describe what is done to it.

criteria.text: w(x) = t(f(x)), that is w = t∘f; the other order gives f(t(x)) = 1/(x + 4), which is not w.
criteria.evidence: Response writes w = t∘f (adding 7 to the output of f) and shows the reverse order differs, for example f(t(x)) = 1/(x + 4) ≠ f(x) + 7, a numerical counterexample, or different domains.
criteria.fix: A vertical translation adds to the output, so t must be applied after f; check the reverse order by substituting.

items.title: Evaluating Logarithms and Reading a Logarithmic Scale
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact values of log₄ 64 and log₉ (1/3). For each, state the exponential equation that confirms your answer.

(b) Without a calculator, find the two consecutive integers between which log₂ 20 lies, and the two consecutive integers between which log 0.05 lies. Explain each answer.

(c) On the logarithmic scale described above, find the position of the value 0.001. Point P is at position 1.7 and point Q is at position 4.7. How many times as large as the value at P is the value at Q? Explain.
items.stimulus:
In this question, log v with no base written means the common logarithm, base 10.

A number line is marked with a base-10 logarithmic scale: each positive value v is placed at position log v. For example, the value 100 is placed at position 2, and the value 1 is placed at position 0.
items.answer:
(a) log₄ 64 = 3, because 4³ = 64.
log₉ (1/3) = −1/2, because 9^(1/2) = 3, so 9^(−1/2) = 1/3.

(b) 2⁴ = 16 and 2⁵ = 32. Since 16 < 20 < 32, the exponent that turns 2 into 20 is between 4 and 5, so log₂ 20 lies between 4 and 5.
10^(−2) = 0.01 and 10^(−1) = 0.1. Since 0.01 < 0.05 < 0.1, log 0.05 lies between −2 and −1.

(c) 0.001 = 10^(−3), so the value 0.001 is at position log 0.001 = −3.
Q is 4.7 − 1.7 = 3 units to the right of P. On a base-10 logarithmic scale each unit represents multiplication by 10, so the value at Q is 10³ = 1000 times the value at P. (Equivalently, 10^4.7 / 10^1.7 = 10³ = 1000.)

criteria.text: log₄ 64 = 3, because 4³ = 64.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 3 and the confirming equation 4³ = 64.
criteria.fix: Ask what power of the base gives the argument, and confirm by writing base^answer = argument.

criteria.evidence: Response gives −1/2 and the confirming equation 9^(−1/2) = 1/3 (since the square root of 9 is 3 and the negative exponent gives the reciprocal).
criteria.fix: A square root of the base is exponent 1/2, and a reciprocal is a negative exponent; combine them.

criteria.text: log₂ 20 is between 4 and 5, because 2⁴ = 16 < 20 < 32 = 2⁵.
criteria.evidence: Response names 4 and 5 and brackets 20 between the powers 2⁴ = 16 and 2⁵ = 32.
criteria.fix: List consecutive powers of the base until you pass the argument; the exponents on either side bound the logarithm.

criteria.evidence: Response names −2 and −1 and brackets 0.05 between 0.01 = 10^(−2) and 0.1 = 10^(−1).
criteria.fix: For a value between 0 and 1, write nearby powers of 10 with negative exponents, such as 0.01 and 0.1.

criteria.text: The value 0.001 is at position −3, because 0.001 = 10^(−3).
criteria.evidence: Response gives −3 and writes 0.001 as 10^(−3) (or states log 0.001 = −3).
criteria.fix: Write the value as a power of 10; the exponent is its position on a base-10 logarithmic scale.

criteria.text: The value at Q is 1000 times the value at P, because Q is 3 units to the right of P and each unit on a base-10 logarithmic scale represents multiplication by 10, so the factor is 10³ = 1000.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1000 and explains it from the 3-unit gap with each unit a factor of 10 (or from 10^4.7/10^1.7 = 10³).
criteria.fix: Find the distance between positions, then raise 10 to that distance; each unit is a factor of 10, not an added amount.

items.title: Values, Asymptotes and Range of Secant and Cotangent
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact values of sec(2π/3) and cot(7π/6). Show the work that leads to each answer.

(b) Find all values of θ in the interval 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π at which the graph of y = cot θ has a vertical asymptote, and give a reason. Then state whether cot θ is increasing or decreasing on the interval between the first two of these values.

(c) Explain why the equation sec θ = 1/2 has no solution. Then give the range of y = sec θ.
items.stimulus: This question concerns the functions y = sec θ and y = cot θ. Give exact values.
items.answer:
(a) sec(2π/3) = 1/cos(2π/3). The angle 2π/3 is in quadrant II with reference angle π/3, so cos(2π/3) = −1/2. Therefore sec(2π/3) = 1/(−1/2) = −2.
cot(7π/6) = cos(7π/6)/sin(7π/6). The angle 7π/6 is in quadrant III with reference angle π/6, so cos(7π/6) = −√3/2 and sin(7π/6) = −1/2. Therefore cot(7π/6) = (−√3/2)/(−1/2) = √3.

(b) cot θ = cos θ/sin θ, so the graph has vertical asymptotes where sin θ = 0 (where tan θ = 0), since cos θ is ±1 there. In 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π this happens at θ = 0, θ = π and θ = 2π.
Between the consecutive asymptotes θ = 0 and θ = π, cot θ is decreasing. (For example, cot(π/4) = 1 and cot(3π/4) = −1.)

(c) sec θ = 1/cos θ, and −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1 with cos θ ≠ 0 wherever secant is defined, so |sec θ| = 1/|cos θ| ≥ 1. A value of 1/2 would require cos θ = 2, which is impossible, so sec θ = 1/2 has no solution.
The range of y = sec θ is (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞).

criteria.evidence: Response writes secant as the reciprocal of cosine, uses cos(2π/3) = −1/2, and gets −2.
criteria.fix: Rewrite secant as 1/cos θ, find the exact cosine with the correct quadrant sign, then take the reciprocal.

criteria.evidence: Response gets √3 using cot θ = cos θ/sin θ with cos(7π/6) = −√3/2 and sin(7π/6) = −1/2, or using cot θ = 1/tan θ with tan(7π/6) = √3/3 (or 1/√3).
criteria.fix: Rewrite cotangent as cos θ/sin θ; in quadrant III both are negative, so the quotient is positive.

criteria.text: θ = 0, π and 2π, because there sin θ = 0 (equivalently tan θ = 0), so cot θ = cos θ/sin θ is undefined while cos θ is not 0.
criteria.evidence: Response lists exactly θ = 0, π, 2π and gives the reason that sin θ = 0 (or tan θ = 0) at these values.
criteria.fix: Write cot θ = cos θ/sin θ and find where the denominator sin θ is zero in the interval, including both endpoints.

criteria.text: cot θ is decreasing on 0 < θ < π.
criteria.evidence: Response states that cot θ is decreasing on the interval between θ = 0 and θ = π.
criteria.fix: Remember that cotangent decreases between consecutive asymptotes, the opposite of tangent; test two values such as π/4 and 3π/4.

criteria.text: Explains that sec θ = 1/cos θ and −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1 (cos θ not 0), so |sec θ| ≥ 1 and sec θ cannot equal 1/2; equivalently, sec θ = 1/2 would need cos θ = 2, which is impossible.
criteria.evidence: Response gives a valid reason that rules out 1/2: secant is the reciprocal of cosine and −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1 (so cos θ = 2 is impossible), or |sec θ| ≥ 1 for every θ, so 1/2 is not an output of secant.
criteria.fix: Rewrite sec θ = c as cos θ = 1/c and check whether 1/c lies between −1 and 1.

criteria.text: The range of y = sec θ is (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞).
criteria.evidence: Response gives the range as all values less than or equal to −1 together with all values greater than or equal to 1.
criteria.fix: Reciprocals of numbers between −1 and 1 (excluding 0) have absolute value at least 1, so the range excludes (−1, 1).

items.title: Using Pythagorean and Sum Identities to Evaluate and Solve
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use a Pythagorean identity to find the exact value of cos α. Then find the exact value of tan α. Show the work that leads to your answers.

(b) Use the sum identity for sine to find the exact value of sin(α + β). Show the work that leads to your answer.

(c) Use a Pythagorean identity to rewrite the equation 2cos²x + 3 sin x − 3 = 0 in terms of sin x only. Then find all solutions of the equation in the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π.
items.stimulus:
Angle α satisfies sin α = 3/5 and π/2 < α < π.
Angle β satisfies sin β = 12/13 and cos β = 5/13.
items.answer:
(a) By the Pythagorean identity, cos²α = 1 − sin²α = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos α = ±4/5. Because π/2 < α < π, α is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative, so cos α = −4/5.
tan α = sin α/cos α = (3/5)/(−4/5) = −3/4.

(b) sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β = (3/5)(5/13) + (−4/5)(12/13) = 15/65 − 48/65 = −33/65.

(c) Using cos²x = 1 − sin²x:
2(1 − sin²x) + 3 sin x − 3 = 0
2 − 2sin²x + 3 sin x − 3 = 0
−2sin²x + 3 sin x − 1 = 0
2sin²x − 3 sin x + 1 = 0
(2 sin x − 1)(sin x − 1) = 0, so sin x = 1/2 or sin x = 1.
In 0 ≤ x < 2π, sin x = 1/2 gives x = π/6 and x = 5π/6, and sin x = 1 gives x = π/2. The solutions are x = π/6, π/2 and 5π/6.

criteria.text: cos α = −4/5: from the Pythagorean identity, cos²α = 1 − sin²α = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, and cos α < 0 because π/2 < α < π.
criteria.evidence: Response uses sin²α + cos²α = 1 to get cos²α = 16/25 and chooses the negative root because α is in quadrant II.
criteria.fix: After using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, choose the sign of the square root from the quadrant of the angle.

criteria.text: tan α = −3/4, for example tan α = sin α/cos α = (3/5)/(−4/5) = −3/4.
criteria.evidence: Response gets tan α = −3/4 with valid work, such as sin α/cos α, or tan²α = sec²α − 1 = 9/16 with the negative root because α is in quadrant II.
criteria.fix: Compute tan α as sin α divided by cos α using the signed values just found, then check the sign against the quadrant.

criteria.text: Writes sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β = (3/5)(5/13) + (−4/5)(12/13).
criteria.evidence: Response applies the sine sum identity and substitutes all four values, including cos α = −4/5.
criteria.fix: Write sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β before substituting; never add the two sines.

criteria.evidence: Response simplifies the substituted expression to −33/65.
criteria.fix: Put both products over the common denominator 65 and keep the negative sign from cos α.

criteria.text: Replaces cos²x with 1 − sin²x to get 2sin²x − 3 sin x + 1 = 0, which factors as (2 sin x − 1)(sin x − 1) = 0, so sin x = 1/2 or sin x = 1.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the substitution cos²x = 1 − sin²x, an equivalent quadratic in sin x, and the two values sin x = 1/2 and sin x = 1.
criteria.fix: Substitute cos²x = 1 − sin²x, collect terms into a quadratic in sin x, then factor or use the quadratic formula.

criteria.text: The solutions are x = π/6, π/2 and 5π/6.
criteria.evidence: Response lists exactly π/6, π/2 and 5π/6, from sin x = 1/2 (two angles) and sin x = 1 (one angle).
criteria.fix: For each sine value find every angle in 0 ≤ x < 2π; sin x = 1/2 has solutions in quadrants I and II.

items.title: Converting Between Polar, Rectangular and Complex Forms
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the rectangular coordinates of point A. Then describe where A is located relative to the terminal ray of the angle 2π/3.

(b) Find polar coordinates (r, θ) for point B with r > 0 and 0 ≤ θ < 2π. Show the work that leads to your answer.

(c) Write w in the form a + bi, where a and b are exact real numbers. Then give polar coordinates (r, θ) for the point corresponding to w with r = −4 and 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
items.stimulus:
In the xy-plane, point A has polar coordinates (r, θ) = (−4, 2π/3), and point B has rectangular coordinates (−3, 3√3).

In the complex plane, the complex number w corresponds to the point with polar coordinates (4, 5π/4).
items.answer:
(a) x = r cos θ = −4cos(2π/3) = −4(−1/2) = 2 and y = r sin θ = −4 sin(2π/3) = −4(√3/2) = −2√3. So A = (2, −2√3).
The terminal ray of 2π/3 points into quadrant II. Because r = −4 is negative, A lies 4 units from the origin on the line containing that ray, but in the opposite direction from the ray, which places A in quadrant IV.

(b) r = √((−3)² + (3√3)²) = √(9 + 27) = √36 = 6.
Since x = −3 < 0, θ = arctan(y/x) + π = arctan(3√3/(−3)) + π = arctan(−√3) + π = −π/3 + π = 2π/3. Check: 6cos(2π/3) = −3 and 6 sin(2π/3) = 3√3. So B has polar coordinates (6, 2π/3).

(c) w = 4cos(5π/4) + i·4 sin(5π/4) = 4(−√2/2) + i·4(−√2/2) = −2√2 − 2√2 i.
With r = −4, the point must lie opposite the terminal ray of θ. The point (−2√2, −2√2) is in direction 5π/4, so the opposite direction is 5π/4 − π = π/4, and the polar coordinates are (−4, π/4). Check: −4cos(π/4) = −2√2 and −4 sin(π/4) = −2√2.

criteria.text: A = (2, −2√3), from x = r cos θ = −4cos(2π/3) = 2 and y = r sin θ = −4 sin(2π/3) = −2√3.
criteria.evidence: Response obtains (2, −2√3) by a valid conversion, such as x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ with r = −4, or first rewriting A as (4, 5π/3) and then converting.
criteria.fix: Substitute the negative r directly into x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ; do not drop its sign.

criteria.text: Because r = −4 is negative, A is 4 units from the origin on the line containing the terminal ray of 2π/3, but in the direction opposite to that ray (so A is in quadrant IV).
criteria.evidence: Response explains that a negative r places the point 4 units from the origin in the opposite direction of the terminal ray of 2π/3.
criteria.fix: For negative r, go |r| units along the line through the terminal ray but on the opposite side of the origin.

criteria.evidence: Response gets r = 6 with valid work, such as r = √(x² + y²), or r = y/sin θ = (3√3)/sin(2π/3) once θ = 2π/3 is found.
criteria.fix: Use r = √(x² + y²) with both coordinates squared, then simplify the square root exactly.

criteria.text: θ = 2π/3: since x < 0, θ = arctan(3√3/(−3)) + π = arctan(−√3) + π = −π/3 + π = 2π/3.
criteria.evidence: Response gives θ = 2π/3 with a reason that accounts for x < 0, such as adding π to arctan(y/x) or using cos θ = −1/2 and sin θ = √3/2.
criteria.fix: When x < 0, add π to arctan(y/x); check that the angle's quadrant matches the signs of x and y.

criteria.text: w = −2√2 − 2√2 i, for example from 4cos(5π/4) + i·4 sin(5π/4) with cos(5π/4) = sin(5π/4) = −√2/2.
criteria.evidence: Response gives w = −2√2 − 2√2 i. Any valid method is accepted, such as r cos θ + i·r sin θ, or quadrant III with equal parts and a² + b² = 16.
criteria.fix: Write a complex number with polar coordinates (r, θ) as r cos θ + i·r sin θ, using exact values with correct signs.

criteria.text: (−4, π/4), because the terminal ray of π/4 points opposite to the point, so r = −4 along it reaches (−2√2, −2√2); π/4 = 5π/4 − π.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the polar coordinates (−4, π/4).
criteria.fix: To use a negative r, change the angle by π so the terminal ray points opposite the point, then check by converting back.

items.title: Distance from the Origin and Average Rate of Change of a Polar Function
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) On the interval 2π/3 < θ < π, is the distance between the point (f(θ), θ) and the origin increasing or decreasing? Give a reason for your answer.

(b) Find the average rate of change of r with respect to θ over the interval π/3 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Then use this average rate of change to estimate f(5π/12).

(c) On the interval 2π/3 < θ < 4π/3, the function f has exactly one relative extremum. Find the value of θ at which it occurs and state whether it is a relative minimum or a relative maximum of f, with a reason. Then determine whether the corresponding point on the curve is relatively closest to or relatively farthest from the origin, and explain.
items.stimulus: Let f be the function given by f(θ) = 1 + 2cos θ. Consider the polar curve r = f(θ) for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. For each θ, the point on the curve has polar coordinates (f(θ), θ).
items.answer:
(a) f(2π/3) = 1 + 2(−1/2) = 0 and f(π) = 1 + 2(−1) = −1. Since cos θ is decreasing on 0 < θ < π, f(θ) = 1 + 2cos θ is decreasing on 2π/3 < θ < π, and its values go from 0 down to −1, so f(θ) is negative there. Because f is negative and decreasing, the distance between the point (f(θ), θ) and the origin is increasing on 2π/3 < θ < π.

(b) f(π/3) = 1 + 2(1/2) = 2 and f(π/2) = 1 + 2(0) = 1.
Average rate of change = (f(π/2) − f(π/3))/(π/2 − π/3) = (1 − 2)/(π/6) = −6/π, about −1.910 units of r per radian.
Estimate: f(5π/12) ≈ f(π/3) + (−6/π)(5π/12 − π/3) = 2 + (−6/π)(π/12) = 2 − 1/2 = 1.5.

(c) cos θ is decreasing on 2π/3 < θ < π and increasing on π < θ < 4π/3, so f changes from decreasing to increasing at θ = π. Therefore f has a relative minimum at θ = π, with f(π) = −1.
The distance from the origin is |f(θ)|. For θ near π in this interval, f(θ) is between −1 and 0, so |f(θ)| < 1 = |f(π)|. The point on the curve at θ = π is relatively farthest from the origin.

criteria.text: On 2π/3 < θ < π, f(θ) is negative (its values go from 0 to −1) and f is decreasing (because cos θ is decreasing on 0 < θ < π).
criteria.evidence: Response states both that f(θ) < 0 on the interval (for example f(2π/3) = 0 and f(π) = −1) and that f is decreasing there.
criteria.fix: Check two things separately on the interval: the sign of r and whether r is increasing or decreasing.

criteria.text: The distance from the origin is increasing, because f is negative and decreasing on this interval.
criteria.evidence: Response concludes that the distance is increasing and bases this on r being negative and decreasing.
criteria.fix: When r is negative and decreasing, |r| grows, so the point moves away from the origin.

criteria.text: Average rate of change = (f(π/2) − f(π/3))/(π/2 − π/3) = (1 − 2)/(π/6) = −6/π.
criteria.evidence: Response evaluates f(π/3) = 2 and f(π/2) = 1 and divides the change in r by the change in θ, π/6, to get −6/π.
criteria.fix: Divide the change in signed radius, f(b) − f(a), by the change in θ in radians, b − a.

criteria.evidence: Response uses the average rate of change times the change in θ from a known endpoint to estimate f(5π/12) as 1.5.
criteria.fix: Estimate a value inside the interval by starting at a known endpoint and adding the average rate times the change in θ.

criteria.text: At θ = π, f changes from decreasing to increasing (equivalently, f(θ) ≥ −1 = f(π) because cos θ ≥ −1), so f has a relative minimum at θ = π.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies θ = π as a relative minimum with a valid reason, such as f changing from decreasing to increasing there, or 1 + 2cos θ ≥ −1 with equality only at θ = π. The value f(π) is not required.
criteria.fix: Find where r switches from decreasing to increasing; that change, not the sign of r, decides minimum versus maximum.

criteria.text: The point is relatively farthest from the origin: for θ near π in this interval, f(θ) is between −1 and 0, so its distance |f(θ)| from the origin is less than |f(π)| = 1.
criteria.evidence: Response concludes relatively farthest and explains using distance |r|, for example that nearby r-values have absolute value less than 1, or that |f(θ)| increases before θ = π and decreases after it.
criteria.fix: Distance from the origin is |r|; a negative relative minimum of r gives a point relatively farthest from the origin.

items.title: Periodic Water Level in a Storage Tank
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the period of h. A student claims that the period of h is 20 because h(t + 20) = h(t) for all t ≥ 0. Explain why the student's claim is incorrect.

(b) For 20 ≤ t ≤ 30, give the interval on which h is increasing and the interval on which h is decreasing. Explain how the periodic behavior of h gives your answer.

(c) Find all times t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 30, at which the height of the water is 40 centimeters. Show the work that leads to your answer.
items.stimulus:
The height of the water in a storage tank follows a repeating schedule. Let h(t) be the height of the water, in centimeters, at time t minutes, for t ≥ 0.

The schedule starting at t = 0 is as follows.
From t = 0 to t = 4, water is pumped in and the height increases at a constant rate from 20 centimeters to 60 centimeters.
From t = 4 to t = 6, the height stays at 60 centimeters.
From t = 6 to t = 10, water drains out and the height decreases at a constant rate from 60 centimeters to 20 centimeters.

After this, the same pattern of filling, holding and draining repeats exactly, over and over, for all t ≥ 0.
items.answer:
(a) In one cycle the height rises from 20 to 60 centimeters for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4, stays at 60 for 4 ≤ t ≤ 6, and falls back to 20 for 6 ≤ t ≤ 10; then the same pattern starts again. So h(t + 10) = h(t) for all t ≥ 0. No shorter length works, because within a cycle the height is 20 only at the start and at the end. The period of h is 10 minutes.
The student's claim is incorrect. The period is the smallest positive value k for which h(t + k) = h(t) for all t. It is true that h(t + 20) = h(t), but h(t + 10) = h(t) is also true and 10 < 20, so 20 is a multiple of the period, not the period.

(b) Every characteristic of a periodic function in one period appears in every period. In the first cycle h is increasing on 0 < t < 4 and decreasing on 6 < t < 10. The interval 20 ≤ t ≤ 30 is the first cycle shifted by 20 = 2·10 minutes. So h is increasing on 20 < t < 24 and decreasing on 26 < t < 30 (h is constant at 60 on 24 < t < 26).

(c) While filling, the height rises 40 centimeters in 4 minutes, which is 10 centimeters per minute: 20 + 10t = 40 gives t = 2. While draining, it falls 10 centimeters per minute: 60 − 10(t − 6) = 40 gives t − 6 = 2, so t = 8. Because the period is 10, h(t) = 40 also at 2 + 10 = 12, 8 + 10 = 18, 2 + 20 = 22 and 8 + 20 = 28. The times are t = 2, 8, 12, 18, 22 and 28 minutes.

criteria.text: States that the period of h is 10 minutes because the pattern of filling, holding and draining takes 10 minutes and then repeats, so h(t + 10) = h(t) for all t ≥ 0.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 10 minutes as the period and connects it to one complete cycle of the schedule or to h(t + 10) = h(t).
criteria.fix: Find where the output pattern starts repeating; the length of one complete cycle is the period.

criteria.text: Explains that the period is the smallest positive value k with h(t + k) = h(t) for all t, and 10 is such a value smaller than 20, so 20 is not the period.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the period must be the smallest positive repeat length (smallest k) and notes that h(t + 10) = h(t) with 10 < 20.
criteria.fix: Check whether a smaller positive k also gives h(t + k) = h(t); the period is the smallest such k, not a multiple of it.

criteria.text: h is increasing on 20 < t < 24, because this is the filling stage 0 < t < 4 shifted by two periods (20 minutes).
criteria.evidence: Response gives 20 to 24 as the interval of increase (open or closed endpoints both accepted) and links it to the interval 0 to 4 shifted by 20, or to the characteristics repeating every period.
criteria.fix: Shift each interval of increase in the first cycle by a whole number of periods to find the matching interval in a later cycle.

criteria.text: h is decreasing on 26 < t < 30, because this is the draining stage 6 < t < 10 shifted by two periods (20 minutes).
criteria.evidence: Response gives 26 to 30 as the interval of decrease (open or closed endpoints both accepted) and links it to the interval 6 to 10 shifted by 20, or to the characteristics repeating every period.
criteria.fix: Add the same multiple of the period to both endpoints of the draining interval, 6 and 10, to locate it in the later cycle.

criteria.text: Finds the two times in the first cycle: t = 2 while filling (20 + 10t = 40) and t = 8 while draining (60 − 10(t − 6) = 40), using the constant rate of 10 centimeters per minute.
criteria.evidence: Response finds t = 2 and t = 8 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 with valid supporting work, such as the rate of 10 centimeters per minute, or noting that 40 is midway between 20 and 60 so it is reached halfway through each 4-minute stage.
criteria.fix: Find each stage's constant rate, 40 centimeters over 4 minutes, then solve for when the height equals 40 within the first cycle.

criteria.text: Uses the period 10 to list all six times: t = 2, 8, 12, 18, 22 and 28 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Response lists exactly 2, 8, 12, 18, 22 and 28, either by adding 10 and 20 to the first-cycle times or by solving within each 10-minute cycle.
criteria.fix: After solving within one period, add each whole multiple of the period that keeps the time inside the given interval.

items.title: Ratios on a Circle and Radian Measure
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact values of sin θ and cos θ. Show how each value is obtained from the coordinates of P.

(b) Find the coordinates of the point Q where the terminal ray of θ intersects the unit circle. Then find the exact value of tan θ and state what tan θ represents for the terminal ray.

(c) Find the radian measure of α. Then find the exact value of the negative angle that is coterminal with α and is closest to 0, and state the direction of rotation that this negative angle represents.
items.stimulus:
An angle θ is in standard position. Its terminal ray intersects the circle of radius 13 centered at the origin at the point P = (−5, 12).

A second angle α is in standard position. On the circle of radius 4 centered at the origin, the angle α subtends an arc of length 10, measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.
items.answer:
(a) P is on the circle of radius 13, so the distance from the origin to P is 13 (check: √((−5)² + 12²) = √169 = 13).
sin θ = (vertical displacement of P from the x-axis)/(distance from origin to P) = 12/13.
cos θ = (horizontal displacement of P from the y-axis)/(distance from origin to P) = −5/13.

(b) On the unit circle, the point on the terminal ray has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), so Q = (−5/13, 12/13). This is P with both coordinates divided by 13.
tan θ is the slope of the terminal ray: tan θ = (12 − 0)/(−5 − 0) = −12/5. Equivalently, tan θ = sin θ/cos θ = (12/13)/(−5/13) = −12/5.

(c) The radian measure is the arc length divided by the radius: α = 10/4 = 2.5 radians.
Coterminal angles differ by whole revolutions of 2π. Since 0 < 2.5 < 2π, subtracting one revolution gives the negative coterminal angle closest to 0: 2.5 − 2π radians, approximately −3.78. Because it is negative, it represents a clockwise rotation from the positive x-axis.

criteria.text: sin θ = 12/13: the vertical displacement of P from the x-axis, 12, divided by the distance from the origin to P, 13.
criteria.evidence: Response gives sin θ = 12/13 and shows it as the ratio of the y-coordinate 12 to the distance 13.
criteria.fix: On a circle of radius r, divide the point's y-coordinate by r to get the sine, keeping the coordinate's sign.

criteria.text: cos θ = −5/13: the horizontal displacement of P from the y-axis, −5, divided by the distance from the origin to P, 13.
criteria.evidence: Response gives cos θ = −5/13, keeping the negative sign from the x-coordinate of P, and shows the ratio to 13.
criteria.fix: Divide the point's x-coordinate by the radius to get the cosine; a point left of the y-axis gives a negative cosine.

criteria.text: Q = (−5/13, 12/13), because on the unit circle the point on the terminal ray has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ) (equivalently, P scaled by 1/13).
criteria.evidence: Response gives Q = (−5/13, 12/13), from cos θ and sin θ or from dividing the coordinates of P by 13.
criteria.fix: The point where the terminal ray meets the unit circle has x-coordinate cos θ and y-coordinate sin θ.

criteria.text: tan θ = −12/5, which is the slope of the terminal ray, (12 − 0)/(−5 − 0), equivalently sin θ/cos θ.
criteria.evidence: Response gives tan θ = −12/5 and identifies it as the slope of the terminal ray.
criteria.fix: Find tangent as the slope of the terminal ray: divide the y-coordinate by the x-coordinate of any point on the ray.

criteria.text: α = 10/4 = 2.5 radians, the arc length divided by the radius of the circle.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the arc length 10 by the radius 4 to get α = 2.5 radians.
criteria.fix: Radian measure equals arc length divided by the radius of the same circle; do not divide by the circumference.

criteria.text: The coterminal angle is 2.5 − 2π radians (approximately −3.78), because coterminal angles differ by whole revolutions of 2π, and a negative angle is a clockwise rotation from the positive x-axis.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 2.5 − 2π (or an equivalent exact form) and states that the rotation is clockwise.
criteria.fix: Subtract one full revolution, 2π, for a coterminal negative angle; negative measures mean clockwise rotation from the positive x-axis.

items.title: Exact Positions of Runners on a Circular Track
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact coordinates of runner A's final position. Show the work that leads to your answer.

(b) Find the exact coordinates of runner B's final position. Show the work that leads to your answer.

(c) Is runner C or runner A farther from the x-axis at their final positions? Justify your answer using exact values.
items.stimulus:
A circular running track has radius 8 meters. A coordinate system, with distances in meters, is placed so that the center of the track is at the origin. Three runners each start at the point (8, 0) and run along the track. Each runner's final position is on the terminal ray of an angle θ in standard position, measured in radians.

Runner A moves counterclockwise through an angle of 5π/6.
Runner B moves clockwise through an angle of 3π/4.
Runner C moves counterclockwise through an angle of 4π/3.

Give all answers as exact values.
items.answer:
(a) A point on a circle of radius 8 at angle θ has coordinates (8cos θ, 8 sin θ). The angle 5π/6 is in quadrant II with reference angle π/6, so cos(5π/6) = −√3/2 and sin(5π/6) = 1/2.
A = (8(−√3/2), 8(1/2)) = (−4√3, 4).

(b) A clockwise rotation of 3π/4 is the angle θ = −3π/4, whose terminal ray is in quadrant III with reference angle π/4. So cos(−3π/4) = −√2/2 and sin(−3π/4) = −√2/2.
B = (8(−√2/2), 8(−√2/2)) = (−4√2, −4√2).

(c) The angle 4π/3 is in quadrant III with reference angle π/3, so sin(4π/3) = −√3/2 and cos(4π/3) = −1/2. C = (8(−1/2), 8(−√3/2)) = (−4, −4√3).
Distance from the x-axis is the absolute value of the y-coordinate. Runner C is 4√3 meters from the x-axis and runner A is 4 meters from it. Since √3 > 1, 4√3 > 4, so runner C is farther from the x-axis.

criteria.text: x-coordinate of A is 8cos(5π/6) = 8(−√3/2) = −4√3.
criteria.evidence: Response gets −4√3 with valid work, such as x = 8cos(5π/6) with cos(5π/6) = −√3/2, or a reference triangle with angle π/6 and hypotenuse 8 and a negative sign for quadrant II.
criteria.fix: Use (r cos θ, r sin θ); find the reference angle, π/6 here, then make cosine negative for a quadrant II angle.

criteria.text: y-coordinate of A is 8 sin(5π/6) = 8(1/2) = 4.
criteria.evidence: Response gets 4 with valid work, such as y = 8 sin(5π/6) with sin(5π/6) = 1/2, or the side opposite π/6 in a reference triangle with hypotenuse 8.
criteria.fix: Multiply the radius by the sine of the angle; the sine of a quadrant II angle is positive, so use sin(π/6) = 1/2.

criteria.text: x-coordinate of B is −4√2: the clockwise rotation of 3π/4 ends in quadrant III with reference angle π/4, so x = 8cos(−3π/4) = 8(−√2/2) = −4√2.
criteria.evidence: Response locates B's terminal ray in quadrant III (for example with the angle −3π/4, the coterminal 5π/4, or a reference angle of π/4 below the negative x-axis) and gets x = −4√2.
criteria.fix: Write a clockwise rotation as a negative angle, locate its quadrant (III here), then compute r cos θ with the correct sign.

criteria.text: y-coordinate of B is 8 sin(−3π/4) = 8(−√2/2) = −4√2.
criteria.evidence: Response gets y = −4√2 with valid work, such as sin(−3π/4) = −√2/2, or an isosceles right reference triangle with hypotenuse 8 and a negative sign below the x-axis.
criteria.fix: Below the x-axis the sine is negative; use sin(π/4) = √2/2 from the isosceles right triangle, then attach the sign.

criteria.text: Runner C is 4√3 meters from the x-axis: |8 sin(4π/3)| = 8 sin(π/3) = 4√3 (C's position is (−4, −4√3)).
criteria.evidence: Response finds C's distance from the x-axis as 4√3 with valid work, such as |8 sin(4π/3)|, or 8 sin(π/3) from the reference angle π/3.
criteria.fix: Distance from the x-axis is the absolute value of the y-coordinate r sin θ; for 4π/3 use the reference angle π/3.

criteria.text: Runner C is farther, because 4√3 > 4, where 4 is runner A's distance from the x-axis.
criteria.evidence: Response compares 4√3 with A's distance 4 (from part (a)) and concludes runner C is farther from the x-axis.
criteria.fix: Compare absolute values of the y-coordinates, not the signed values, when asked about distance from the x-axis.

items.title: Sine and Cosine from a Point Moving Around the Unit Circle
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) As θ increases from π/2 to π, describe how the position of P changes. Use this to determine whether f is increasing or decreasing and whether g is increasing or decreasing on the interval π/2 < θ < π.

(b) Explain why the equation sin θ = 0.7 has at least one solution, but the equation cos θ = 1.3 has no solution.

(c) Find the interval of θ values, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, on which f is decreasing and g is increasing at the same time. Explain your reasoning in terms of the motion of P.
items.stimulus:
A point P moves counterclockwise around the unit circle centered at the origin. When P is where the terminal ray of an angle θ in standard position intersects the unit circle, the y-coordinate of P is sin θ and the x-coordinate of P is cos θ.

Let f(θ) = sin θ and g(θ) = cos θ.
items.answer:
(a) As θ increases from π/2 to π, P moves along the unit circle from (0, 1) to (−1, 0), through quadrant II. P moves down toward the x-axis, so its y-coordinate decreases from 1 to 0: f(θ) = sin θ is decreasing on π/2 < θ < π. P also moves to the left, so its x-coordinate decreases from 0 to −1: g(θ) = cos θ is decreasing on π/2 < θ < π.

(b) As θ increases, sin θ, the y-coordinate of P, oscillates between −1 and 1 and takes every value in between. Since −1 < 0.7 < 1, there is at least one angle with sin θ = 0.7.
cos θ is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, so −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1 for every θ. Since 1.3 > 1, no angle has cos θ = 1.3.

(c) f is decreasing when P moves downward, which happens for π/2 < θ < 3π/2 (from the top of the circle to the bottom). g is increasing when P moves to the right, which happens for π < θ < 2π (from the leftmost point to the rightmost point). Both happen only for π < θ < 3π/2. On this interval P moves through quadrant III from (−1, 0) to (0, −1), so its y-coordinate falls from 0 to −1 while its x-coordinate rises from −1 to 0. The interval is π < θ < 3π/2.

criteria.text: f is decreasing on π/2 < θ < π, because P moves from (0, 1) toward (−1, 0), so its vertical displacement from the x-axis decreases from 1 to 0.
criteria.evidence: Response states f is decreasing and explains with P moving downward, its y-coordinate going from 1 to 0.
criteria.fix: Track the y-coordinate of P as it moves through the quadrant; sine increases only while P moves upward.

criteria.text: g is decreasing on π/2 < θ < π, because P moves to the left, so its horizontal displacement from the y-axis changes from 0 to −1.
criteria.evidence: Response states g is decreasing and explains with P moving left, its x-coordinate going from 0 to −1.
criteria.fix: Track the x-coordinate of P; cosine decreases whenever P moves to the left, even when the values are negative.

criteria.text: sin θ = 0.7 has a solution because sin θ takes the value 0.7: sine oscillates between −1 and 1 and takes every value in between (for example, the y-coordinate of P goes through every value from 0 to 1 as θ goes from 0 to π/2).
criteria.evidence: Response gives a valid reason that sine attains 0.7, such as: sine takes every value from −1 to 1, or the y-coordinate of P takes every value from 0 to 1 as θ increases from 0 to π/2.
criteria.fix: Show the target value lies among the y-coordinates P passes through, for example every value from −1 to 1.

criteria.text: cos θ = 1.3 has no solution because cos θ is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, so −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1, and 1.3 > 1.
criteria.evidence: Response states that cosine values are never greater than 1 (x-coordinates on the unit circle lie from −1 to 1) and that 1.3 is outside this range.
criteria.fix: Before solving, compare the target value with the output range −1 to 1; values outside it give no solution.

criteria.text: Gives the interval π < θ < 3π/2.
criteria.evidence: Response states π < θ < 3π/2 (open or closed endpoints both accepted) as the interval on which f decreases and g increases.
criteria.fix: Find where P moves both downward and to the right at once, and write that set of angles as one interval.

criteria.text: Justifies with the motion of P: P moves downward only for π/2 < θ < 3π/2 and to the right only for π < θ < 2π, so both happen only for π < θ < 3π/2, as P goes from (−1, 0) to (0, −1).
criteria.evidence: Response explains that on this interval the y-coordinate of P decreases (0 to −1) while its x-coordinate increases (−1 to 0), and that outside it at least one of these fails. Any valid explanation earns the point, including identifying Quadrant III and describing P moving down and to the right there; an explicit argument that every other angle fails is not required.
criteria.fix: List where each coordinate of P decreases or increases separately, then intersect the two sets of angles.

items.title: Amplitude, Midline, Period and Symmetry of Sinusoidal Functions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the amplitude of h and the equation of the midline of the graph of h. Show the work that leads to your answers.

(b) Find the period and the frequency of h. Explain how the frequency is related to the period.

(c) Find the values of sin(−a) and cos(−a). Justify each answer using the symmetry of the graphs of y = sin θ and y = cos θ.
items.stimulus:
Let h be a sinusoidal function of x. The graph of h has a maximum value of 14 at x = 3, and the next maximum after x = 3 occurs at x = 11. The minimum value of h is 2.

Separately, let a be a real number such that sin a = 0.6 and cos a = 0.8.
items.answer:
(a) The amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum values: (14 − 2)/2 = 6.
The midline is the average of the maximum and minimum values: (14 + 2)/2 = 8, so the midline is y = 8.

(b) Consecutive maxima occur at x = 3 and x = 11, and the pattern of h repeats from one maximum to the next, so the period is 11 − 3 = 8.
The period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals, so the frequency is 1/8: h completes one-eighth of a cycle per unit of x.

(c) The graph of y = sin θ has rotational symmetry about the origin, so sine is an odd function: sin(−a) = −sin a = −0.6.
The graph of y = cos θ has reflective symmetry over the y-axis, so cosine is an even function: cos(−a) = cos a = 0.8.

criteria.text: Amplitude = (14 − 2)/2 = 6, half the difference between the maximum and minimum values.
criteria.evidence: Response computes half of the difference between 14 and 2 to get an amplitude of 6.
criteria.fix: Amplitude is half of (maximum − minimum); do not use the maximum value itself as the amplitude.

criteria.text: Midline y = (14 + 2)/2 = 8, the average of the maximum and minimum values.
criteria.evidence: Response averages 14 and 2 to get the midline y = 8.
criteria.fix: Find the midline as the average of the maximum and minimum values and write it as an equation y = constant.

criteria.text: Period = 11 − 3 = 8, the horizontal distance between consecutive maximum points, where the pattern of h repeats.
criteria.evidence: Response gives a period of 8, computed as the distance between the consecutive maxima at x = 3 and x = 11.
criteria.fix: Measure the period as the horizontal distance from one maximum to the next maximum, not from a maximum to a minimum.

criteria.text: Frequency = 1/8, because the period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals.
criteria.evidence: Response gives frequency 1/8 and states that frequency is the reciprocal of the period (one-eighth of a cycle per unit of x).
criteria.fix: Take the reciprocal of the period to get the frequency, the number of cycles completed per unit of input.

criteria.text: sin(−a) = −0.6, because the graph of y = sin θ has rotational symmetry about the origin (sine is odd), so sin(−a) = −sin a.
criteria.evidence: Response gives sin(−a) = −0.6 and cites that sine is an odd function or that its graph is symmetric about the origin.
criteria.fix: Use the odd symmetry of sine, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, which comes from the graph's rotational symmetry about the origin.

criteria.text: cos(−a) = 0.8, because the graph of y = cos θ has reflective symmetry over the y-axis (cosine is even), so cos(−a) = cos a.
criteria.evidence: Response gives cos(−a) = 0.8 and cites that cosine is an even function or that its graph is symmetric over the y-axis.
criteria.fix: Use the even symmetry of cosine, cos(−θ) = cos θ, which comes from the graph's reflection symmetry over the y-axis.

items.title: Period, Asymptotes and Behavior of a Transformed Tangent Function
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the period of g. Then find the equations of all vertical asymptotes of the graph of g.

(b) The interval −π/4 < θ < π/4 lies between two consecutive vertical asymptotes of the graph of g. On this interval, determine whether g is increasing or decreasing, and describe the concavity of the graph of g. Give a reason for each answer.

(c) Find the exact value of g(π/6). Then find the value of θ, with π/2 < θ < π, for which g(θ) = g(π/6), and explain how the period of g gives your answer.
items.stimulus: Let g be the function given by g(θ) = −2 tan(2θ) + 3.
items.answer:
(a) g(θ) = −2 tan(2θ) + 3 has the form a·tan(bθ) + d with b = 2 (a horizontal dilation by a factor of 1/2), so its period is π/|b| = π/2.
The graph of tan u has vertical asymptotes where cos u = 0, that is u = π/2 + kπ for integers k. Setting 2θ = π/2 + kπ gives θ = π/4 + kπ/2. The vertical asymptotes are θ = π/4 + kπ/2 for every integer k.

(b) Between consecutive asymptotes, tan(2θ) is increasing. Multiplying by −2 is a vertical dilation by a negative factor, which involves a reflection over the x-axis, so g is decreasing on −π/4 < θ < π/4.
Between consecutive asymptotes, the graph of tan(2θ) changes from concave down to concave up at θ = 0. The reflection reverses this, so the graph of g is concave up on −π/4 < θ < 0 and concave down on 0 < θ < π/4, with a point of inflection at (0, 3), since g(0) = −2·0 + 3 = 3.

(c) g(π/6) = −2 tan(π/3) + 3. tan(π/3) = sin(π/3)/cos(π/3) = (√3/2)/(1/2) = √3, so g(π/6) = 3 − 2√3.
Because the period of g is π/2, g(π/6 + π/2) = g(π/6). π/6 + π/2 = 2π/3, which is between π/2 and π. (Check: g(2π/3) = −2 tan(4π/3) + 3 = 3 − 2√3.) The next value with the same output, 7π/6, is greater than π, so θ = 2π/3.

criteria.text: The period of g is π/2 (for example, a·tan(bθ) + d has period π/|b| with b = 2, or consecutive asymptotes are π/2 apart).
criteria.evidence: Response gives the period π/2 by any valid method, such as π divided by |b| = 2 (horizontal dilation factor 1/2) or the spacing between consecutive vertical asymptotes.
criteria.fix: Divide tangent's base period π by the absolute value of the coefficient of θ.

criteria.text: The vertical asymptotes are θ = π/4 + kπ/2 for every integer k, where 2θ = π/2 + kπ (where cos(2θ) = 0).
criteria.evidence: Response gives θ = π/4 + kπ/2 for all integers k (or an equivalent description of every asymptote), by any valid method, such as solving 2θ = π/2 + kπ or repeating θ = π/4 every period π/2.
criteria.fix: Set the argument of tangent equal to π/2 + kπ, where cosine of the argument is zero, and solve for θ.

criteria.text: g is decreasing on −π/4 < θ < π/4, because tan(2θ) is increasing between consecutive asymptotes and the factor −2 is negative, which involves a reflection over the x-axis and reverses the direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states g is decreasing and attributes this to the negative vertical dilation factor −2 applied to an increasing tangent function.
criteria.fix: Identify whether tangent increases, then reverse that direction when its output is multiplied by a negative coefficient.

criteria.text: The graph of g is concave up on −π/4 < θ < 0 and concave down on 0 < θ < π/4, changing at θ = 0; this reverses tangent's change from concave down to concave up because a = −2 < 0.
criteria.evidence: Response states concave up then concave down, with the change at θ = 0, and links this to the reflection by the negative factor. The coordinates of the inflection point are not required.
criteria.fix: Tangent goes from concave down to concave up between asymptotes; reflect this order when a is negative, switching at the center point.

criteria.evidence: Response evaluates tan(π/3) = √3 and obtains g(π/6) = 3 − 2√3.
criteria.fix: Substitute the input into 2θ first, then use tan = sin/cos with exact unit-circle values before multiplying by −2 and adding 3.

criteria.text: θ = π/6 + π/2 = 2π/3, because g repeats every π/2, and 2π/3 is the only such value in π/2 < θ < π.
criteria.evidence: Response adds the period π/2 to π/6 to get 2π/3 and notes that it lies in the interval π/2 < θ < π.
criteria.fix: Add whole multiples of the period to a known input to find other inputs with the same output, then keep the one in the interval.

items.title: Inverse Trigonometric Values on Restricted Domains
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact values of arccos(−1/2) and arctan(−√3). For each, explain why your value is the correct output.

(b) Find the exact value of arcsin(sin(5π/6)). Explain why the answer is not 5π/6.

(c) State the domain and the range of y = arctan x. Then explain why arctan x is defined for every real number x, but arcsin x is defined only for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.
items.stimulus: The functions arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x are the inverse functions of sine, cosine and tangent, defined using the usual restricted domains of those functions. Give exact values.
items.answer:
(a) arccos(−1/2) = 2π/3. The output of arccos must be an angle in [0, π], the restricted domain of cosine, and cos(2π/3) = −1/2 with 2π/3 in [0, π]. Cosine is one-to-one on [0, π], so this is the only such angle.
arctan(−√3) = −π/3. The output of arctan must be in (−π/2, π/2), and tan(−π/3) = sin(−π/3)/cos(−π/3) = (−√3/2)/(1/2) = −√3, with −π/3 in (−π/2, π/2).

(b) sin(5π/6) = 1/2, so arcsin(sin(5π/6)) = arcsin(1/2). The output of arcsin must be in [−π/2, π/2], the restricted domain of sine. 5π/6 is greater than π/2, so it cannot be the output. The angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is 1/2 is π/6, so arcsin(sin(5π/6)) = π/6.

(c) The domain of y = arctan x is all real numbers, and the range is −π/2 < y < π/2.
For an inverse function, the input and output values are switched, so the domain of the inverse is the range of the restricted original function. On (−π/2, π/2), tan θ takes every real value, so arctan x is defined for every real x. On [−π/2, π/2], sin θ takes only values from −1 to 1, so arcsin x is defined only for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.

criteria.text: arccos(−1/2) = 2π/3, because cos(2π/3) = −1/2 and 2π/3 is in [0, π], the restricted domain of cosine.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 2π/3, shows cos(2π/3) = −1/2, and states that 2π/3 lies in [0, π].
criteria.fix: Look for the angle in [0, π] with the given cosine; arccos never outputs a negative angle.

criteria.text: arctan(−√3) = −π/3, because tan(−π/3) = −√3 and −π/3 is in (−π/2, π/2), the restricted domain of tangent.
criteria.evidence: Response gives −π/3, shows tan(−π/3) = −√3, and states that −π/3 lies in (−π/2, π/2).
criteria.fix: Look for the angle strictly between −π/2 and π/2 with the given tangent; negative inputs give negative angles.

criteria.text: Evaluates the inner expression: sin(5π/6) = 1/2 (equivalently, sin(5π/6) = sin(π/6)).
criteria.evidence: Response evaluates sin(5π/6) as 1/2, or shows that sin(5π/6) = sin(π/6) using the reference angle π/6, so the composition equals arcsin(sin(π/6)).
criteria.fix: Evaluate the inner function first using the reference angle π/6, with sine positive in quadrant II.

criteria.text: arcsin(1/2) = π/6, because arcsin outputs only angles in [−π/2, π/2]; 5π/6 is outside this interval, and π/6 is the angle in it whose sine is 1/2.
criteria.evidence: Response gives π/6 and explains that the output of arcsin must lie in [−π/2, π/2], which excludes 5π/6.
criteria.fix: Check that the final angle lies in the restricted domain of sine, [−π/2, π/2]; if not, find the angle there with that sine.

criteria.text: The domain of arctan x is all real numbers, and its range is −π/2 < y < π/2.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the domain as all real numbers and the range as the open interval (−π/2, π/2).
criteria.fix: Swap inputs and outputs: the range of arctan is the restricted domain of tangent, (−π/2, π/2), with endpoints excluded.

criteria.text: Explains that the inputs of an inverse function are the outputs of the original function: on (−π/2, π/2) tangent takes every real value, while sine takes only values from −1 to 1, so arcsin x needs −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.
criteria.evidence: Response connects the domain of each inverse function to the range of the corresponding restricted function (tangent outputs all reals; sine outputs only [−1, 1]).
criteria.fix: The domain of an inverse function is the range of the original; compare the output ranges of restricted tangent and sine.
